Impacts of EU research and innovation projects: Innovations developed as part of the Genk nature-based solution mainstreaming process have relevance to cities globally. In particular, they have direct relevance to the plethora of small/medium sized cities across the EU. Recognising some of the advantages and challenges of public administration on this scale, the Stiemervallei exemplar, and its spin-off innovations, represent excellent templates for maximising the value of limited public authority resources through a community-focused, and engaged, co-creation approach to regenerating a neglected community and city asset. Further information: Genk is situated 80 km from the city of Brussels on the border with the Netherlands. Through the Albert Canal, the city is connected to Antwerp and Liège, which was pivotal in the development of local industries. Until 1988, the coal industry was a very important driver for the city's economy. Of the city’s 66,000 population, 54% are of foreign origin from about 107 different nationalities, mostly Italians, Turkish, and Dutch, much of this diversity derives from the legacy of this industry. Like many cities, Genk faces multifaceted challenges, ranging from securing a sustainable economic future, to building resilience in the face of climate change. This includes needs to: Find solutions to increasingly frequent episodes of flooding and stormwater overflow. Create new business models that create local jobs. Increase the attractiveness and quality of the landscape and local ecosystems to create a desirable location to live and visit. The Stiemervallei represents an opportunity to deliver a nature-based solution for Genk to support its ambition to increase its attractiveness as a place to live and work, that is connected with nature and the local environment: The Stiemer is a forgotten stream that flows through Genk for about 8 km and is under severe pressure. It originates in Waterschei, from there runs diagonally through the city, connects to the ponds of De Maten and flows into Diepenbeek into the Demer. On a regional scale, the Stiemervallei is part of De Wijers, a unique wetland area of around 700 ha around the cities of Hasselt and Genk. Parts of the valley have been completely enclosed by buildings over the last sixty years, with other parts of the area hidden and forgotten. The stream itself was straightened and thus largely lost contact with its valley area. Nevertheless, in some places the valley still contains valuable natural elements and large parts are protected as a recognized nature reserve. Tackling water issues in the valley is crucial. The sewage system of all surrounding neighbourhoods feeds into collectors on both sides of the Stiemer.

title: Wallasea Island Wild Coast Project – A landmark conservation and engineering scheme | BIONEXT — section 1 of 4
parent_title: Wallasea Island Wild Coast Project – A landmark conservation and engineering scheme | BIONEXT
text: Wallasea Island Wild Coast Project – A landmark conservation and engineering scheme | BIONEXT Case study Wallasea Island Wild Coast Project – A landmark conservation and engineering scheme Image: Area characterisation: Within the Wallasea Project, land-raising and landscape engineering was innovatively approached by creating a novel public private partnership. Materials from the Crossrail tunneling project were transported to a low-lying coastal area at high risk of flooding, in order to raise the land. Objective: Extensive public engagement and consultation processes were carried out during the planning and incep-tion phases (building block 1) in order to address stakeholder concerns and generate support for the project. Start/end date: 1 January 2015 Financing: Private investment Potential impacts/benefits: The project safeguards communities and local wildlife from rising sea levels, including providing a habitat for the arrival of species from further south in Europe, such as Black-winged Stilt, which are expected to colonise southern England as the climate continues to change. It also created education and recreation opportunities for the surrounding community and serves as a tourist destination more broadly. The project was designed on the basis of an estimated 1m of sea level rise over the next 100 years, and is intended to be ‘climate proof.’ It is anticipated that the project will be robust, whether sea level rise is very rapid or rather slow. If sea levels rise rapidly, there will be a lot of coastal erosion and a lot of sediment in the system. Consultation events, discussions with interested parties and the instigation of a Local Liaison Group combined with education about the potential impacts of climate change and the risks of sea level rise have ensured widespread support for the project. Actions: The project established a precedent for using largely waste material generated by a major infrastructure project to meet biodiversity conservation and climate change adaptation aims elsewhere. Financing stemmed from both the private company Crossrail as well as from the Environment Agency, with all parties profiting due to the economic as well as environmental benefits set off by recycling the leftover materials. With Crossrail on board as a delivery partner, the project represents a partnership between Europe's largest civil engineering project and Europe's largest intertidal habitat creation project. Enabling factors Instead of paying to remove waste materials from tunnel construction, Crossrail opted to transport them to Wallasea Island. An unloading facility enabled the materials to be shipped and then distributed across the island to build the habitats. Crossrail covered most costs (e.g. land purchase and some staff costs), with the Environment Agency (RA) funding the rest. The EA `bought` into the project to deliver replacement habitats for areas impacted/lost within the local Natura 200 network.

Crossrail covered most costs (e.g. land purchase and some staff costs), with the Environment Agency (RA) funding the rest. The EA `bought` into the project to deliver replacement habitats for areas impacted/lost within the local Natura 200 network. The project answers to a technical advisory panel (TAP), which meets every six months. This is comprised of a wide range of relevant stakeholders, both directly and indirectly affected by the project. Relevant parties include: Natural England, the Environment Agency (four or five individuals representing each of various arms of the EA that are involved – the environmental permitting team, the land drainage consent team, and the seawall maintenance team), the Crouch Harbour Authority, the local planning authority, Defra, the Essex County Council authorities, the Rochford District Council’s head of planning, Crossrail representatives, the RSPB, individuals from the Centre for Environment, Fisheries, and Aquacultural Sciences (local fisheries advisors), and the Wallasea Island landowner (Wallasea Farms Inc). This panel was a critical source of expertise and analysis during early implementation, and continues to provide advice as the project is completed on potential barriers and means to overcome these. Enabling factors The existence of the TAP provided an underlying sense of confidence in the planning and implementation process, in order to deal with foreseen barriers. The panel supported extensive modelling, environmental impact assessments, and redesign of solutions. In particular, the design of three smaller managed realignments rather than one large one helped to overcome the problem of scale which was faced in the project. For Wallasea Island, the public was largely content with creating new habitat in place of low-productivity agricultural land, but objected to the loss of farmland and potential impacts on recreation sailing, oyster fisheries and estuary processes. Another issue was the sense that past generations had worked hard to reclaim these areas from the sea and that this should not be reversed. However, according to the Environment Agency’s flood risk maps, the project estimated that hundreds of years of such reclamations had resulted in thousands of hectares along the Essex coastline that should be inundated. Extensive public engagement and consultation processes were thus carried out during the planning and inception phases of this project to gain understanding and support. Public engagement took place in the form of consultation events, talks to interest groups, site visits for key stakeholders, new updates for involved stakeholders, the establishment of a Local Liaison Group and the appointment of a public engagement manager in April 2010.

title: Wallasea Island Wild Coast Project – A landmark conservation and engineering scheme | BIONEXT — section 3 of 4
parent_title: Wallasea Island Wild Coast Project – A landmark conservation and engineering scheme | BIONEXT
text: nning and inception phases of this project to gain understanding and support. Public engagement took place in the form of consultation events, talks to interest groups, site visits for key stakeholders, new updates for involved stakeholders, the establishment of a Local Liaison Group and the appointment of a public engagement manager in April 2010. Enabling factors Public engagement during the design phase was particularly important to gain public support, as the project entailed destroying productive agricultural land in favor of habitat creation. Targeted outreach and dissemination activities helped to raise awareness and understanding of potential damaging climate change related impacts (i.e. flooding) and the range of benefits which would be offered by the project (e.g. recreational opportunities, flood risk management, increased amenity values etc). Lessons learnt: While sufficient buy-in was obtained by RSPB to buy the land, funds had not initially been collected to carry out the project itself. At this point, Crossrail came forward with an offer of materials and funding that permitted the project to move forward with more confidence. The main lesson learned is thus to think ‘outside the box’ and consider novel (public-private) partnerships to tap into previously unconsidered resources, and making sure to highlight the range of benefits which will be delivered to each party as a result of the project. Furthermore, a strong relationship with the landowner was particularly important in the early design phases of the project, as this led to the ability of RSPB to take out a two-year purchase option. This meant that, for a two-year period, RSPB could purchase the majority of the island if they decided to, and the price would be fixed at the beginning of this period, thereby creating some certainty surrounding the initial costs of the project. In a project with such a high chance of technical barriers as in Wallasea Island, a technical advisory panel can be instrumental in a smooth and successful planning and implementation process. The function is essentially to support the identification of both technical and regulatory barriers and development of means to overcome these prior to project implementation. Early and comprehensive consultation are key to ensuring successful implementation and generating public support for many EbA projects, the extent of which depends on the sensitivity of the location and/or proximity of residential areas and socio-economic resources. In the case of Wallasea, early and frequent public consultations required significant education about potential climate change impacts and the risks of sea level rise in order to gain acceptance for the planned project activities. s: Chris Tyas RSPB Wallasea Island Project Manager This habitat restoration project aimed to offset coastal habitat loss while reducing flood risk and transforming an area from a carbon source to sink.

text: Waterevolution: an integrated approach to maritime cluster sustainability | BIONEXT Case study Waterevolution: an integrated approach to maritime cluster sustainability Image: Area characterisation: The Waterevolution solution represents a practical example that nature conservation and human progress are not mutually exclusive. It is a credible and accessible technological model, based on Computational Sustainability, that can promote general welfare in ways that support and even enhance our planet’s natural assets. The model links together industry-focused and scientific-based computational sustainability with marine conservation and is able to provide a win-win situation. It allows a substantial reduction of the environmental and energy footprint of the industry through an optimisation of the production process that is able to generate significant cost savings, a part of which is reinvested into marine conservation programs In the pilot project the savings were reinvested into various marine conservation projects including the strategic planning of the IUCN Joint SSC-WCPA Marine Mammal Protected Areas Task Force (started in February 2015) to develop Important Marine Mammal Areas (IMMAs). Thanks to this financial support, the Criteria for IMMA identification (currently undergoing public scrutiny) were drafted and broad consensus and full support on IMMAs were gained within the relevant IUCN Commissions and Sub-Committees. The funding allowed participation of the two main researchers as experts to EBSA Workshops organised by the Secretariat of the Convention on Biological Diversity (Sri Lanka and Dubai), and the provision of information on IMMA development to potential institutional partners such as the French Marine Protected Areas Agency, Pew Charitable Trusts, UNEP’s World Conservation Monitoring Centre, Secretariat of the Convention on Migratory Species, and Secretariat of the Pacific Regional Environment Programme, particularly in view of a possible joint organisation of the South Pacific region Year of the Whale 2016. The Waterevolution model has the potential to not only drive changes into the super yacht business, where the pilot project was implemented, but also within the entire yachting sector and the maritime cluster as a whole while generating structural funding opportunities for marine conservation initiatives worldwide. Objective: Waterevolution is a comprehensive, evidence-based model that involves a sustainable corporate management approach to reduce environmental footprint, which generates structural funding to support marine science and conservation projects and facilitates industry commitment to ocean responsibility.

text: On your roofs, get set, green! – Hamburgs green roof strategy implement NbS at different level | BIONEXT Case study On your roofs, get set, green! – Hamburgs green roof strategy implement NbS at different level Image: Objective: Hamburg was the first major German city to launch a comprehensive Green Roof Strategy. Its goal is to green at least 70 per cent of both new buildings and suitable flat or gently pitched roofs that are being renovated. The Ministry for Environment, Climate, Energy, and Agriculture supports the project with three million euros until the end of 2024. In 2014 the goal was set to create 100 hectare (ha) green roofs in Hamburg within one decade. Starting from 80 ha we are on track having in 2020 about 168 ha green roofs in Hamburg.* Nevertheless, there are still many roofs in Hamburg that can offer microhabitat for insects (increase biodiversity), reduce the stormwater runoff (flood management), improve the microclimate (urban heat island) and provide many other services for the growing population of Hamburg. *The numbers dont represent entire Hamburg but include about 70 % of Hamburgs population. Start/end date: 4 December 2020 Images Financing: The financing of the strategy and the subsides are provided by the city. The funding can cover up to 40 % of the installation costs for a green roof and maximum 100 000 €. To derive the support, the roof must be larger than 20 squaremeters, the soil layer must be thicker than 12 cm and the green roof must be a voluntary descistion of the house owner. Beside the general funding, a premium funding is profided for the following reasons: location in the city center, usage of roof top for e.g. recreational purposes, improvement of statik of exisiting buildings, combination with energy production, runoff reduction. More detailed information about the conditions for public funding can be derived on our website and on the website of the investment and development bank . Actions: The green roof strategy has four main action points: promotion, dialogue, stipulation and scientific support . Promotion of green roofs is done via multiple media by developing visualisations that show a potential green roof top of Hamburg. But also in practice the city itself works as leading example by realising green roofs on novel city own buildings whenever possible. The promotion also includes the funding program for green roofs and facades. The program started in 2014 running for 10 years and provides about 5 million euro. Detailed information how the funding works and can be derived is provided on the website www.hamburg.de/gruendach and will be explained in more detail in the financing section. Dialog is the second action point to motivate private house owners to invest into a green roof too. Therefore all the advantages of the green roof or facade are described in print and digital publications that are frequently used to explain the structure and functions of a green roof.

Therefore all the advantages of the green roof or facade are described in print and digital publications that are frequently used to explain the structure and functions of a green roof. The third action point is stipulation via the landuse plan, landscape plan or the climate plan of Hamburg. All this tools are used to define green roofs as obligatory for further urban development. Scientific support is the fourth action point that generates knowledge for the before mentioned points. In practice, several universities are conducting research on green roofs of Hamburg regarding different services (currently micro climate, water retention, biodiverstiy are monitored). Lessons learnt: Integration of the green roof strategy into overarching stategies (e.g. Hamburgs climate plan) gave the strategy a wide and stable fundament by including strategic goals from other strategies into the green roof strategy. Communication and dialogue/involvement is key to changing practices and creating a demand for green roofs among residents and companies. This requires a dedicated full-time communication officer and structured co-creation processes. Co-creation was formalised in a stakeholder group consisting of housing estate companies, constructors, landscape architects and urban planners. The group took part in dialogues with other cities, co-designed the incentive programme and continue to meet for evaluation of the Green Roof Strategy bi-annually. The combination of regulation, dialogue, financial incentives and science advice and evaluation is key to successful urban NbS implementation. The green roof financial support programme is in combination with public relations and dialogue the most important in creating awareness. The main driving force for expanding green roofs in Hamburg is the demand for greening buildings with vegetation. There is still a strong need to gather evidence of effectiveness, e.g. for water retention and temperature reduction. The lack of evidence means that the impact of green roofs is currently not recognised in the DIN norms for retaining and slow down run-off on buildings. title: Communicating the Results | BIONEXT — section 1 of 2
text: Communicating the Results | BIONEXT Image: Communicating the Results In this phase, the outcomes of the decision analysis are presented to stakeholders in a clear, transparent, and understandable way. Objectives of the phase Present the results in an understandable format (e.g. rankings, trade-offs and sensitivities). Explain the reasoning, assumptions, and applied methods behind the results. Support informed decision-making and stakeholder acceptance. Ensure transparency and credibility of the decision process. Achieve a shared understanding of the results among stakeholders. Modes of communication The communication may take different forms depending on the audience and context: Technical reports (detailed and method-focused). Summaries for decision-makers (concise and action-oriented). Visual presentations (charts, dashboards, interactive tools). Participatory workshops or discussions (most interactive). Effective communication requires tailoring the level of detail and technicality to the audience. Outcome of the phase: A clear and transparent presentation of the decision analysis results to support final decision-making and implementation. Follow up Questions for the AI Ask the following questions to get more information from the AI: What are the key principles of effective communication of the decision analysis results? How can complex decision analysis results be explained to non-experts? What types of visualisations are best suited for presenting results? See also visualisations in Comparing Alternatives and Sensitivity Analysis . How can conflicting stakeholder perspectives be presented? This is especially important in terms of ensuring stakeholder acceptance, transparency and credibility of the decision process Image: Image: Ask BIONEXT Explore BIONEXT knowledge through a conversational AI assistant Ask a question Benefits and Risks of Using AI Image: Benefits (++) - Translating technical results into accessible language for different audiences. - Automatically generating summaries and reports. - Creating visualisations (charts, dashboards, comparison figures). - Tailoring communication to different stakeholder groups. - Highlighting key insights, trade-offs and uncertainties. - Supporting interactive exploration of results (e.g. Q&A formats). Benefit Scoring: ++ Medium More on Benefits Image: Risks (!!) - Oversimplification or misrepresentation of complex results leading to generation of misleading or biased narratives. - Loss of methodological transparency. - Inconsistent interpretation of results across different outputs. - All the above can lead to reduced trust of stakeholders if communication is not aligned with actual analysis Risk Scoring: !! Medium More on Risks Questions to Better Understand the Benefits and Risks of AI Questions to make use of the benefits Prerequisite for each of these questions is that the results of the analysis as well as sensitivity analysis are available.

These kinds of questions can easily lead AI to add arguments that may not be valid. title: Comparing the Alternatives | BIONEXT — section 1 of 2
text: Comparing the Alternatives | BIONEXT Image: Comparing the Alternatives In this phase the performance of the different alternatives is systematically evaluated and compared across the selected criteria. Objectives of the phase Assess and compare how well each alternative performs with respect to each criterion. Compare the overall scores of the alternatives obtained by aggregating the performance information of the alternatives with respect to criteria and stakeholder preferences. Identify trade-offs between alternatives and possible dominance relationships. Elements of comparison Simple scoring and ranking of the alternative. Compare the results of aggregated multicriteria models (e.g. weighted sums, value functions). Pairwise comparisons of alternatives. Dominance or outranking analysis The alternatives are typically compared together with stakeholders so that the facilitator presents the results and explains the reasoning behind them to increase understanding of the strengths and weaknesses of the alternatives and of the trade-offs to be made when selecting the alternatives. The results are typically visualised, for example, with stacked bar graphs or radar charts to illustrate the contributions of different criteria to the results Outcome of the phase: A structured comparison of alternatives (e.g. overall scores or ranking of the alternatives, or dominance relations) and identification of the most preferred alternative(s) from different viewpoints. Follow up Questions for the AI Ask the following questions to get more information from the AI: What is the purpose and key characteristics of the comparison phase in decision analysis? How does the comparison of the alternatives differ between different methods (e.g. ranking, scoring, and outranking methods)? There are fundamental differences between the methods in terms of how the results are presented. Can you describe and illustrate typical visualisation techniques for comparing the alternatives? Image: Image: Ask BIONEXT Explore BIONEXT knowledge through a conversational AI assistant Ask a question Benefits and Risks of Using AI Image: Benefits (++) - Identifying patterns, dominance relations, and trade-offs between alternatives. - Automating ranking or classification of alternatives. - Generating intuitive visualisations (e.g. radar charts, heatmaps, rankings). - Explaining complex comparison results in understandable terms. Benefit Scoring: ++ Medium More on Benefits Image: Risks (!!) - Lack of transparency in how the aggregate values used to compare alternatives are derived. - Use of inappropriate or implicit aggregation logic and oversimplification of complex trade-offs. - Misinterpretation of the measurement scales of input preference data.

title: Decision Analysis: The Basics | BIONEXT — section 1 of 3
text: Decision Analysis: The Basics | BIONEXT Image: Decision Analysis: The Basics Decision analysis is a systematic and analytical approach that supports informed decision-making in problems involving multiple alternatives and criteria. It provides a transparent means of combining data about the impacts of the alternatives on different criteria and stakeholders’ preferences regarding the criteria. The aim is to support well-informed decisions about the most appropriate practice or policy-oriented actions. Elements of decision analysis problems Decision maker(s) (people making the decision). Stakeholders (people who are affected by the decision) Experts (people knowledgeable about the issues related to the problem and facilitators providing support for the process). Objectives (things that the people involved want to achieve). Alternatives (available options when trying to reach the objectives). Criteria (dimensions for measuring how well the objectives are met). Impacts (consequences of alternatives in terms of different criteria). Values (underlying preferences and priorities that shape the decision). Uncertainties (external factors affecting the outcomes). To analyse these problems, decision analysis provides: Decision rules (means of structuring these elements to support transparent, reasoned, and defensible decision-making). Decision process (a structured pathway to reach the decision). Support for making trade-offs between the criteria (various methods to elicit the trade-offs). Support for participation (means of involving stakeholders and decision-makers). Decision analysis is most useful in complex decision problems, such as large environmental problems, where multiple and diverse dimensions are otherwise very difficult to deal with. Note: Decision analysis, used here in its broadest sense, as an umbrella term for a range of systematic and analytical approaches that support rational decision-making. Decision analysis approaches are often divided into two broad categories: Approaches based on expected utility theory, which support decision-making under uncertainty through the explicit use of probabilities. In some fields, the term decision analysis is used specifically to refer to these approaches rather than to decision analysis as a whole, which can cause confusion. Multi-criteria decision analysis (MCDA)-based approaches focusing on trade-offs between multiple objectives. In these approaches, uncertainties are typically not explicitly integrated into the model as probabilities, but they are analysed afterwards, for example, with sensitivity analyses. Outcome of the phase: An understanding of the basic principles and possibilities of applying decision analysis to support environmental decision-making.

title: Decision Analysis in Environmental Decision Making | BIONEXT

text: Decision Analysis in Environmental Decision Making | BIONEXT Image: About Ask BIONEXT Case Studies Decision Analysis Resources Decision Analysis in Environmental Decision Making AIDA: AI-assisted Decision Analysis Like the protagonists of Verdi's Aida, decision-makers often face difficult choices involving competing objectives, stakeholder interests, uncertainties, and values. Decision analysis helps make these tensions explicit, supports the systematic exploration of alternatives, and enhances transparency in decision-making. The AIDA tool (AI-assisted Decision Analysis) provides guidance on how generative AI can be used responsibly and effectively throughout the decision-analysis process. It does not make decisions for people; it helps people in using AI to make better-informed decisions for themselves. The AIDA module introduces the fundamentals of the decision-analysis process and provides guidance on how to use generative AI responsibly and transparently to support decision analysis, particularly in environmental decision-making. It also provides example prompts that can be used to obtain meaningful responses from generative AI. Note: On this page, the term AI refers to generative AI unless otherwise stated. Generative AI: Generative AI is a subset of AI capable of generating text, images, video or other forms of output by using probabilistic models trained across one or more domains. These models learn from large amounts of specially-curated training data to discern and replicate complex patterns and structures. The output generated by these models mimics the characteristics learned from that training data, enabling many novel applications – ranging from personalised content generation, to advanced analysis and evaluation, and aiding creative processes.[ definition from GOV.UK ] Image: What is Decision Analysis? title: Decision Analysis: Objectives | BIONEXT — section 1 of 2
text: Decision Analysis: Objectives | BIONEXT Image: Decision Analysis: Objectives Fundamental objectives of decision analysis include: Supporting rational choices Not finding “the right answer” but supporting better-informed decision-making- its objectives are therefore procedural as much as outcome-oriented. To acknowledge rather than eliminate uncertainty and ambiguity – it helps decision-makers to address them through a well-informed, well-structured and transparent process Make values, trade-offs, and assumptions explicit Separating facts (what may happen) from values (what is preferred). Making trade-offs between competing objectives explicit. This transparency is often more important than the final ranking or recommendation Improve quality of decisions Emphasis on decision quality, not outcome quality. A “good decision” is one that uses the best available information, reflects the decision-maker’s values consistently and follows a defensible reasoning process– even if the outcome later turns out badly. Enable learning, deliberation, and insight Promoting structured thinking. Improving communication among analysts, experts and stakeholders. Supporting learning about what drives outcomes and where disagreements originate. In participatory decision analysis, this learning objective is often as important as choice Enhance accountability and justifiability Justification of decisions to others. Traceability of reasoning. Defensibility against critique. Especially important in public and environmental decisions. Key Principles of Decision Analysis Focus on decision. Explicit structuring of the decision problem. Separation of facts and values. Explicit treatment of uncertainty. Internal consistency (normative coherence). Value-Focused Thinking (“What do we care about?” before “What should we choose?”). Conditional and context-dependent recommendations (never claims universal optimality). Human accountability and learning through exploration and (supports decisions rather than making them). Image: Outcome of the phase: Understanding of the reasoning behind applying decision analysis. Follow up Questions for the AI Ask the following questions to gather more information from the AI: Can you elaborate the fundamental objectives and the key principles of decision analysis? Can you elaborate approaches for achieving these fundamental objectives and the key principles of decision analysis? Can you give examples of how these objectives can be observed in typical applications of decision analysis in environmental decision-making problems? Can you give examples of how [some specific objective or principle] can be observed in typical applications of decision analysis in environmental decision-making problems? title: Decision/Policy Recommendations | BIONEXT — section 1 of 2
text: Decision/Policy Recommendations | BIONEXT Image: Decision/Policy Recommendations In this phase the results of the decision analysis are translated into concrete, actionable recommendations to support implementation. Objectives of the phase Formulate clear recommendations based on the results. Link the analytical outcomes to practical decisions and policy actions. Consider feasibility, constraints and real-world implications. Support decision-makers in selecting and implementing the preferred alternative(s) Tasks involved in the phase This phase is typically led by the facilitator or decision analyst and builds directly on the results that have been communicated and the feedback provided by stakeholders. The phase involves the following tasks: Identifying the recommended alternative(s) or policy options. Outlining implementation steps and required resources for possible options. Considering institutional, legal and practical constraints. Integrating stakeholder perspectives and acceptance considerations. The recommendations may include several options, recognising that different stakeholders or perspectives may favour different alternatives. The aim is not to identify a single "best" option, but rather to support decision-makers and policy-makers by providing informed recommendations and explaining the implications of the available alternatives. Outcome of the phase: Clear and justified decision or policy recommendation(s) for the decision makers and practical guidance for implementation. Follow up Questions for the AI Ask the following questions to get more information from AI: What are the key principles for translating analysis results into operational action recommendations? What additional factors beyond the results of decision analysis model should be considered in decision-making? How should uncertainty and sensitivity results influence recommendations? What are good practices for presenting actionable policy advice? Image: Image: Ask BIONEXT Explore BIONEXT knowledge through a conversational AI assistant Ask a question Benefits and Risks of Using AI Image: Benefits (++) - Supporting the formulation of structured and evidence-based recommendations. - Translating analytical results into actionable steps. - Identifying implementation considerations (e.g. risks, constraints, stakeholders). - Generating alternative policy options or scenarios. - Structuring justification and argumentation for the recommendations Benefit Scoring: ++ Medium More on Benefits Image: Risks (!!) - Providing normative or prescriptive recommendations without understanding full context. - Ignoring important real-world constraints (political, institutional, legal). - Overstepping the role of decision-makers by suggesting final decisions leading to loss of accountability and ownership in decision-making. - False sense of objectivity in recommendations derived from AI. - Misalignment between AI-generated recommendations and stakeholder values.

title: Designing the Application Process of Decision Analysis | BIONEXT — section 1 of 2
parent_title: Designing the Application Process of Decision Analysis | BIONEXT
text: Designing the Application Process of Decision Analysis | BIONEXT Image: Designing the Application Process of Decision Analysis The purpose of this phase is to design a practical process for carrying out the decision analysis. While the previous phases focus on understanding the decision problem and selecting an appropriate decision-analytical approach , this phase focuses on how the process will be organised and implemented in practice. Key questions to consider: Including but not limited to: Which phases of the decision analysis process will be carried out? Which stakeholders should participate in each phase of the process? What information needs to be collected and when? What interaction methods will be used (e.g. workshops, interviews, surveys, expert panels)? What resources, competencies, and tools are needed? What is the schedule of the process? How will uncertainties, stakeholder preferences, and communication be handled? How will transparency, traceability, and quality assurance be ensured? Competing objectives to balance Analytical rigor Intensity of stakeholder participation Transparency Availability of resources Timeliness Practical feasibility There is no universally optimal process design. The most appropriate design depends on the characteristics of the decision problem, stakeholders, available resources, decision context, and intended use of the results. Outcome of the phase: A documented plan for conducting the decision-analysis process, including the phases of the process, stakeholder involvement strategy and their roles, applied interaction methods, required data and expertise and schedule and resource allocation and quality assurance and communication procedures. Follow up Questions for the AI Ask the following questions to get more information from the AI: Can you describe typical ways of organising a decision-analysis process? What factors should be considered when designing a participatory decision-analysis process? What are the advantages and disadvantages of different stakeholder interaction approaches? How can analytical rigor and stakeholder participation be balanced in decision-analysis projects? What are the key resource requirements in typical decision-analysis applications? How can transparency and traceability be ensured throughout the process? Benefit Scoring: ++ Medium More on Benefits Image: Risks (!!) - Oversimplification of complex organisational and social processes.

title: Eliciting Stakeholder Preferences | BIONEXT — section 1 of 3
text: Eliciting Stakeholder Preferences | BIONEXT Image: Eliciting Stakeholder Preferences Preference elicitation is a phase where the stakeholders’ values, priorities, and trade-offs are formally identified and structured so they can be incorporated into a decision model. Objectives of the phase Identify the importance of different criteria relative to others in terms of the possible impacts in this decision context and to. Capture trade-offs between criteria for different stakeholders. The practical implementation of the weight elicitation process depends greatly on the decision analysis approach that has been selected in the selection of the decision analysis phase. In practice, there are different ways to interact with stakeholders to elicit their preferences. How to find stakeholder preferences Expert-based analysis (least interactive). Questionnaires/survey-based elicitation. Facilitated group workshops. Structured individual interviews (most interactive). The more interactive the approach is, the more committed participants typically are to the process, but the more resource-intensive the process becomes. Outcome of the phase: Data indicating the relative importance of the criteria for different stakeholder groups (e.g. in the form of weights). Follow up Questions for the AI Ask the following questions to get more information from the AI: What is the purpose and key characteristics of the preference elicitation phase in decision analysisWhat is the interpretation of the criteria weights in decision analysis and how does the context of the problem affect them? The core of weight elicitation in decision analysis is to understand that the weights should reflect the importance of the criteria and the scales of their impacts in the current context, but not the general importance of the criteria. Why is "Which is more important, economy or environment?" a bad question in decision analysis? One cannot answer this question without knowing the scales of the impacts. This is one of the most critical issues to be understood when planning preference elicitation in decision analysis. What are the pros and cons of approaches to interact with the stakeholders in preference elicitation in decision analysis and for what types of problems the approaches are best suited to? The aim is to find an approach that best suits the needs of the problem. What issues should be considered when selecting the way to interact with the stakeholders to elicit their preferences with different decision analysis approaches [or with the approach selected here] What kind of trade-offs there typically are in environmental decision making problems and can you give examples of those? There are differences in how different interaction approaches are suitable for use with different decision analysis approaches.

title: Framing of the Problem | BIONEXT — section 1 of 2
text: Framing of the Problem | BIONEXT Image: Framing of the Problem Framing of the problem defines the decision context and the dimensions of the analysis. The aim is that after this phase the problem is defined clearly and meaningfully and that all stakeholders interpret the problem similarly. Issues to consider framing the problem What situation triggered the need for a decision? Who is the decision maker and stakeholders, and in what issues can the decision maker have an impact? What is the fundamental goal of the problem that you are trying to achieve? What are the scope and boundaries of the decision (Too narrow scope may miss important factors, but too broad can become unmanageable)? What is included (and what is not)? What are the different dimensions from which we should analyse the problem (time frame, spatial extent, included viewpoints of the stakeholders, level of governance, etc.)? Can relaxing the system boundaries give some new innovative viewpoints to the framing The framing of the problem is often carried out iteratively with the phases of identifying objectives/criteria , alternatives and uncertainties . For example, the framing typically has an impact on what kinds of alternatives it is reasonable to consider, whereas the availability of alternatives has an impact on how the problem should be framed. Innovative framing of the problem often requires out-of-the-box thinking and relaxing the system boundaries. For example, a problem of a forest owner of finding an optimal strategy for a certain forest stand may in a broader picture appear to be part of a larger system, when more efficient solutions could be found through designing an optimal regional forest management strategy for the whole area. Outcome of the phase: Description of the problem including the boundaries of the decision making situation and the dimensions of the problem to be solved Follow up Questions for the AI Ask the following questions to get more information from the AI: Could you please describe the fundamentals of framing the problem in decision analysis? What issues should be considered when framing the problem? What are the typical dimensions to be considered when framing the problem in environmental decision making and can you give examples of these? title: Identifying and Generating Alternatives | BIONEXT — section 1 of 2
text: Identifying and Generating Alternatives | BIONEXT Image: Identifying and Generating Alternatives Alternatives represent different ways to achieve the objectives, and they may include, for example, different policies (e.g. emission reduction strategies), projects (e.g. location options for a wind farm) or actions (e.g. conservation measures). The aim of this phase is to create a set of feasible and meaningful options to compare. This phase should not be limited to existing options. Brainstorming, expert input and other structured approaches can help stimulate creativity and encourage the exploration of new alternatives. For example, value-focused thinking begins by identifying objectives and then asking questions such as, "How can these objectives be achieved?" This helps generate alternatives that are designed to fulfil the stated objectives, rather than simply selecting from an existing set of options. Characteristics of a good alternative include feasibility (incl. technical, legal and practical), relevancy to the objectives, meaningfulness and being implementable. A set of good alternatives should be internally consistent and cover a sufficient range of options (including diverse approaches, viewpoints and possibly a status quo) so that the alternatives are sufficiently distinct from one another Outcome of the phase: A set of alternatives to be analysed for the problem. Follow up Questions for the AI Ask the following questions to get more information from the AI: Can you describe the characteristics of a good alternative and also a good set of alternatives in decision analysis? Can you give examples of the sets of good alternatives in environmental cases? What methods are available for increasing creativity and exploration in the development of the alternatives? Image: Image: Ask BIONEXT Explore BIONEXT knowledge through a conversational AI assistant Ask a question Benefits and Risks of Using AI Image: Benefits (+) - Support for carrying out creative and explorative alternative generation approaches, including value-focused thinking. - Getting suggestions of various alternatives that are considered in similar cases Benefit Scoring: + Low Benefit More on Benefits Image: Risks (!!) - Limited creativity and bias toward familiar or dominant solutions. - Generation of alternatives is the phase that truly requires creativity, but AI generates alternatives based on existing data and patterns, rather than through genuine creativity. - Lack of contextual understanding about the local situation leading to a poor set of alternatives. - Inadequate understanding of local ecological conditions and cultural or institutional factors may lead to alternatives that are generic, impractical, or inappropriate for the specific case. - Narrowing rather than expanding the solution space. - If used improperly, AI can focus attention on a limited set of plausible options and discourage exploration beyond those suggestions.

title: Identifying and Structuring of Objectives/Criteria | BIONEXT — section 1 of 2
parent_title: Identifying and Structuring of Objectives/Criteria | BIONEXT
text: Identifying and Structuring of Objectives/Criteria | BIONEXT Image: Identifying and Structuring of Objectives/Criteria The aim of this phase is to define what the decision aims to achieve and how success will be measured by identifying relevant objectives and structuring them into clear, usable evaluation criteria. Definitions Objectives Objectives reflect the values and preferences of stakeholders and may encompass multiple dimensions, including environmental, economic, social, and technical considerations. Criteria Criteria translate broad objectives into measurable indicators that can be used to evaluate how well the alternatives achieve those objectives. Characteristics of a good criterion include, for example, relevance, non-redundancy, measurability, understandability, independence, sensitivity to differences and feasibility of assessment. The objectives/criteria can be structured hierarchically as a value tree, with main objectives at the top, sub-objectives beneath them, and on the lowest level criteria against which the alternatives are measured (e.g. indicators). The set of objectives/criteria should comprehensively cover all the issues that are relevant to the decision, but on the other hand also be concise enough to be operational. There is no general answer for the level of detail, but it depends on the aims of the analysis. Value-focused thinking can be used to enhance identification of the objectives. With questions like “What do we want to achieve, and why?” one can get deeper into the fundamental (main) objectives behind the problem. With questions like “What are the means of achieving these objectives” we can identify sub-objectives and criteria. Outcome of the phase: A set of objectives relevant to stakeholders, with criteria under each objective for measuring how well the alternatives achieve it Follow up Questions for the AI Ask the following questions to get more information from the AI: Can you give examples of hierarchical objective and criteria structures in environmental decision problems? Can you elaborate the value-focused thinking process? What are the characteristics of good criteria [or a good set of criteria] in decision analysis? title: Identifying Key Stakeholders | BIONEXT — section 1 of 2
text: Identifying Key Stakeholders | BIONEXT Image: Identifying Key Stakeholders Identifying key stakeholders and including them in the process is extremely important in environmental decisions, as these decisions typically concern many different groups. What are stakeholders? Stakeholders are individuals, groups, or organisations that: Are directly or indirectly affected by the decision outcome. Have the power to influence the decision process. Have an interest (financial, social, environmental, political, etc) in the impacts of the decision Typical key stakeholder groups Identification of key stakeholders and including them in the process is extremely important in environmental decisions, as these decisions typically concern many different groups such as: Private sector/industry. Wider public and society, including local communities and residents. Environmental NGOs and advocacy groups. Government and regulatory authorities. Scientists and experts. Financial institutions and funders. In terms of inclusiveness, transparency and stakeholders’ commitment, it is very important to include all key stakeholder groups in the process. There are various systematic stakeholder analysis approaches for identifying stakeholders and their roles based, for example, on their power/influence, their interest in the decision and the level of impact on them. Outcome of the phase: A list of stakeholders to be included in the process. Follow up Questions for the AI Ask the following questions to get more information from the AI: Can you elaborate the roles of typical stakeholder groups related to environmental decisions? What approaches can be used to systematically identify and classify the stakeholders? What issues should be considered when categorising the stakeholders and deciding who to include in the process? What are the means to ensure that all the different viewpoints of the stakeholders would become included in the process? title: Identifying Uncertainties | BIONEXT — section 1 of 2
text: Identifying Uncertainties | BIONEXT Image: Identifying Uncertainties In this phase, sources of uncertainty relating to the decision problem, input data, model assumptions, and outcomes are systematically recognised and described. Objectives of this phase: Identify different types of uncertainties affecting the decision problem. Understand how uncertainty may influence the assessment and comparison of alternatives. Distinguish between reducible (epistemic) and irreducible (aleatory) uncertainties. Prepare for subsequent analysis (e.g. sensitivity analysis and risk assessment). Uncertainties may arise from: Limited or incomplete data. Measurement errors or variability. Model structure and methodological choices. Future developments and external conditions. Stakeholder judgments and preferences. Depending on the characteristics of the case, these uncertainties may be modelled explicitly by using dedicated methods for modelling uncertainties or implicitly in the sensitivity analysis . Explicit methods for modelling uncertainties include those relying on probabilities and expected utilities (e.g. multi-attribute utility theory) and those relying on imprecision ranges of parameter input (e.g. preference programming). Outcome of the phase: A structured list and classification of the key uncertainties affecting the decision problem (e.g. data-, model-, scenario- and preference-related uncertainties) and, when explicit methods are used, a model for analysing them. Follow up Questions for the AI Ask the following questions to get more information from the AI: Can you elaborate what types of uncertainties are relevant in decision analysis and what are the sources of different types of uncertainties? Can you elaborate the differences between the methods that model uncertainties by probabilities and expected utilities (e.g. multi-attribute utility theory) and the methods that model imprecision by ranges of parameter inputs? What methods can be used to deal with uncertainty in later phases of the process? Image: Image: Ask BIONEXT Explore BIONEXT knowledge through a conversational AI assistant ask a question Risks and Benefits of AI Image: Benefits (+) - Identifying potential sources of uncertainties based on available information. - Structuring and categorising uncertainties systematically. - Supporting documentation and explanation of uncertainty sources. - Suggesting methods for dealing with different types of uncertainties. Benefit Scoring: + Low More on Benefits Image: Risks (!!) - Overlooking context-specific uncertainties not present in training data. - Misinterpreting the nature or importance of uncertainties. - Creating a false sense of completeness in uncertainty identification. - Lack of transparency in how uncertainties are inferred - Ignoring stakeholder-specific perceptions of uncertainty.

title: Impact Assessment | BIONEXT — section 1 of 2
text: Impact Assessment | BIONEXT Image: Impact Assessment The goal of impact assessment is to understand what will happen if a decision is implemented and to quantify and characterise the effects of possible solutions across relevant criteria (e.g. environmental, economic, social). The impact assessment phase defines the consequences of implementing each alternative for each criterion by using suitable indicators for measuring the impact. Impact assessment methods There are various ways to assess impacts, including: Expert assessments. Results from field studies. Environmental models. Simulation models. Impacts are typically presented in the form of a two-dimensional matrix, with alternatives on one dimension and criteria on another, where the cells describe the consequence of each alternative for each criterion Outcome of the phase: A matrix describing the impacts of each alternative against each criterion or indicator. Follow up Questions for the AI Ask the following questions to get more information from the AI: Can you elaborate the different ways of assessing the impacts and in which kinds of cases they are suitable? What issues should be taken into account when deciding which method to use when assessing the impact? Image: Image: Ask BIONEXT Explore BIONEXT knowledge through a conversational AI assistant Ask a question Benefits and Risks of Using AI Image: Benefits (+) - Support for finding studies assessing the impacts of actions in these kinds of cases. - Support for verifying the scale and direction of the impacts. - Support for identifying means of measuring the impact. Benefit Scoring: + Low More on Benefits Image: Risks (!!) - Use of generic impact estimates without being able to take the current decision context into account. - Loss of transparency due to the use of methods that are not mathematically rigorous. - Loss of stakeholders’ commitment to the process due to AI not being able to assess the impacts correctly. - False feeling of objectivity when using AI to assess the impacts – impacts are typically context-dependent. Risk Scoring: !! Medium More on Risks Questions to understand the benefits and risks of AI Questions to make use of the benefits of AI I have this criterion/indicator: [name of the criterion/indicator]. Can you suggest different ways in which the impacts of the alternatives are typically measured in terms of this criterion? The impacts themselves are typically context dependent, but AI can give suggestions on how to measure them. I have this problem: [problem description including criteria and alternatives]. Can you give me examples of how earlier studies have assessed the impacts within a similar context? After getting the response, the decision analyst should carefully analyse whether the conditions of the earlier study are sufficiently similar to allow the results here. I have these alternatives and criteria in my problem: [description of criteria and alternatives].

title: Implementation of the Chosen Alternative | BIONEXT — section 1 of 2
parent_title: Implementation of the Chosen Alternative | BIONEXT
text: Implementation of the Chosen Alternative | BIONEXT Image: Implementation of the Chosen Alternative This is the phase in which the selected alternative or policy is put into practice. Objectives of the phase Execute the chosen decision in a real-world context. Translate plans and recommendations into concrete actions. What to expect in this phase This phase typically involves: Detailed planning of actions, timelines, and responsibilities. Coordination between different actors and organisations. Allocation of financial, human, and technical resources This is typically a phase carried out by the problem owner, but the stakeholders should be kept informed about the actions being taken. Even if this phase is an essential part of a decision analysis process, the topics discussed here are generally applicable to any implementation process of an alternative. Outcome of the phase: The chosen alternative is implemented in practice. Follow up Questions to ask the AI Ask the following questions to get more information from the AI. What are the key steps in implementing a decision or policy? What are common barriers to implementation and how can they be addressed? What are good practices for adaptive implementation? Image: Image: Ask BIONEXT Explore BIONEXT knowledge through a conversational AI assistant Ask a question Benefits and Risks of Using AI Image: Benefits (+) - Supporting planning of implementation steps and timelines. - Identifying potential risks, bottlenecks and resource gaps. - Assisting in coordination and task allocation. Benefit Scoring: + Low More on Benefits Image: Risks (!) - Over reliance on generic implementation advice without context-specific understanding. - Lack of accountability if AI-generated plans are followed without scrutiny. - False sense of control or predictability in complex implementation environments. - Potential misalignment between AI suggestions and stakeholder realities. Risk Scoring: ! Low More on Risks Questions to Better Understand the Benefits and Risks of AI Questions to make use of the benefits Prerequisite for each of these questions is that a decision has been approved on the alternative to be implemented. Can you propose mitigation measures for potential implementation barriers? title: Monitoring | BIONEXT — section 1 of 2
text: Monitoring | BIONEXT Image: Monitoring The monitoring phase is where the implementation of the chosen alternative is systematically followed and evaluated over time. Objectives of the phase Track whether the implementation is progressing as planned. Measure actual outcomes against expected impacts. Detect deviations, emerging issues and unintended consequences. Provide feedback for corrective actions and future decision-making What to expect in this phase This phase typically involves: Defining indicators and metrics for tracking performance. Collecting and analysing data on implementation and outcomes. Comparing observed results with expected results from the analysis. Continuously reporting progress to relevant stakeholders. Identifying the need for adjustments or corrective measures. In practice, monitoring can be automated, for example, with technical monitoring systems or it can be carried out through participatory assessment involving experts and/or stakeholders. In the latter case, the approaches vary from data-driven reporting systems to interactive participatory monitoring for example, through interviews Regular and systematic information on implementation progress and evidence on achieved impacts and performance. Follow up Questions for the AI Ask the following questions to get more information from the AI. What are the key principles of effective monitoring in decision processes? How should indicators for monitoring be selected and defined? What is the difference between monitoring and evaluation? How can deviations from expected outcomes be interpreted? What types of data collection methods are appropriate for monitoring? Image: Image: Ask BIONEXT Explore BIONEXT knowledge through a conversational AI assistant Ask a question Benefits and Risks of Using AI Image: Benefits (++) - Automating data collection, processing and reporting. - Detecting patterns, trends and anomalies in monitoring data. - Supporting real-time dashboards and visualisation tools for tracking performance against defined indicators. - Identifying early warning signals of implementation problems Benefit Scoring: ++ Medium More on Benefits Image: Risks (!!) - Misinterpretation of monitoring data without domain-specific understanding. - Over reliance on automated analysis without human validation. - Lack of transparency in AI-driven monitoring tools. - False alarms or missed signals due to limitations of the model Risk Scoring: !! title: BIONEXT | Oppla
text: BIONEXT | Oppla Image: About Ask BIONEXT Case Studies Decision Analysis Resources BIONEXT BIONEXT is a research and innovation project that joins the fight for nature and biodiversity. The project produces new evidence to better understand biodiversity loss and demonstrates how biodiversity underpins every aspect of life; the water we drink, the food we eat, and our health. To secure and protect these values, the project demands transformative change: BIONEXT’s goal is a sustainable society, where links between biodiversity, water, food, energy, transport, climate, and health are acknowledged and nature and biodiversity are a part of everyday choices and policymaking. BIONEXT creates and offers science-based solutions and tools for reversing biodiversity loss and achieving regenerative, nature-centered futures and societies. Image: Keywords: biodiversity transformative change policy

text: Prerequisites for Applying Decision Analysis | BIONEXT Image: Prerequisites for Applying Decision Analysis Understanding the prerequisites for applying Decision Analyais (DA) is essential for its successful application. General prerequesists include: Decision problem that can be clearly formulated (including criteria/alternatives). Decision maker/stakeholders that are committed to the process. Skilled facilitator or analyst. Appropriate methods and tools that are suited to the problem. Data and/or expert judgments available. Resources and time available for the process. When considering the application of decision analysis, one should carefully analyse whether these prerequisites are met in relation to the problem. Outcome of the phase: An understanding of the kinds of situations in which decision analysis can be applied. Follow up Questions for the AI Ask the following questions to gather more information from the AI: Can you elaborate the above-mentioned prerequisites and discuss other possible prerequisites? title: Biodiversity case studies indicating transformative change | BIONEXT — section 1 of 2
parent_title: Biodiversity case studies indicating transformative change | BIONEXT
text: Biodiversity case studies indicating transformative change | BIONEXT Resource Jump to resource Biodiversity case studies indicating transformative change Image: Resource description: In the BIONEXT project D3.1, we’ve collected a critical mass of case studies from around the globe, all indicating transformative change. Transformative change is needed to address the major challenges to nature and humankind, such as biodiversity loss, climate change, and social injustices. Transformative change means that we move beyond just fixing problems and instead fundamentally shift how we interact with the natural world. Generating such fundamental shifts in our mindsets, policies, and practices demands action from all, from citizens to policymakers. A change is only transformative if it shakes up ecological, technological, and socio-economic systems. All the case studies we’ve collected relate to biodiversity and at least two other nexus elements, such as climate, water, transport, energy, health, or food. They centre around an effort to intervene in ecosystems, within habitats, or specifically with species. Examples of these case studies range from NAREI’s implementation of Mangrove restoration in Guyana to Interreg’s restoration of peatlands in Die Weiden, Netherlands. Method We sourced and collected case studies from open-source knowledge repositories. The case studies were existing real-world nexus-related projects and initiatives from across societal and cultural contexts. This allowed us to identify key archetypes of transformative processes. Main findings Case studies that address three or more nexus elements, appear more likely to achieve transformative change. This means that by addressing biodiversity, in combination with other nexus elements (climate, water, transport, energy, health or food), you may be more likely to succeed with transformative change. Creating impact through other dimensions, such as social, political, and economic change, is always a strong indication of the transformative potential of case studies. Projects that ensure cooperation between communities, civic, business, and public bodies are also more likely to be long-term successes in achieving transformative change. Shared governance and cross-collaboration between public, private and community bodies has also similarly emerged as important factor. Transformative change remains difficult to identify and define! Transformative change often isn’t mentioned in the case studies and there is no universally agreed criteria for “what is a transformative change case study”. Most case studies that have created transformative change set out to ensure that the impacts of their change were viable for the long-term. There is also limited focus on transport and energy within case studies: these are nexus elements that would benefit from further research. We have also found that case studies that address water issues, nearly always also have benefits for biodiversity and climate change.

title: BIONEXT European Policy Brief | BIONEXT
text: BIONEXT European Policy Brief | BIONEXT Resource Jump to resource BIONEXT European Policy Brief Image: Resource description: Many recent international science-policy assessments emphasise that Business-as-Usual is no longer sustainable and transformative change of our socio-economic systems is required for tackling issues such as biodiversity loss and climate change. Evidence on what portfolio of transformative solutions are sufficient and effective is urgently needed to mainstream biodiversity and climate change in public and private decision-making. This requires the development of holistic and transdisciplinary approaches, data-driven science, and new tools, models and scenarios that address the main causes of biodiversity loss and explore options for transformative change that are socially just. This is vital to meet many EU objectives, strategies, and commitments such as the EU Biodiversity Strategy 2030, the Nature Restoration Law and the associated national restoration plans. title: Composting conflict: a BIONEXT zine and in-depth case studies | BIONEXT
parent_title: Composting conflict: a BIONEXT zine and in-depth case studies | BIONEXT
text: Composting conflict: a BIONEXT zine and in-depth case studies | BIONEXT Resource Jump to resource Composting conflict: a BIONEXT zine and in-depth case studies Image: Resource description: This is a zine for you… if you’re involved in fundamental change for nature! The BIONEXT project presents three European case studies that show: addressing injustice is often overlooked as a key component in accelerating transitions to a nature-positive society. And to amplify the key messages of these case studies, we’re accompanying them with an eye-catching and brain-stimulating mini magazine that you can print and fold yourself. Read the zine or download a print copy (with folding instructions). You can also find the in-depth case-studies here: The Netherlands , Belgium and Finland. Embrace the heat There’s plenty of conflict in the transition to a nature-positive society. Dealing with conflict is like turning a compost heap: it creates heat which breaks down the scraps of injustice to create a superb substance with which you can grow something new. Without heat, nothing transforms – and the rot leaks out in more dangerous ways. So – in the fight for nature and biodiversity – embrace the heat of conflict like you would stimulate the funk of a compost heap. That’s what stands out from the experiences of policy-workers and other involved professionals ‘doing justice’ in three nature-positive practices: nature-inclusive agriculture in The Netherlands, nature-on-prescription in Belgium and continuous-cover forestry in Finland. A zine for you Zines are small-batch magazine publications, often created without the help of a publisher or financier. Creators of zines (also called ‘zinesters’) see these circumstances not as limitations but rather as ideal conditions to create something experimental and outspoken. Research institute DRIFT created a zine together with various experts also involved in the BIONEXT project to hammer home the essence of what ‘doing justice’ ought to be in nature-positive practices. With 8 small pages no bigger in total than an A3 sheet, getting to the point was non-negotiable. Using cut-and-paste visuals, a quirky printing technique (risography) and a surprising metaphor throughout, the resulting booklet is something that will certainly spark conversations when tactically dropped at the right meeting room, conference or lunch table! title: Constructing a conceptual understanding of transformative change in the biodiversity nexus | BIONEXT
parent_title: Constructing a conceptual understanding of transformative change in the biodiversity nexus | BIONEXT
text: Constructing a conceptual understanding of transformative change in the biodiversity nexus | BIONEXT Resource Jump to resource Constructing a conceptual understanding of transformative change in the biodiversity nexus Image: Resource description: BIONEXT is an innovative research project that produces action-oriented knowledge to halt biodiversity loss. The project demonstrates how biodiversity underpins every aspect of life through the nexus elements of water, food, climate, health, energy, and transport. BIONEXT’s goal is to mainstream biodiversity into policymaking and provide concrete options on how to initiate, accelerate, and upscale biodiversity-relevant transformative change in society. Transformative changes are fundamental shifts in the way we think, act, and organise our society. A change is only transformative if it shakes up ecological, technological, and socio-economic systems. BIONEXT work package 2 ‘Triggering Transformative Change’ aims to find what that change is and how we can set it in motion. And, how we can monitor and evaluate transformative change. The aim of Work Package 2 is to create a conceptual understanding as a basis for the project. In this conceptualisation we build on literature on transformative change, spanning all nexus elements. Building on this literature review, we create an understanding of transformative change in the biodiversity nexus. In addition, this task will work towards defining “signposts for change” – which can be understood as seeds of the future in the present – that can be used to identify practices that have transformative potential. This has been explored through an extensive literature review of transformative change in research describing the nexus elements; to map an understanding of transformative change across these nexus elements and identify how they relate to biodiversity; and illustrate necessary changes for and obstructions to transformative change in the nexus. Author/ : Aniek Hebinck, Amanda Krijgsman, Mara de Pater (DRIFT), Heli Saarikoski, Helena Valve, Dalia D’Amato (SYKE), and Hans Keune (University of Antwerp) Publication date: 30 August 2023 Resource download: Deliverable_D2.1.pdf (1.21 MB) Image: Keywords: biodiversity transformative change Resource type: Report Project: BIONEXT

title: D1.1 Scientific paper on the review of nexus interlinkage | BIONEXT
parent_title: D1.1 Scientific paper on the review of nexus interlinkage | BIONEXT
text: D1.1 Scientific paper on the review of nexus interlinkage | BIONEXT Resource Jump to resource D1.1 Scientific paper on the review of nexus interlinkage Image: Resource description: Biodiversity underpins the functioning of ecosystems and the diverse benefits that nature provides to people, yet is being lost at an unprecedented rate. To halt or reverse biodiversity loss, it is critical to understand the complex interdependencies between biodiversity and key drivers and sectors to inform the development of holistic policies and action. We conducted a literature review on the interlinkages between biodiversity and climate change, food, water, energy, transport and health (“the biodiversity nexus"). Evidence extracted from 194 peer-reviewed articles was analysed to assess how biodiversity is being influenced by and is influencing climate, food, water, energy, transport and health. Out of the 354 interlinkages evidenced between biodiversity and other nexus elements in the review, 53% were negative, 29% were positive and 18% contained both positive and negative influences. Most studies provide evidence of the negative influence of the nexus elements on biodiversity, highlighting the substantial damage being inflicted on nature from human activities. The main types of negative impacts were related to land or water use/change, land or water degradation, direct species fatalities through collisions with infrastructure, and climate change. Alternatively, evidence of biodiversity having a negative influence on the other nexus elements is mainly limited to the effects of invasive alien species and vector-borne disease. Furthermore, a range of studies provided evidence of how co-benefits could be achieved between biodiversity and other nexus elements, such as through agroecological practices, green and blue infrastructure, nature-based solutions, ecosystem restoration and sustainable diets. The review highlighted the complexity and context-dependency of interlinkages within the biodiversity nexus, but clearly demonstrates the importance of biodiversity in underpinning human well-being and ensuring a sustainable future for people and the planet. Author/ : HyeJin Kim, Anita Lazurko, George Linney, Lindsay Maskell, Elizabeth Díaz-General, Romana Jungwirth Březovská, Hans Keune, Chrysi Laspidou, Henna Malinen, Soile Oinonen, Joanna Raymond, Mark Rounsevell, Simeon Vaňo, Marina Demaria Venâncio, Alejandrina Viesca-Ramirez, Ayesha Wijesekera, Katie Wilson, Konstantinos Ziliaskopoulos, Paula A.
