In most integrated models, biodiversity is still treated primarily as an impact endpoint rather than a dynamic driver of system behaviour that influences other nexus outcomes (e.g., Leclère et al., 2020). This is despite abundant evidence that changes in species distributions, habitat quality and ecosystem service provision can propagate through food, water, energy, transport and health systems with significant policy implications (IPBES, 2024a; Kim et al. 2024). The limited representation of biodiversity in integrated assessments, therefore, constrains our ability to evaluate nature-positive or transformative pathways. This challenge is reinforced by the findings of the IPBES Nexus Assessment, which emphasised the need for studies that quantify the role of biodiversity in interlinkages among nexus elements, for models that can simulate sustainable pathways, and for scenarios and models that capture diverse policy response options and their interactions across three or more nexus elements (IPBES, 2024a). The nexus approach The term “nexus” refers to the interlinkages and interdependencies between different sectors/elements (IPBES, 2024a). Nexus approaches are valuable for addressing sustainability challenges by identifying synergistic outcomes across multiple sectors, minimizing or balancing trade-offs, and avoiding potential unintended consequences of decisions. The recently approved Nexus Assessment from the Intergovernmental science-policy Platform on Biodiversity and Ecosystem Services (IPBES) synthesises the diverse and often fragmented literature that examines interlinkages between sectors, such as the water-energy-food, climate-biodiversity-health or water-energy-food-biodiversity nexus (e.g., Newell 2023; Adeola et al. 2022; Moreno Vargas et al. 2023). The findings highlight a wide range of more synergistic response options for nature and people and emphasises the need for more holistic governance to identify and minimize trade-offs between actions targeting different sectors (IPBES, 2024a) WP1 of the BIONEXT project informed the IPBES nexus assessment through Deliverable 1.1, a literature review of the current state of the biodiversity nexus in Europe, i.e., between biodiversity and a more comprehensive range of elements including water, food, health, energy, transport and climate change (Kim et al. 2024). Deliverable 1.2 addressed the need for better integration of biodiversity and nature into scenarios exploring plausible societal trajectories to capture feedbacks between socio-economic and environmental systems (Lazurko et al. 2025a) and to co-create visions of desirable nature-positive futures to inspire and inform pathways of action (Lazurko et al. 2025b). This Deliverable addresses two key knowledge gaps related to modelling emerging from the recently approved assessment. First, it addresses an empirical gap in evidence regarding the impact of response options on multiple nexus elements before and after implementation to understand synergies and trade-offs. To do so, a nexus modelling framework was used to evaluate the ability of co-created pathways of actions to achieve ambitious visions of a nature-positive future in Europe (Section 2.2). Second, it addresses a methodological gap in the representation of cross-sector interactions, feedbacks and the implications of multiple response options in models by leveraging three complementary models together into a nexus modelling framework (Section 2.3). 2.2.

The BIONEXT transformative visions and pathways The co-creation of nature-positive visions and pathways is a key component of the BIONEXT transdisciplinary methodology. This methodology is carried out through the BIONEXT stakeholder workshop series alongside additional consultation including webinars, focus groups and interviews undertaken over the period May 2023 to May 2026. This Deliverable draws on two major components of this transdisciplinary methodology (Figure 2). First, three nature-positive visions for Europe were co-created during Workshop (WS) 1 (May 2023), providing the desirable endpoint in 2050 for biodiversity and the nexus elements, as well as indirect drivers of biodiversity loss including the state of the economy, governance and human-nature relations [Page 9] 6 (Deliverable 1.2). Second, just transition pathways were then co-created during WS2 (May 2024), proposing strategic actions to achieve the three visions across sectors from present to 2030, 2040 and 2050 (Deliverable 2.3). These pathways were then reinforced based on an interim evaluation of their impacts in WS3 (May 2025). The nexus modelling framework was used to evaluate the impacts of a modellable subset of actions proposed in the pathways. The inputs to the nexus modelling framework were parameterised according to the subset of actions in the three pathways (see section 2.4). The outputs of the modelling framework quantitatively describe the outcomes of the pathways across nexus elements, representing the extent to which the pathways achieve the desirable outcomes in the visions. It is recognised that models cannot represent all the rich aspects of the pathways, so the model outputs described in this deliverable will be integrated in future work with a qualitative pathway evaluation to holistically evaluate whether the three pathways achieve the three visions. The BIONEXT nexus modelling framework The nexus modelling framework comprises three complementary models: (i) JUNIPER, a systems dynamic model developed specifically for BIONEXT; (ii) CRAFTY-Europe, an existing agent-based model that has been further enhanced in BIONEXT; and (iii) IAP2/dIAP, an existing regional integrated assessment model. JUNIPER complements the other components of the BIONEXT nexus modelling framework by providing a transparent, computationally efficient representation of how national-scale sectoral trends interact over time, and by generating a coherent set of indicators that can be compared across baseline and pathway runs. In the integrated workflow, JUNIPER provides boundary-condition trajectories (e.g., energy demand, sector pressures and emissions) that can also be used to inform and constrain other modelling components. JUNIPER is implemented in STELLA Architect and follows a system dynamics structure using stocks, flows, auxiliary variables and feedback loops.

In the integrated workflow, JUNIPER provides boundary-condition trajectories (e.g., energy demand, sector pressures and emissions) that can also be used to inform and constrain other modelling components. JUNIPER is implemented in STELLA Architect and follows a system dynamics structure using stocks, flows, auxiliary variables and feedback loops. Each nexus element is represented as a sectoral module with explicit equations and parameter values, so that users can trace causal chains and understand why a given trajectory emerges. The model runs at an annual time step and is designed for repeated scenario exploration, enabling rapid testing of pathway assumptions, sensitivity analysis and comparison across multiple regions. A baseline run is first calibrated against observed time series (where available) to ensure that the model reproduces key historical patterns before it is used for forward-looking pathway analysis (typically extending to 2050). Structurally, JUNIPER is organised around six interconnected modules (Water, Energy, Food, Transport, Health and Biodiversity) plus an emissions/climate component that consolidates GHG pressures from production and mobility systems and transmits their impacts to health and ecosystems (Laspidou et al., 2020). The modular design makes it straightforward to refine or expand a specific sector without re- building the whole model and to apply a consistent modelling logic while adjusting country- or pathway- specific inputs (e.g., resource endowments, energy mix, agricultural structure or transport activity). A simplified overview of the main modules and linkages used in BIONEXT is provided in Figure 3. The Water module estimates total freshwater withdrawals from agriculture (irrigation and livestock), households, industry, desalination and thermoelectric power generation. It integrates demand signals originating from the Food module (irrigation and livestock water requirements), the Energy module (cooling-water needs) and socio-economic drivers (population- and GDP-linked domestic and industrial demand). A key water-stress indicator generated by the model is the Water Exploitation Index (WEI), which expresses total withdrawals as a share of total renewable water resources and provides a consistent metric for tracking water stress over time and across scenarios. The Energy module represents primary energy supply by source (e.g., coal, oil, gas and renewables) and allocates energy demand across end-use sectors (transport, industry, agriculture, services and households). Fuel-specific emission factors are used to estimate energy-related CO₂-equivalent emissions, which then feed into the emissions/climate component. Energy–water coupling is captured through thermoelectric cooling requirements and other water-dependent energy processes (e.g., desalination), while energy demand originating in the Transport and Food modules is accounted for to preserve cross-sector consistency.

The Food module quantifies crop and livestock production and associated resource requirements, distinguishing major crop categories and animal products. Production volumes are linked to (i) energy inputs for food production and processing and (ii) GHG emissions from agricultural activities using crop- and livestock-specific coefficients. These outputs connect directly to the Water module through irrigation and livestock water demand and to the emissions/climate component through agricultural GHG emissions. Food production and consumption are major determinants of land use pressures and diffuse pollution (e.g., nutrient loading and pesticide use) and therefore provide one of the strongest pathways through which socio-economic change can affect biodiversity outcomes. In the current JUNIPER implementation, the Food module primarily drives other modules (rather than receiving strong feedback from them), which keeps pathway assumptions explicit and avoids introducing poorly constrained endogenous responses where data are limited. The Transport module simulates passenger and freight activity across major modes (road, rail and aviation) and estimates both energy demand and pollutant emissions (e.g., CO₂, NOx, SOx and PM2.5). Transport energy demand is passed to the Energy module, while transport-related air pollution provides a direct pathway to health outcomes through the exposure variables used in the Health module. Transport infrastructure and activity also contribute to biodiversity pressures (e.g., habitat fragmentation and disturbance). Similar to the Food module, transport is treated mainly as a driver within JUNIPER, enabling pathway narratives (e.g., electrification, modal shift, demand reduction) to be imposed transparently and then traced through to emissions, health and biodiversity impacts. The Health module translates environmental exposures and socio-economic conditions into two composite outcome indices: Length of Life (LoL) and Quality of Life (QoL). LoL captures physical health outcomes and is influenced by factors such as air-pollution exposure (PM2.5), pesticide use, antibiotic consumption, healthcare capacity and climate-related temperature changes.

In this model, land managers are represented through Agent Functional Types (AFTs), characterised by their behaviours and their form of land management (e.g. profit-maximising intensive farmers). Agents compete for land, represented as a grid of cells, and use socio-economic and natural capitals defined for each cell to produce a range of ecosystem services (Murray-Rust et al. 2014). CRAFTY-Europe is part of the LandSyMM modelling framework (https://landsymm.earth/), which provides the natural capital inputs (from LPJ-GUESS, a dynamic global vegetation model) and the demands for some material services, specifically food and timber (from PLUM, a global food trade model) (Figure 4). The process The model operates at the cell level (Figure 4). Each cell has location attributes defined by the capitals and has one agent assigned to it. In turn, each agent has specific attributes related to competition and [Page 17] 14 productivity capacities for determined services. The configuration of these attributes can change depending on the scenario simulated. A cell can change ownership through the current agent abandoning it when competitiveness falls below a threshold, or when a competing agent has a competitive advantage above another threshold. Simulations start from a baseline map built on the historical land use reconstruction HILDA+ (Winkler et al., 2021) and the European land systems map of Dou et al. (2021), giving land cover and management intensity for each cell. Food and timber production baselines are taken from PLUM v2 (Arendarczyk et al. 2025), and the energy baseline is taken from Saxena et al. (2023). Socio-economic capitals (social, human, manufactured, and financial) were empirically generated based on data primarily from EUROSTAT and the European Social Survey (Raymond et al., in review). Natural capitals, which represent the suitability to produce different crops and plants, were taken from LPJ-GUESS (Arendarczyk et al. 2025).

The location of protected areas for pathways in 2020 was based on the 2019 World Database on Protected Areas (WDPA) protected area distribution in Europe, from which strictly protected areas were defined as those corresponding to IUCN categories Ia, Ib and II. Strict area coverage was expanded first by converting semi-strict areas to strict. Cells with more extensive semi-strict protection were converted first. Secondly, cells with the highest proportion of strict areas were increased so the entire cells were strictly protected. If the total area under strict protection was still short of the target, random cells were selected for protection outside intensively-managed areas. The cells are ranked randomly before the process starts using the same random seed, so that for each pathway, the same cells are allocated randomly first. Following the strict area allocation, semi-strict protection was allocated by first increasing coverage of cells that were partially covered by strict protection, so that the entire cells were protected to some level. If the semi-strict area target was still not met, then cells were allocated randomly based on the precomputed random order. This method was chosen as being conceptually justifiable, but is biased towards places already protected pre-2025, and the random ordering does not ensure that new areas were spread evenly between countries. Similarly, urban areas were also implemented as a reduction of natural capitals, but were kept constant across all pathways and years. From these settings and inputs, simulations ran on annual timesteps until 2050, following the conditions defined by each pathway. The reported values are the averages of 5-year time slices (e.g., 2030 is the average from 2026 to 2030) to minimise the effect of any fluctuations. The European and country-level outputs for BIONEXT are the result of averaging the respective cells. More details will be forthcoming in Díaz-General et al. (in prep.). To facilitate the cross-sectoral model linkages and to reduce model run-time within the web-based software environment, a meta-modelling approach was used whereby computationally efficient or reduced-form models that emulate the performance of more complex models was developed. As an example of these interlinkages, the Rural Land Allocation Model optimises the spatial rural land allocation to meet scenario food demand by selecting between intensive agriculture (arable or dairying), extensive agriculture (grass-based livestock systems), managed forest, unmanaged forest or unmanaged land based on profit maximisation under a range of constraints. Land use selection is constrained by land that is unavailable for agricultural use due to urbanisation (from the Urban Model), frequency of flooding (from the Flooding Model), protected area status or physical constraints (e.g., soil depth). Crops are selected on the basis of relative profitability, which depends on their simulated rainfed and irrigated yields (from the Crop Yield Model) and the maximum allowed water withdrawals for irrigation in a given river basin (from the Water Availability Model). Managed versus unmanaged forest is determined on the basis of whether simulated timber yields (from the Forestry Model) for the baseline tree species achieve sufficient profit. Capital, people and trade flows are treated exogenously within the dIAP, so that GDP, population and food imports are specified as scenario variables. Crop and livestock production prices are not set but are iteratively adjusted within each dIAP run so that farm profits allow sufficient agricultural area to meet the required European food demand. As European food demand increases, imports decrease and/or agri-environment measures (such as buffer strips, set-aside, etc.) increase, then simulated food prices will increase (Dunford et al. 2015).

Discussion and Conclusions The application of the nexus modelling framework to the just transition pathways enables evaluation of the impacts, synergies and trade-offs in the pathways and tests their potential efficacy in achieving sustainable, nature-positive and equitable futures. In this section, we present a high-level overview of the pathway impacts across the nexus elements and discuss their similarities and differences and policy implications, as well as synthesising remaining knowledge gaps. 4.1. The three BIONEXT just transition pathways—NAC (Nature as Culture), NFN (Nature for Nature) and NFS (Nature for Society)—demonstrate that nature-positive futures for Europe are reachable through multiple, value consistent routes. Despite their contrasting philosophies, each pathway delivers similar directional improvements across the biodiversity nexus (Figure 20): (i) biodiversity status increases (Red List Index of Ecosystems and mean species abundance); (ii) food production increases within Europe but shifts towards more plant-based or mixed agricultural systems that support healthy nutritional needs; (iii) water withdrawals and the Water Exploitation Index decline, while flood regulation increases; (iv) GHG emissions fall markedly with deep cuts in fossil energy replaced by substantial growth in renewables; (v) conventional car use and transport emissions shrink; and (vi) population health [Page 42] 39 improves in both length and quality of life. This convergence of outcomes contrasts with the divergence of causal mechanisms—from localised governance, biocultural landscapes and agroecology (NAC), to strict protection and societal sufficiency (NFN), to innovation-led efficiency and circularity (NFS). Together, the results suggest that policy design can leverage multiple approaches that can be tailored to societal contexts without sacrificing long-term sustainability outcomes, if actions remain coherent within a whole nexus perspective. Across pathways, biodiversity gains appear smaller in magnitude than other sectoral improvements by 2050, not because pressures are unresponsive, but because reduced disturbance, land use change and restoration measures take time to translate into species and ecosystem outcomes in the modelling framework. These time lag assumptions are deliberate to avoid overstating short-term recovery; they imply that post-2050 trajectories would likely show larger biodiversity gains if the same pressure reductions are sustained. Importantly, the quality of life improvements we simulate are consistent with these biodiversity trends, capturing part of the co-benefits from cleaner air, greener spaces and improved environmental conditions that accompany nature recovery. 4.1.1 Different routes to sustainability: mechanisms that matter NAC achieves improvements primarily by reducing system pressures at source through cultural and behavioural change—lower livestock and meat consumption, biocultural principles, widespread agroecology, organic fertilisation, local lifestyles and supply chains driving strong reductions in private car use and aviation, and large behavioural energy savings embedded in community-owned, localised systems. Protected areas increase but are largely semi-strict, enabling low intensity multifunctional landscapes to contribute to food provision and biodiversity.

title: Deliverable D1.3 — section 54 of 80
text: ic fertilisation, local lifestyles and supply chains driving strong reductions in private car use and aviation, and large behavioural energy savings embedded in community-owned, localised systems. Protected areas increase but are largely semi-strict, enabling low intensity multifunctional landscapes to contribute to food provision and biodiversity. The result is cross-cutting reductions in pollution and disturbance that enhance biodiversity and improve health and air quality, with moderate energy electrification complemented by demand contraction. NFN improves outcomes by maximising “space for nature” through a strong, top-down eco-vision—the most ambitious expansion of protected areas (50% land; 37.5% strict), strong sufficiency measures (largest decrease in meat consumption, deep cuts in aviation, near elimination of conventional cars), and behavioural water and energy savings. Food production is displaced outside strict PAs, intensifying where necessary, while preventative health and ecological literacy complement environmental gains. This pathway obtains the largest total GHG reductions through combined sufficiency in mobility, energy and diets, and strict spatial protection that reduces land use pressures. NFS relies on technology and market-shaped efficiency: large yield increases, circular economy instruments (material budgets, differential pricing), economic valuation of nature, high electrification of energy and transport, and wide deployment of nature-based solutions. Moderate PA expansion is paired with extensive potential rewilding of abandoned land, and AI-enabled, decentralised healthcare bolsters health gains. This route decouples resource demand from services via innovation and governance reforms, moderating pressures while sustaining service delivery and access. These distinct mechanisms are not interchangeable; they shape different co-benefit bundles and risk profiles. For example, strict protection (NFN) rapidly improves the species Red List Index where pressures are excluded, while agroecological mosaics (NAC) improve the Red List of ecosystems index via diffuse pressure reduction and multifunctional land sharing. Across all three pathways, the results reveal a strong predominance of synergies, with improvements in one sector often reinforcing gains in others. Reductions in livestock numbers, fertiliser use, fossil fuel dependency, and private car travel, for example, consistently deliver co-benefits for biodiversity, water, air quality, climate mitigation and health. These reinforcing dynamics demonstrate the value of integrated policy portfolios that act on shared pressure points within the system. At the same time, each pathway exhibits distinctive trade-offs, arising not from contradictions in overall strategy but from the different mechanisms through which the pathways attempt to achieve nature- positive outcomes. The modelling shows that similar endpoints are reached through different combinations of land system change, technological innovation, sufficiency measures and governance choices, and these combinations produce pathway specific pressure shifts across the nexus. In the biodiversity–food nexus, for example, gains in biodiversity can arise through three different routes: (i) strict protection and dietary changes reducing agricultural land (NFN); (ii) widespread agroecology and pressure reduction within biocultural landscapes (NAC), or (iii) freeing land via high agricultural yields and circular systems (NFS). While all three approaches improve biodiversity overall, they have different implications for where food production is intensified, how much land becomes available for natural regeneration, and which habitats expand or contract outside protected areas. Similarly, water–food–energy interactions show that all pathways reduce water stress, but through different means. NFN achieves this primarily through behavioural change and reducing irrigated land, NAC combines agroecological practices with irrigation efficiency, while NFS relies more heavily on technological water savings and circular water management that decouples water use from GDP. These differences shape not only the magnitude of water savings but also their distribution across sectors and basins, emphasising the need to consider local hydrological contexts in implementation. Energy–land interactions illustrate how renewables can both reinforce and challenge biodiversity and land use goals. All pathways reduce fossil fuels substantially but differ in the composition of renewables: NAC includes a larger role for bioenergy within a low demand system; NFN and NFS expand solar and wind more extensively but rely less on bioenergy. These distinctions lead to different land use footprints and siting pressures, showing that the nature-positivity of energy transitions depends not only on the scale of renewables but also on their spatial configuration and land competition dynamics.

[Page 44] 41 4.2 Policy implications Several broad policy implications emerge from assessing the outcomes of applying the nexus modelling framework to the just transition pathways. These centre on designing context-specific portfolios that draw on the strengths of each pathway and align with local values, capacities and institutional conditions. Key principles include: • Embracing plurality. Policymakers can select and combine elements from NAC, NFN and NFS to match local values and institutional capacity, so long as the portfolio reduces core pressures across the nexus. • Sequencing actions. Early gains can be achieved from demand-side actions (such as dietary shifts and mobility sufficiency), no-regret efficiency measures (for water and energy), and spatial protections where social licence exists. However, long-lead investments (such as electricity grid/storage upgrades, nature-based solutions, agroecology transitions, workforce skills) need to be scaled up in parallel to achieve impacts at the needed time scales. • Planning spatially and governing participatorily. Renewable energy deployment, protected area expansion, rewilding and agroecology must be spatially explicit, co-designed with communities and integrated with transport and health-access planning to maximise co-benefits and minimise local trade-offs. • Locking in the gains. Legal reforms (e.g., rights of nature, long-term sustainability frameworks), financing tools (e.g., material budgets, circular incentives), and just transition mechanisms are needed to stabilise transformations beyond 2050. • Strengthening multi-level governance and cooperation.

Their complementary logics provide a richer basis for understanding how the pathways propagate impacts across sectors and scales. These complementary modelling approaches strengthen inference where they align and illuminate uncertainties where they diverge. [Page 47] 44 Across models and indicators, the direction of change for the core nexus outcomes is consistently positive: lower GHGs and water withdrawals/WEI, higher renewable energy deployment, increased plant-based food production, improved biodiversity indicators and better health outcomes. This cross- model coherence strengthens confidence in the robustness of the broad patterns and interactions simulated for the different pathways.

Alternatively, JUNIPER has independent models at country and European scales based on a common structure, revealing more consistent trends in impacts between the six countries and Europe. These divergences are informative as they identify sensitive mechanisms or assumptions (e.g., where strict protected areas limit establishment of certain forest types; where intensified plant-based production outside protected areas affects local diversity), and guide priorities for empirical validation and future model refinement. The combined use of three models enables triangulation. Areas of strong agreement mark high confidence signals where policy action can proceed with fewer concerns about model uncertainty. Conversely, areas of divergence identify sensitive system levers—such as strictness of protected areas, renewable energy siting, or the treatment of abandoned land—where outcomes depend heavily on assumptions and where policy should proceed with clearer spatial planning, adaptive management or additional evidence gathering. First, the model highlights strong structural inertia in the land system: entrenched patterns such as the dominance of G1 over G2 bioenergy persist even under ambitious pathway interventions. These limitations relate not only to model structures, data inputs, and modelling assumptions but also to the kinds of changes that [Page 48] 45 can be represented, and to the uncertainties introduced through the stakeholder co-creation process that informed the parameterisation of the pathways. A first set of limitations concerns the representation of qualitative, experiential and relational dimensions of transformative change. The models are designed to quantify pressures, flows and biophysical outcomes, but they cannot fully capture aspects such as how people experience nature, how access and wellbeing are shaped by cultural practices, or how governance transformations alter relationships between communities and landscapes. For example, in the NFN pathway, strict protection and large-scale resettlement raise important questions about people’s ability to access nature, the cultural acceptability of restrictions, and the social meaning of restored landscapes—none of which can be represented directly in the modelling framework. Similarly, NAC’s emphasis on biocultural reciprocity and local stewardship is only partially approximated through variables such as low-input agriculture, meaning that key relational aspects of transformation remain outside the quantitative analysis. These qualitative dimensions are critical to understanding both feasibility and legitimacy, yet they require complementary non-modelling approaches.

A second source of uncertainty arises from the stakeholder process used to quantify pathway parameters. Although the co-production approach ensured a transparent and participatory translation of pathway narratives into numerical trends, stakeholder inputs inevitably reflected varying levels of confidence, interpretation and familiarity with quantitative ranges. Stakeholders were asked to estimate their level of confidence in their parameter trends on a scale from 0 to 10, where 0 reflected no confidence and 10 very confident. The scores ranged from 1 to 9 (average = 5.8), highlighting that some parameters—such as food imports and most of the transport parameters—were more intuitive for participants to estimate, while others (e.g., protected areas, tree planning and land use intensity trajectories) were less immediately accessible and required significant facilitation and interpretation by the modelling teams. This creates embedded uncertainties not only in the magnitude of parameter values but also in the assumptions that underpin them. Related to this is the challenge of managing expectations about what is modellable and what is not. During workshops and webinars, stakeholders often proposed actions that were conceptually transformative but not easily translatable into model parameters (e.g., shifts in social norms, legal rights for nature, new governance cultures, or changes in political narratives). Several proposed actions also operate at local scales or targeted indirect drivers not embedded in the models, such as educational reforms. Because the three models operate at European and national scales, it is difficult to incorporate highly specific or locally governed changes that fall outside the regulatory reach of those levels. Although modellers worked to approximate these elements through proxy variables or contextual assumptions, important gaps remain between the richness of pathway narratives and the subset of actions that can be meaningfully represented within the modelling framework. Recognising these gaps is essential to avoid over-interpreting the quantitative results as complete representations of the pathways. A third limitation concerns the underlying assumptions and structural constraints of each model, including the treatment of biodiversity dynamics and land system processes. Biodiversity indicators (RLI, RLIe, MSA, naturalness) respond to changes in pressures and land use but do not encompass ecological thresholds, species interactions or socio-ecological feedbacks.

The BIONEXT work reported here addresses these gaps in several ways. First, it operationalises a biodiversity-centred nexus by coordinating three complementary models (JUNIPER, CRAFTY-Europe, dIAP) to quantify interactions across biodiversity, water, food, energy, transport, health and climate. Second, it co-creates visions and just transition pathways with stakeholders and parameterises them for modelling through an iterative, transparent process.

Conclusions The BIONEXT assessment shows that Europe’s journey to nature-positive futures is not singular. Community-based biocultural landscape management and agroecology (NAC), strict ecological prioritisation and societal sufficiency (NFN), and innovation-led efficiency and circularity (NFS) each converge on improved biodiversity, lower resource pressures, deep decarbonisation and better health. While their action logics and distributional footprints differ, all three work when designed as coherent nexus portfolios. This plurality is a strength: it widens the political and cultural coalition for change, allowing governments, regions and communities to pursue context-fit transformations that together bend the curve for nature while improving human wellbeing. The task ahead is to orchestrate these routes—sequencing quick wins, investing in enabling infrastructures and embedding justice—so that diverse European societies can travel their chosen paths towards their nature-positive vision. Nature Communications, 12, 2501. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41467-021-22702-2 [Page 57] 54 Annex 1: CRAFTY-Europe model output indicators This annex provides a detailed description of the model output indicators from the CRAFTY-Europe model used to represent the biodiversity nexus. They represent the services produced by the agents, and also the land use types that are relevant to the delivery of those services. Nexus element Type of CRAFTY output Description Biodiversity, Water, Health and Climate (see details in the description for each nexus element) Forest land use types (in km2) • Intensive forests: Broadleaf or conifer trees with intensive forest management, including clear- felling (as standard or where permitted, optimum rotation lengths, thinning and species • Extensive forests: Broadleaf or conifer trees with extensive forest management, no clear-felling, less intense selective logging and other forest services • Multifunctional mixed woodland: Mixed trees with extensive forest management • Conserved woodland: Protected forests with no/low management • Agroforestry: Agroforestry systems with a mix of broadleaf trees and crop cultivation (cereals, fruit and vegetables, oil crops) Land use type (km2) Unmanaged land: Unlabelled, sparsely or unmanaged land (mining areas, wetlands, shrubs, barren land, rocks and ice) Emergent land use type (km2) Abandoned lands: Land uses of any type abandoned due to changes in the competitive capacities of agents (see process description of the model in Section 2.3.2) Biodiversity Service • Naturalness (ranking from 1 to 6): The degree of naturalness, indicating the anthropogenic influence on biodiversity. Ranking of land use types, based on the degree of naturalness from Rüdisser, Tasser and Tappeiner (2012). AFT categories were mapped onto the land use types within the naturalness classification. • Mean Species Abundance (MSA, from 0 to 1): MSA is a biodiversity intactness index. Here we only represent the land use effects on MSA. MSA values are assigned for each AFT based on the GLOBIO3 MSA land use values from Alkemede et al 2009. Abandoned lands are assigned a value of 1, the same as conservation woodland and unmanaged land. When the AFTs change, MSA will decrease instantly if it’s not favourable for biodiversity, but if it’s to a higher MSA value e.g. from intensive pasture to very extensive pasture, then there is a recovery period. We use the SSE biodiversity net gain advisory Annex E “Habitat creation” as a proxy for how long each AFT would take to increase to the maximum possible MSA value. • Landscape heterogeneity (from 0 to 1): Diversity within and between land uses in a landscape. Calculated using the Shannon Diversity Index for each 1km² grid cell in Europe based on EUNIS habitat level 2 data (100m spatial resolution) and averaged per AFT and country for the baseline year.

It considers rainfall erositivity projections under RCP4.5 Relevant land use types (km2) • Flood regulation: All forest land uses (intensive and extensive), unmanaged and abandoned lands, and pastoral lands • Soil retention: All forest land uses (intensive and extensive), pastoral lands, and unmanaged lands. Calculated for each grid cell following Vallecillo et al. (2019), based on the ESTIMAP project (Parrachini et al. 2014; Zulian et al. 2018). The approach takes into account human inputs to the land system that are essential for accessibility of the land for recreational activities as well as the ecosystem-based potential of land to be used for recreational activities. The approach is based on advanced look-up tables for particular values that are used to assign scores for ecosystem services to land cells based on a cross-tabulation fed by overlaying maps (Schröter et al., 2015 in Vallecillo et al., 2019). Protected areas increase the recreation score, regardless of the level of protection as they represent more nature elements. Abandoned lands do not contribute to recreation as they are assigned a recreation value of 0. Relevant land use types (km2) All forest land uses, food land uses for pasture and fruit and vegetable, and abandoned lands? Climate Service The carbon sequestration estimation is taken from LPJ-GUESS runs that assume static alternative land uses, and includes vegetation biomass only. As non-forest biomass is not generally preserved, values are given only for forest types. Because runs a pre-defined, the history, length of management or growth of a forest does not affect the carbon value. • Carbon sequestration (tons): Potential carbon sequestration by forested land, calculated using input data from LPJ-GUESS, as outlined above. • Carbon sequestration with abandoned lands (tons): As in the Carbon sequestration service above, but modified to account for abandoned land as forested areas such that they also use the potential carbon sequestration (in particular they use the Mixed Woodland carbon values).

Introduction BIONEXT is an innovative research project that produces action-oriented knowledge to halt biodiversity loss. The project demonstrates how biodiversity underpins every aspect of life through the nexus elements of water, food, climate, health, energy, and transport. BIONEXT’s goal is to mainstream biodiversity into policymaking and provide concrete options on how to initiate, accelerate, and upscale biodiversity-relevant transformative change in society. Transformative changes are fundamental shifts in the way we think, act, and organise our society. A change is only transformative if it shakes up ecological, technological, and socio-economic systems. BIONEXT work package 2 ‘Triggering Transformative Change’ aims to find what that change is and how we can set it in motion. And, how we can monitor and evaluate transformative change. The aim of Work Package 2 is to create a conceptual understanding as a basis for the project. In this conceptualisation we build on literature on transformative change, spanning all nexus elements. Building on this literature review, we create an understanding of transformative change in the biodiversity nexus. In addition, this task will work towards defining “signposts for change” – which can be understood as seeds of the future in the present – that can be used to identify practices that have transformative potential. This has been explored through an extensive literature review of transformative change in research describing the nexus elements; to map an understanding of transformative change across these nexus elements and identify how they relate to biodiversity; and illustrate necessary changes for and obstructions to transformative change in the nexus. [Page 5] 2 2. State of the art on transformative change 2.1. The need for transformative change in the biodiversity nexus The world is confronted with pressing global crises such as climate change, biodiversity loss, and growing inequality (Vogel and O’Brien 2022). Scholars are increasingly united in the belief that the enormity, urgency, complexity, and interconnectedness of these crises make it impossible to continue a 'business-as-usual' trajectory if we are to ensure both biophysical and social well-being (Shove et al. 2012; Feola 2015). In response, the scientific and policy communities have become more attentive to the need for transformative changes in socio-ecological systems and deliberate steps towards sustainability over the last few decades (Bennett et al. 2019).

title: Deliverable D2.1 — section 4 of 73
text: as-usual' trajectory if we are to ensure both biophysical and social well-being (Shove et al. 2012; Feola 2015). In response, the scientific and policy communities have become more attentive to the need for transformative changes in socio-ecological systems and deliberate steps towards sustainability over the last few decades (Bennett et al. 2019). When highlighting the urgency of the biodiversity crisis, scholars build upon scientific evidence that demonstrates the worldwide deterioration of biodiversity and ecosystems, while underscoring the dependency of human existence on the functioning of natural systems (IPBES 2019; Díaz et al. 2019). Central to research that aims to understand these relations is the ‘nexus’ approach, which entails “A perspective which emphasizes the inter-relatedness and interdependencies of ecosystem components and human uses, and their dynamics and fluxes across spatial scales and between compartments. […] In such complex systems there are trade-offs as well as facilitation and amplification between the different components” (IPBES 2019). To comprehend the loss of biodiversity, researchers generally distinguish between direct and indirect anthropogenic drivers. Among the most influential direct drivers are climate change, natural resource extraction, land-use change, invasive alien species, and pollution (Elbakidze et al. 2018; IPBES 2019), while indirect drivers encompass demographic, sociocultural, economic, technological, and institutional factors (Visseren-Hamakers et al. 2021). Advocates of transformative change argue that previous conservation efforts have proven insufficient in reversing biodiversity loss due to their inadequate response to many of the underlying drivers (IPBES 2019). As a result, the primary goal of transformative change for biodiversity is to tackle these drivers, with a specific focus on the indirect ones, often termed as the root causes, which are deeply influenced by societal values and behaviours (Díaz et al. 2019). 2.2. Conceptualizations of transformative change Due to the increasing recognition of the necessity for transformative change, the terms 'sustainability transformations' and 'transformative change' have become firmly established concepts among both scientists and policymakers (Scoones et al. 2020). However, the interpretations and applications of these terms differ significantly across various disciplines (Feola 2015). In the following sections we will first give a brief overview of the main conceptualizations of transformative change and the main applications of the concept in the academic community. Last, we will give a brief overview of the use of transformative change in the context of biodiversity. 2.2.1. Dominant perspectives to transformative change The concept transformative change is generally understood as a “fundamental, system-wide reorganization across technological, economic and social factors, including paradigms, goals and values” (IPBES 2019).

text: ive a brief overview of the use of transformative change in the context of biodiversity. 2.2.1. Dominant perspectives to transformative change The concept transformative change is generally understood as a “fundamental, system-wide reorganization across technological, economic and social factors, including paradigms, goals and values” (IPBES 2019). Understandings of transformative change stem roughly from three prominent perspectives: social-ecological systems, sustainability transitions and political ecology. [Page 6] 3 Notable is that the terms transition and transformation are often used interchangeably. Some authors stress the differences between the two: Eckersley (2022) and Hordijk et al. (2014) for example, argue that transitions, due to its sectoral focus, imply incremental changes and are less radical and systemic than transformations. A review by Hölscher et al. (2018) shows that the differences in concepts do not necessarily lie in a difference in radicality, but mostly stem from different framings used by different research communities. The elasticity of the use of concepts like transitions and transformations makes it hard to make a clear distinction between them (Feola 2015). Sustainability transitions Sustainability transitions is an interdisciplinary approach to societal changes that occur over multiple decades (Loorbach et al. 2017). Transition scholars generally analyse social, technological, and institutional changes within a societal subsystem or sector such as the energy sector. Change is understood as a phased and multi-level process where different levels (niche, regime, landscape) influence changes toward the reconfiguration of a new regime. A large focus within this field is on initiating processes of change through transition management, which entails experimentation and the development and scaling of (social) innovations at a niche level. More recently attention has broadened to breakdown of unsustainable regimes and the role of power in transitions (Markard 2018; Davidson 2019; Hebinck et al. 2022). Social-ecological systems The social-ecological systems perspective is largely centred on the analysis of system properties such as resilience and adaptation against perturbations or crises, whether naturally occurring or human- induced (Patterson et al. 2017). Transformations were initially perceived as outcomes of disturbances that exceeded a system's adaptive capacity, whether ecological, economic, or social in nature (Fougères et al. 2022). Over time and through contributions from various disciplines, this perspective has broadened its scope, leading to improved understandings of the social component of social- ecological systems. While transformations were initially seen as emergent processes, it is now acknowledged that desired transformations contribute to increased resilience of systems (Folke et al. 2010; Patterson et al. 2017).

title: Deliverable D2.1 — section 6 of 73
text: isciplines, this perspective has broadened its scope, leading to improved understandings of the social component of social- ecological systems. While transformations were initially seen as emergent processes, it is now acknowledged that desired transformations contribute to increased resilience of systems (Folke et al. 2010; Patterson et al. 2017). In this, there is an increasing focus on ‘transformative capacities’ in social-ecological systems literature, responding to the idea that transformation cannot be steered but rather be ‘navigated’ (Moore et al. 2018). Additionally, the processes of transformations can be guided by deliberate and socially complex approaches to learning and decision-making (Fougères et al. 2022). Political ecology Perspectives within the political ecology cluster do not constitute a separate and distinctly defined field like sustainability transitions and social-ecological systems. Instead, they form a cluster of critical social science perspectives on transformative change. Scholars within this field emphasize the potential risks associated with promoting changes that still operate within existing hierarchies of knowledge and power (Massarella et al. 2021). Instead, they advocate for ‘axial change’, which involves breaking free from the status quo by questioning the entire system to uncover innovative and radical approaches to transformation (Massarella et al. 2021). From the perspective of political ecology, the most significant contributions lie in providing valuable insights on themes such as politicizing change, challenging hegemonic power structures, and addressing issues of (in)justice (Patterson et al. 2017; Temper et al. 2018; Massarella et al. 2021). [Page 7] 4 2.2.2. Compatibility of the three disciplinary understandings of transformative change The three main perspectives are not inherently exclusive of each other. They primarily emphasize different aspects of transformation. Transitions literature typically begins with sectors as a basis, while social-ecological systems usually adopt a place-based approach. Perspectives within the political ecology cluster do not necessarily oppose other fields; instead, they draw attention to the deficiencies or risks linked to the existing body of knowledge and prevailing dominant approaches. This does not mean that the concept transformative change is uncontested. Within and across all perspectives debate remains on the desirability and effectiveness of certain deliberate processes of change and the directionality and radicality of the transformative changes being advocated (Feola 2015). In the following sections we outline some of these different approaches in literature. 2.3. Use of and critiques to transformative change in literature The contested nature of the concept transformative change has also resulted in diverse approaches to researching transformative change in the literature.

title: Deliverable D2.1 — section 7 of 73
text: mative changes being advocated (Feola 2015). In the following sections we outline some of these different approaches in literature. 2.3. Use of and critiques to transformative change in literature The contested nature of the concept transformative change has also resulted in diverse approaches to researching transformative change in the literature. For example, while some focus on the cause or need for change, others explore the mechanisms that allow transformative change to take place. Often more than one approach to exploring transformative change is applied at the same time. The most prevalent approach in the literature to exploring transformative change category is one that sheds light on the issues and crises prevailing in societies and advocate the need for change. This category displays contributions from diverse disciplines and is often driven by a “sense of urgency” (Bentz et al. 2022). However, scholars warn for the conflation of the ‘what’ and the ‘how’ of transformative change and to assume that “once we know what needs to be done, then mobilization, organisation, decisions, and action will follow” (Bentz et al. 2022, p. 498). In other words, the knowledge of what needs to change by itself – e.g., a need to reduce emissions 40-50% by 2030 (Rockström et al. 2017) – does not automatically result in action. Only recently, more literature focuses on what needs to change and how such change might unfold and can be fostered. Depending on the school of thought, these are embedded in different ways of understanding the system. For example, the work that understands change processes as unfolding in a ‘non-linear’ way and thus being complex and uncertain, such as the sustainability transitions literature and the social-ecological systems literature, often explore patterns of change through a focus on properties such as complexity, path-dependency, emergence, and contestation (e.g. Hölscher et al. 2018). Literature oriented at the analysis of complex systems, similarly, see change as non-linear, complex, and uncertain, but tend to focus on what aspects influence systems: such as drivers and barriers. These factors encompass both practical aspects, like the availability of resources (Dawson et al. 2017), and systemic characteristics such as the 'vested interest' of institutions (Termeer et al. 2015). Literatures combining both the ‘what’ and ‘how’ of transformative change investigate types of changes and actions that have the potential to result in transformative change. This requires both an idea of the required (or desired) change and an understanding of how change unfolds. Literature that both acknowledges the emergent nature of transformations and the agency to drive transformative change, explore the potential for deliberate interventions and actions (Olsson et al. 2014; Massarella et al. 2021).

title: Deliverable D2.1 — section 8 of 73
text: mative change. This requires both an idea of the required (or desired) change and an understanding of how change unfolds. Literature that both acknowledges the emergent nature of transformations and the agency to drive transformative change, explore the potential for deliberate interventions and actions (Olsson et al. 2014; Massarella et al. 2021). However, significant variations can be observed in the interventions proposed, spanning from technological innovations to policy measures and social innovations (Dias and Partidário 2019; [Page 8] 5 Dorninger et al. 2020). Literature outlining the interventions often makes the connection to the types of changes that the interventions should initiate, such as such as changing norms and values, shifting power dynamics, modifying behaviours, and bringing about institutional and political transformations. These proposals span a spectrum of radicality: from gradual incremental adjustments and reformation of existing structures to more revolutionary and transformative shifts (e.g. as discussed in Burch et al. 2014; Geels et al. 2015). Lastly, a growing group of scholars focusses on the direction of change – or directionality, which revolves around envisioning desired futures or the critical interrogation of where the current course of change is leading towards (Muiderman et al. 2022). Especially in the literature exploring desired futures, the primary emphasis is on striving for sustainable societies and, in numerous instances, societies that prioritize justice and equity (Bennett et al. 2016). Whereas critical interrogation of futures, departs from the understanding that all claims on the future (and thus transformation) are political interventions that hold performative power (Jasanoff and Kim 2015) and aims to uncover how they might exclude certain choices, trajectories, or futures (Muiderman et al. 2022). 2.3.1. Main critiques voiced about transformations literature As transformations and transformative change have become increasingly popular themes in research, they are also subject to critique. Feola (2015) argues that while criticism can signal a vibrant field within the social sciences, it also poses a particular risk when it comes to transformative change. “[T]he high conceptual elasticity and lack of empirical grounding of the conce pt of transformation generate the risk of voiding the term of meaning, and consequently easily co-opted by actors who aim to defend the status quo rather than promoting radical societal change” (Feola 2015, p. 377). Similar dynamics were noted around the use of ‘sustainability’, when use of the term has mainstreamed in diverse scientific communities and societal groups, although with diverse meanings and through diverse approaches (Scoones 2007). Much like the use of sustainability, both transformation and transformative change are susceptible to legitimizing existing or new structures of power that uphold ‘business as usual’ in disguise (Blythe et al. 2018).

title: Deliverable D2.1 — section 9 of 73
text: in diverse scientific communities and societal groups, although with diverse meanings and through diverse approaches (Scoones 2007). Much like the use of sustainability, both transformation and transformative change are susceptible to legitimizing existing or new structures of power that uphold ‘business as usual’ in disguise (Blythe et al. 2018). For example, it may be used by authorities to promote change that serves their own interests or gain public acceptance without questioning distributional consequences. Fougères et al. (2022) demonstrate how the ‘UN 2030 Agenda for Sustainable Development’, the ‘Post-2020 Global Biodiversity Framework’, and ‘Nature 2030’ use the term transformative change in a way to maintain or expand their power over biodiversity, territory, and people. The understanding of transformative change is often modified when translated into policies and practices, risking loss of its transformative potential and raising questions about how these may shape social, political, and environmental change in reality (Blythe et al. 2018; Fiasco and Massarella 2022). Some scholars assign the lack of empirical grounding of the concept to an insufficient understanding of the processes of transformative change. They argue for the need for effective strategies and interventions to facilitate and put such changes in motion (Feola 2015; Bentz et al. 2022). Bentz and colleagues (2022) criticize the disproportionate attention given to the 'why' aspect of transformation, neglecting the crucial 'what' and 'how' aspects. Consequently, ‘what’ the problem exactly is and ‘how’ it can be resolved remain obscure, as well as the plurality of perspectives to the ‘what’ and ‘how’ that may exist (Blythe et al. 2018). This can explain why policies and interventions aimed at transformative [Page 9] 6 change tend to get stuck between the ambitions of change on the one hand, and the ‘real-life’ perceptions, experiences, norms, choices, and practices of society on the other (Gollata and Newig 2017). In addition, Tschakert et al. (2013) argue that processes of transformative change are hampered by insufficient knowledge on vulnerability dynamics, which are required to address fundamental and relational drivers of injustices. In a similar vein, scholars critique the use of transformative change that implicitly assumes that its outcomes are of universal benefit, overlooking losers of change (Blythe et al. 2018; Forsyth et al. 2022). In such cases, the positive effects of change tend to be uncritically embraced rather than subjected to critical analysis. Other scholars warn that the limited awareness of the consequences of transformative change has resulted in insufficient attention to complex legal and institutional circumstances that shape governance of transformative change (Heffron 2021).

title: Deliverable D2.1 — section 10 of 73
text: the positive effects of change tend to be uncritically embraced rather than subjected to critical analysis. Other scholars warn that the limited awareness of the consequences of transformative change has resulted in insufficient attention to complex legal and institutional circumstances that shape governance of transformative change (Heffron 2021). Transformative change implicitly or explicitly relies on cognitive and normative framings of problems, which in turn guide normative and instrumental biases in governance approaches to transformative change. Such biases may be reproduced in the introduction of new norms, values, technologies, knowledge, expertise, principles, rules, and laws to regulate the direction of change. It is essential to consider how relationships between power and resources can influence changing forms of access and control, identifying who benefits and who loses in transformative change (Burch et al. 2014; Blythe et al. 2018; Fougères et al. 2022). Such considerations encompass for example factors like efficiency, productivity, trade-offs, equity, social and legal security, and recognition. Moreover, society must understand and accept possible consequences to ensure the public supports and acts towards a transition (Heffron and McCauley 2018). Especially with transformative change being co-opted by ‘business as usual perspectives’, there is the risk that the necessary radical change is not achieved. Science is expected to play a significant role in reshaping the dominant social paradigm on change and intervening within the sustainability transformations it seeks to understand (Fazey et al. 2018). For example, by addressing underlying drivers of unsustainability (Blythe et al. 2018), and introducing new options and incentives to catalyse transformative change (Ehrlich et al. 2012). The conceptualization of transformative change ideally maintains the flexibility to accommodate diverse perspectives, while retaining its robustness to uphold its radical essence (Scoones et al. 2020). Science being both part of and intervening in processes of transformation, places an enormous responsibility on researchers to be critical and reflexive (Popa et al. 2015; Fazey et al. 2018). Building on these critical perspectives, researchers who advocate for transformative change within the biodiversity nexus must critically engage with the following ‘red flags’: 1. The concept "transformative change" is vulnerable to being co-opted by existing or new structures of power, possibly reinforcing the status quo. Uncertainties persist regarding the true meaning and potential impact of transformative change, especially when it interacts with different actors; 2. The concept of transformative change faces challenges stemming from a lack of empirical grounding and insufficient understanding of the underlying processes of change; 3.

The urgency of climate change and biodiversity loss necessitate an understanding of transformative change as being both rapid and fundamental. Science has a pivotal role in demonstrating the ‘what’ and ‘how’ of such fundamental changes. 2.4. Analytical approaches to transformative change As the review on transformative change highlights, transformative change is a contested concept. The proliferation of the concept of ‘transformative change’ leads to approaches placing diverse emphases within the process of change: ranging from actor-configurations, the role of institutions, or to system dimensions. To come to a conceptual understanding of transformative change in the biodiversity nexus, we need to explore what the concept means and how it is used across diverse research communities. In order to map these diverse understandings, we build on several academic works that attempt to analyse these different perspectives. We identified three papers which particularly underscore the need for transformative change to addresses global sustainability challenges and unite in the critique that existing paradigms and approaches to sustainability transformations do not provide sufficient insight into effective ways to achieve transformations. (2020) similarly argue that it often remains unclear what concrete interventions for transformative change exist, hindering the replication or scaling of promising interventions. Based on a systematic literature review, they uncover several clusters of scientific approaches and their ‘bias’ towards a particular solution space: an ‘engineering’ cluster characterized by technological solutions, a ‘technocratic’ cluster with an emphasis on policy solutions, a ‘sociopolitical’ cluster that focuses on solutions that address social problems, and a ‘social-ecological’ cluster that looks at solutions that have an ecological problem framing. They argue these clusters differently consider fundamental aspects of the system, such as its rules, values, and paradigms. Lastly, we turn to West et al. (2020) who argue that the ‘conventional’ systems perspective to transformative change risks reproducing the separation between the ‘social’ and the ‘ecological’ as embedded in currently dominant system structures, and risks overlooking the continuously changing relations and processes between (non-)human entities. This in turn, limits the transformative potential of insights drawn from such research. They propose that a more relational approach to transformative change, might enable a more dynamic and place-based understanding of processes of change. Limitations to the review The search performed to conduct the review was systematically structured, although limited by time constraints. The search strings used were designed to capture documents dealing with both transformative change and at least one of the nexus items. However, search strings were limited in that they did not include synonyms for both transformative change and for the nexus elements. For example, this meant that literature covering adjacent fields that are influential to transformative change were not included, such as sustainability transitions literature.

Conceptualisation of transformative change The understanding of transformative change in the governance-focused literature is rooted in a system- change perspective. It emphasises the need to re-configure or re-organize the entire system and its interdependent components (i.e., economic, political, cultural, technological, power relations, consumption and production), rather than focussing on a single sub-domain or a sector. Transformative change is regarded as a non-linear, complex, and emergent process that is hard to predict and manage. As such, action for transformative change is considered more as an ‘evolutionary search process’, rather than purposeful design. This includes characteristics such as a lack of a system perspective and lack of ability to connect to diverse values or give space to societal dialogue. While papers covered a range of different countries, governance regimes, and scales, papers within this cluster see the (for their context) dominant governance regime as leading to solutions that are ineffective in the long run, only leading to incremental change and strengthening the status quo. In some documents, rigidly top-down governance was considered conducive to detrimental path dependency and leading to issues such as: lack of inclusiveness and participation (e.g. democratically developed coherent visions and strategies for development); policy incoherence, ineffectiveness and lack of normativity (e.g. perverse incentives or too short-term investments into sustainable alternatives); deregulation trends and failure of markets and financial systems; disconnect between production and consumption, and between local practices and global commitments; need for knowledge (e.g. evidence on transformative change and investments effectiveness, traditional local knowledge). The values embedded in dominant policy processes were seen as problematic, such as the focus on a growth-paradigm and inability to challenge vested interests and injustices. Transformative change is disabled by the co-option (i.e., appropriation or ‘hijacking’) of processes of change towards business as usual, as well as vested interests that are served by keeping the system in its current state. Here, in- effective policy integration and a focus on tech-fixes are mentioned as perpetuating unsustainability.

Another mentioned disabler in governance was the limited suitability of monitoring frameworks. Solution space and enablers of change The required transformative change is described to emerge out of alternative governance paradigms, which especially emphasize the characteristics these new modes of governances should build on. These included an integrated systems-approach (i.e., taking the interconnections between diverse ongoing transition processes into account, for example in food and energy); adaptivity and reflexivity rather than reactivity; accountability and transparency; and inclusiveness and participation (decentralization, stewardship, pluralism). Nature-positive goals and values were also mentioned as a feature of new governance modes, in opposition to mere technological change. In this context, change is enabled for example by changes in the way knowledge and evidence is generated and made available to societal actors (interdisciplinary, transdisciplinary, co-creative), as well as more cross- sectoral collaboration, new business models and social/technical innovations (e.g., agroecology, biomass recycling), policy reforms and integration, changes in values and behaviours (e.g., food consumption). This cluster sees governance as a key problem, but it also sees solutions in directing it to different modes and strengthening somewhat existing factors – rather than overhauling the foundations that it builds on. For example, by having private sector and wealthy nations take more responsibility for change or by making governance more science-based and inclusive through more knowledge co- production in governance. Enablers of transformative change included for instance the knowledge sector (scientists, educators, skilled workforce), the public sector (policy makers, public procurement), [Page 21] 18 private entities (farmers, landowners, suppliers, CSOs and NGOs, citizens, local and indigenous communities) and multilateral arenas. Notable Throughout this cluster, the differences of opinion when it comes to the role of incremental change is notable: Some see incremental change as obstructive to transformative change and possibly even reinforcing existing power relations, while others see incremental change in an adaptive context – allowing to make small adjustments based on real-time information. Here, transformative change is regarding as a learning process where reflexivity is vital.

Cross-cluster analysis and discussion on transformative change The literature collected with the search string proved disparate in terms of their scientific grounding, analytical approaches to transformative change, and focal topics. Within them, transformative change as a broad concept was widely acknowledged and appeared to be used in a rather generic fashion. In fact, the notion of transformative change seemed to be applied in a rather fluid sense: travelling effectively across the diverse groups of papers, differently applied each time, making visible different modes of analytical anchoring. While a structure based on the ‘nexus elements’ did not provide a feasible approach to making sense of the literature, an approach using ‘anchoring-types’ in diverse socio-material contexts did allow us to reflect on the research questions. This section looks across the different clusters and aims to glean insights from their conceptualisation of the concept, their perspective to enablers and disablers of change, their connection to the biodiversity nexus and justice. Here, we highlight elements that the clusters have in common, but also underscore how these clusters differ from one another. Table 6 shows a summary of the analysis results of all clusters. Lack of concreteness as to what fundamental change results in Fundamental change is often emphasised as key within the clusters. However, many clusters are unable (or perhaps unwilling) to explicitly describe what fundamental change entails (i.e., concrete ideas of what fundamental change might look like). This lack of concreteness, which is also rooted in [Page 35] 32 a poor agreement over what are the fundamental causes of unsustainability, brings about two challenges. One, it obscures the interpretation of ‘fundamental’ change and the extent to which it reorganizes the system. In some cases, the need to overhaul the foundation of our society is explicitly mentioned, such as the need to enable structural changes in governance or economic systems. In this regard, the social practices cluster mentions degrowth, while the human-nature relations cluster advocates for enhancing human-nature connectedness. The governance cluster envisions opportunities in establishing coalitions among diverse stakeholders to foster a new shared ideology in governance approaches to enable future possibilities. Whereas in other cases, the extent of change is much narrower. For example, within the social functions cluster, a suggestion was made to explore alternative sources of protein, such as pulse ingredients, that provide nutrition and are sustainable to produce and process. Especially a ‘narrower’ interpretation is prone to under-theorisation of transformative change and thus unable to provide a coherent analytical insight into phenomena they might label as potentially transformative. Second, as already mentioned above, omitting a concrete vision or description of what transformation entails, enables a greenwashing and co-option of transformative change (i.e., the process by which powerful actors incorporate elements of ‘transformative change’ to serve their interests and/or maintain the status quo). Solely describing the change we envision as ‘sustainable’ and ‘just’, does not describe what pathways of solutions are part of that form of sustainability and justice – meaning it is unclear for whom that might be sustainable (Leach et al. 2010). To address this ambiguity, directionality (i.e., deliberate and purposeful orientation of change processes) is key. Enabling directionality requires setting clear goals that provide a sense of clarity and thus cannot be co-opted.

Somewhat paradoxically, these normative pleas for a wholesale change in our mindsets remain quite inconsequential as the proposed solutions— environmental education and information via news and social media—are very conventional and not likely to respond to the urgent need for reorganizing socio-technical systems in a more sustainable way. In a similar way, the papers that emphasize degrowth provide relatively few concrete suggestions on how to achieve transformative change, limiting themselves to suggestions like eco- communalism and time-banking. Box 1. An overview of the conceptualisation of ‘justice’ in just transition and social justice literature Processes of change (be it ‘sustainable development’ or ‘transformation’) involve both winners and losers. Acknowledgement of this has resulted in popularisation of research on social justice and more recently just transitions (Leach et al. 2010) and even the use of the concept in policy contexts and societal discussions (Heffron and McCauley 2018). Literature on justice emphasizes the multi- dimensional nature of justice, crossing and influenced by multiple dynamics – such as economic, political, cultural, etc. Scholars have developed a multi-dimensional framework to make sense of this multi-dimensional concept. Although the focus or choice of dimensions differs across the literature, commonly mentioned dimensions are distributive justice, recognition justice, restorative justice, procedural justice, environmental justice, and cosmopolitan justice (Kaljonen et al. 2023). Most commonly used across justice-related literature are the dimensions of distributive, recognition, and procedural justice. Here, distributive justice is conceptualised as the fair distribution of burdens and benefits, as well as the allocation of opportunities and material goods, such a natural resources, income, and wealth (Menton et al. 2020). Recognition justice refers to the recognition of and respect for different individuals and collective identities, including their specific values, knowledge, practices, needs and liveliho ods (Fraser 2008). Procedural justice describes participatory fairness within political and societal decision-making processes, with specific focus on the fairness and transparency of procedures (Schlosberg 2007).

Overcoming human-centred perspectives to change Understandings of change generally build on a human-centred (or anthropocentric) perspective, in the sense that places human agency, interests, or needs at the centre of transformative change. This has a strong influence of the direction and scope of efforts of transformative change, especially when it comes to the interconnectedness between humans and nature. While nature and biodiversity are often regarded as an important element of the system, they are rarely seen as an active agent. As such, transformative change often is of influence on nature and biodiversity, impacting the status of or the way processes unfold. For example, market-based conservation approaches that centre around tourism (Fiasco and Massarella 2022). Although all clusters, except for the infrastructure cluster, cited a shift in values towards non-anthropocentric values as a solution or vision for transformative change, the consideration of nature and biodiversity as equally crucial components of transformative change, enabling change through them, is less prevalent.
