text: in biodiversity nexus cases by studying interventions, processes, and outcomes. Interventions were deﬁned as speciﬁc actions implemented that catalyse change through intermediary processes; they were categorized as society-related (e.g., governance, equity, gender) and nexus-related (actions across the biodiversity, water, climate, etc., sectors). The society-related interventions consisted of social, governance, economy, equity, gender, and relational actions, representing the principal areas for achieving transformative change (Díaz et al., 2019; Visseren-Hamakers et al., 2021; O’Brien et al., 2025), while the nexus-related interventions included actions in the biodiversity, water, climate, food, energy, transport and health sectors, recognised as the interplay critical for sustainability (Kim et al., 2024; McElwee et al., 2025). Outcomes represented the transformative impacts for society and the biodiversity nexus, conceptualized equivalently as society-related and nexus-related positive impacts. Processes were conceptualized as the central connection mediating non-linear interactions and transformative change between interventions and outcomes, often tackling indirect drivers or root causes of the current crises. To operationalise the analysis of processes, the 12 leverage points framework (Meadows, 1999; 2008; Abson et. al., 2017) was applied as summarized in table 1. This framework served as a diagnostic tool to deconstruct the case-study processes, analyzing complex systems across a spectrum from the shallowest levels (parameters and feedbacks) to the deepest levels (system design and intent). 2.2 Selection of case studies The selection process utilised existing case study repositories including Biodiversity Information System for Europe (https://biodiversity.europa.eu), Panorama Solutions (https://panorama.solutions), ClimateADAPT (https://climate-adapt.eea.europa.eu), Oppla (https://oppla.eu), and the Naturvation - Urban Nature Atlas (https://una.city). A two-tier screening process was employed to assess a case study’s transformative potential by investigating its nexus and societal dimensions. 7 [Page 8] In the ﬁrst-tier screening , case studies had to meet outcomes showing positive impacts on three or more nexus elements (biodiversity, water, climate, food, energy, transport and health) AND objectives related to cross-cutting societal beneﬁts. This stage narrowed the selection down to 500 case studies from an initial review of over 7,000. In the second-tier screening , each case was evaluated against its commitment to at least one of three critical transformative principles (IPBES, 2019; O’Brien et al., 2025; Pascual et al., 2023): (a) pluralism and inclusion (e.g., multi-stakeholder engagement), (b) clear evidence of equity and justice considerations, and/or (c) explicit attention to gender dynamics. Cases were also screened for clear signs of transformative changes in structural arrangements or dominant worldviews.

text: (IPBES, 2019; O’Brien et al., 2025; Pascual et al., 2023): (a) pluralism and inclusion (e.g., multi-stakeholder engagement), (b) clear evidence of equity and justice considerations, and/or (c) explicit attention to gender dynamics. Cases were also screened for clear signs of transformative changes in structural arrangements or dominant worldviews. In the ﬁnal step, cases outside the European context were systematically excluded. This process ﬁltered the sample to 31 case studies deemed to have genuine transformative potential. 2.3 Coding Following the analytical framework, the coding concentrated on the three key aspects: interventions, processes, and outcomes . Supporting qualitative and categorical ﬁelds were also included, such as case identiﬁers and stakeholder characteristics. An iterative coding process was carried out by three coders, involving test coding and benchmarking to establish clear instructions and a ﬁnal codebook. Interventions and outcomes were coded in relation to the nexus-related and society-related elements they addressed or affected. Processes were speciﬁcally coded in relation to the 12 leverage points. The coded data generated were both binary (indicating presence or absence of attributes, used for archetype analysis) and qualitative (providing richer details). 2.4 Archetype analysis The analysis aimed to deﬁne archetypes of transformation mechanisms —recurrent patterns of interventions, processes, and outcomes at an intermediate level of abstraction (Oberlack et al., 2019; Eisenack et al., 2021) that explain transformative outcomes under speciﬁc conditions. Due to the process-oriented conceptualisation of the cases, a process-centered meta-analysis combined with Formal Concept Analysis (FCA) was applied to identify recurrent patterns (Ganter et al., 2005; Villamayor-Tomas et al., 2020; Oberlack, 2016; Oberlack and Eisenack, 2018; Harmáčková et al., 2025) utilizing the coded data of interventions, processes and outcomes. Each resulting recurrent pattern (archetype) comprised two processes and a set of interventions, covering 30 of the 31 case studies. The archetype analysis facilitated the development of these recurrent patterns, the identiﬁcation of the subset of cases associated with each, and the building of meaningful qualitative descriptions. While two overarching processes deﬁned the main features and characteristics of each archetype, the speciﬁc conﬁguration of interventions clariﬁed the types of actions driving those processes, and therefore, the underlying transformative mechanisms observed in the case studies. 8 [Page 9] 3 Archetypes of transformative change mechanisms The analysis resulted in a single optimal suite of four archetypes (N=4) representing transformative mechanisms, each comprising two processes that were coded as equivalent to the leverage points (attribute richness 𝜌 =2) and with a coverage of 30 case studies (nu=30) out of the 31 selected.

Further analysis of the patterns of interventions underlying the processes within each archetype (Figure 2) revealed that ﬁve out of thirteen intervention types were found in all the cases, namely the nexus-related Biodiversity, Water, Climate actions, and the society-related Society and Governance actions. These were therefore considered necessary conditions, like the always-present processes described above. The other eight intervention types were analyzed through FCA and constituted 10 different recurring patterns, structured in pairs of interventions. Figure 2. Flowchart of analyzed interventions and processes (12 leverage points) feeding into archetypes of transformative mechanisms. 10 [Page 11] These patterns allowed us to identify the presence of and synergies between types of interventions that co-occur with different processes, forming speciﬁc archetypes that are described in more detail below. To showcase context-speciﬁc examples, Appendix A covers an example of the “Steering deep societal change” archetype and its manifestation in the case of “The Garden Factory, Netherlands” (NL1). Building co-governance: redistributing power and enhancing nature stewardship This archetype is typical for initiatives where the main trigger of change is the modiﬁcation or establishment of new top-down rules. Often, new policy tools, frameworks and regulations are coupled with new modes of governance, where stakeholders' involvement is key, therefore reorganising social structures, establishing new relationships and re-distributing power in terms of decision-making and agency over the commons. The sense of ownership, responsibility and stewardship are central to these co-governance models and are promoted through top-down rules, with positive outcomes for nature and people. Frequently, the cases covered by this archetype describe a local government that changes rules and opens its structure to scale the change, allowing for broader collaboration with local actors, private and public entities, including interinstitutional and intersectoral collaboration.

Frequently, the cases covered by this archetype describe a local government that changes rules and opens its structure to scale the change, allowing for broader collaboration with local actors, private and public entities, including interinstitutional and intersectoral collaboration. The typical actions throughout the archetype include introducing policies and guidelines, establishing social networks, starting social enterprises around nature-based solutions, and spurring cross-sectoral collaborations, among others. These align with a dominant focus on interventions through Economic factors with eminent equity and inclusion aspects, Relational values, and a strong orientation towards the Food and Energy sectors. For instance, in the Portuguese case (PT1), the Lisbon city administration developed a Master Development Plan to regenerate the city through ecological restoration and sustainable urbanization, thus implementing nature-based solutions while tackling social challenges. In the Hungarian case (HU1), on the other hand, a wide array of stakeholders was considered in the planning and implementation of a ﬂoodplain farming community, redesigning and restoring the Great Plains ecosystem to develop a more sustainable and resilient land use, while combatting droughts that threatened livelihoods of local farmers. It hence relies on multi-stakeholder participation to create social learning and knowledge exchange as a driver of change. This archetype is similar to the previous one “Building co-governance” in the sense that both establish new rules, policies and regulations to nest system change under a top-down scheme. Here, however, the new rules do not focus on changing the social structures and re-distributing governance agency, but on promoting information structures and ﬂows, including the access to and exchange of information and practices. The widely spread actions behind this archetype are, for example, awareness and educational events, training and capacity building programs, hands-on initiatives, or hubs, that aim to create a collaborative environment and maximise human capacities and resources for innovations in social-ecological practices. These correlate with the archetype’s most typical interventions through Economy, Equity and Relational values that are also connected to the Food, Health and Energy sectors of the biodiversity nexus.

It emphasizes the shifting understandings, norms, behaviours, values, mindsets, or paradigms. Similarly to the previous archetype, “Cultivating social capital”, this archetype also focuses on communication ﬂows and engagement structures. However, the key difference lies in its focus on bottom-up intra-personal and inter-personal change, building on a sense of belonging, place attachment, and nature connectedness to foster positive human-nature relationships. Consequently, this archetype is characterized by processes and actions that aim for deeper, transformative social change. Typical activities include communication platforms or campaigns designed for education and awareness-raising, as well as public and stakeholder engagement. The overreaching goal is to mobilize local communities and create momentum for change. Stakeholders are considered both as target groups and drivers of change, hence frequently contributing to shaping and inﬂuencing the project design and implementation, ensuring that diverse 13 [Page 14] societal needs are recognized and addressed. This archetype particularly focuses on promoting actions around social equity and justice through the inclusion of underrepresented and vulnerable groups, as well as promoting gender equity.

Furthermore, the pairs where Economy is present typically exhibit high rates of co-occurrence within the interventions themselves (for example, an intervention where ﬁnancial incentives trigger consumption patterns change). This suggests that there is synergy or necessity between economic change and change in other elements or structures. Conversely, the association Economy-Relational values exhibits rather low co-occurrence rates, which may raise questions as to why this particular pair does not typically come together within one intervention and whether there are possibilities for connections. Also, we can see that 16 [Page 17] Relational Values appear twice as related to Equity, which may indicate some synergies yet to be explored. On the other hand, even when Biodiversity, Water, Climate, Social and Governance-related interventions are present in all the cases, there are differences across the archetypes. For instance, archetypes “Building co-governance” and “Steering deep societal change” are more oriented towards urban greening and green infrastructure, while archetype “Adaptive change” tends towards ecosystem restoration and archetype “Cultivating social capital” exhibits both tendencies. Other signiﬁcant differences can be appreciated when analysing, for example, the Economy angle of the archetypes, where archetypes “Building co-governance” and “Steering deep societal change” are more inclined towards the entanglement of Economy and Equity, while archetype “Adaptive change” deals more with relational economy, and archetype “Cultivating social capital” exhibits a dominant merely economic pattern. The interventions that most repeated for all the archetypes were: stakeholder involvement, co-production approach/processes, interventions towards social justice, urban greening, ecosystem restoration, aquatic ecosystem restoration, measures for climate adaptation, energy saving. The Economy, Food and Relational values interventions, even when exhibiting an important presence across cases and archetypes, nonetheless, did not exhibit very repetitive interventions, hence illustrating the plurality of the cases as well as traits of the archetypes. Conclusions The investigation into transformative change within the Biodiversity nexus identiﬁed four complementary and non-exclusive mechanisms, which serve as guidance for fostering change in interlinked social-ecological systems. These include ‘Building co-governance’ , ‘Cultivating social capital’ , ‘Steering deep societal change’ , and ‘Adaptive change’ .

title: Deliverable D3.3 — section 13 of 16
text: The investigation into transformative change within the Biodiversity nexus identiﬁed four complementary and non-exclusive mechanisms, which serve as guidance for fostering change in interlinked social-ecological systems. These include ‘Building co-governance’ , ‘Cultivating social capital’ , ‘Steering deep societal change’ , and ‘Adaptive change’ . Among these, ‘Steering deep societal change’ was revealed as the most prevalent and often self-standing mechanism, operating by reshaping deep-seated social values, norms, and paradigms, and fostering human-nature relationships via community-driven, learning-oriented approaches. This prominence underscores the importance of transforming fundamental societal beliefs and tackling underlying root causes and drivers of social challenges, placing emphasis on equity and gender perspectives as essential components of deep change (O’Brien et al., 2025; Barragan-Jason et al., 2021; West et al., 2020; IPBES, 2019). The mechanisms often display synergistic interactions , highlighting the importance of collective agency and mutually reinforcing actions for sustained transformation. For instance, ‘Cultivating social capital’ and ‘Building co-governance’ are frequently observed to co-occur across cases, both stressing a systemic, top-down perspective on restructuring institutional and governance arrangements through structural and procedural transformations. ‘Cultivating social capital’ resonates with calls for meaningful community and multi-actor engagement to mobilize diverse knowledge and sow the undergrowth for lasting transformations (Tuckey et al., 2023; Visseren-Hamakers et al., 2021; Valve et al., 2025; Gurung et al., 2025). ‘Building co-governance’ actively creates or reshapes institutionalized structures by emphasizing shared responsibility, power redistribution, and policy innovation. Systemic transformations require both the restructuring of governance modes and decentralization, involving civil society and local communities as local stewards, which also helps to promote justice, equity, 17 [Page 18] and nurture reciprocal human–nature relationships (O’Brien et al., 2025; Gurung et al., 2025; de Castro et al., 2025; Buijs et al., 2024; Diver et al., 2024). Ultimately, these archetypal mechanisms are intended to be of practical use , which was also explored in Bionext Workshop 3 with stakeholders. They provide useful guidelines or 'building blocks' for policymakers seeking to optimize policies across sectors (nexus) and for practitioners designing new projects. By illustrating how transformations unfold and operate at various levels and scales, these mechanisms offer an empirical foundation for embedding transformative actions and processes into new initiatives.

Introduction The BIONEXT consortium has an extensive past and current engagement with the Intergovernmental Science-Policy Platform on Biodiversity and Ecosystem Services (IPBES) assessments, task forces and technical support units. In the methodological approach of the project, Work Package 4 (WP4) has the role of synthesising knowledge generated in the project and promoting science brokerage for IPBES assessments. This function is reflected in Task 4.1 ‘Delivering information in the IPBES rolling programme of work up to 2030’, which is composed of Subtask 4.1.1 ‘Establishing collaboration with IPBES bodies’ (linked to Milestone 4.1 and submitted in February 2023) and Subtask 4.1.2 ‘Knowledge for IPBES’ (linked to Milestone 4.2, submitted in February 2024; and Deliverable 4.1, described in this report). The IPBES rolling work programme up to 2030 includes the following assessments:  Thematic assessment of the interlinkages among biodiversity, water, food and health (Nexus assessment)  Thematic assessment of the underlying causes of biodiversity loss and the determinants of transformative change and options for achieving the 2050 Vision for Biodiversity (Transformative change assessment)  Business and biodiversity (methodological assessment)  Second global assessment  Monitoring biodiversity and nature’s contributions to people (Monitoring assessment)  Integrated biodiversity-inclusive spatial planning and ecological connectivity (Spatial planning assessment) The BIONEXT project primarily intended to make direct contributions to the Nexus and the Transformative Change assessments, but both are already concluded and were approved at IPBES 11 in December 2024. Therefore, in this deliverable we also refer to potential contributions to the other assessments in the IPBES rolling work programme, which are already in progress or plan to be started this year. Deliverable 4.1 ‘Documents and databases for IPBES assessments’ is based on Milestone 4.2 ‘Draft reports and database developed’, which presented a preliminary version together with a database used to gather the project outcomes from the BIONEXT partners.

BIONEXT outcomes by thematic outlines of IPBES assessments The thematic outlines of IPBES assessments were summarised in nine categories: IPBES Conceptual Framework, transformative change and pathways, nexus interlinkages, scenarios and models, justice, knowledge systems and plurality, options for action, biodiversity monitoring, and capacity building. 4.1 IPBES Conceptual Framework The six elements of the IPBES Conceptual Framework are embedded in multiple BIONEXT outcomes that can represent opportunities for improvement of the framework and its implementation. 1. ‘Nature’ is considered as the biodiversity nexus element and is present in all outcomes. Additionally, more-than-human, sentient and non-sentient nature, or the non-human world are explicitly included in the transformative change framework (WP2) and in the quality-of-life framework (WP1) 2. ‘Anthropogenic assets’ such as built infrastructure, technology and financial assets are part of the SSP scenarios and NFF pathway narratives, co-created in WP1 and WP2, and as indirect drivers in the Nexus Modelling Framework (see section 4.4.2), 3. ‘Nature’s contributions to people’ are considered in the outputs of the land use models (IAP2 and CRAFTY-Europe) of the Nexus Modelling Framework. They are also used as inputs to model quality of life (see section 4.4) 4. ‘Institutions and governance systems and other indirect drivers’ are also considered in the co- created narratives (WP1, WP2). In particular, the NFF pathway narratives use this framework element for the co-creation of actions for change. In addition, policy actions will be co-created and tailored by quality-of-life simulations, transformative change archetypes and justice considerations (WP1, WP2, WP3, WP4) 5. ‘Direct drivers’ include the co-created transformative NFF pathway actions (WP2), and land use changes and climate change scenarios in the Nexus Modelling Framework (see section 4.4.2) 6.

(in review)  Milestones and deliverables in section 4.4.2 4.2 Transformative change and pathways Transformative change (TC) is a core component of BIONEXT. WP2 and WP3 are the responsible to analyse existing knowledge and co-create pathways with stakeholders. In turn, WP4 is in charge of synthesising the findings and transform them into policy actions to facilitate transformative change. Rather than make a new framework, WP2 created a 'lay of the land' or understanding of what different perspectives there are to TC - i.e. how is TC as a definition utilised by different groups and what does that say about their theory of change. The associated deliverable (D2.1) describes different ‘anchoring types’ present in the literature and how they view transformative change. As a consequence of this work, there is a bibliographic database that shows how WP2 categorised the different papers. [Page 11] 11 Key options for transformative change and their scaling potential are presented in an academic paper setting out 7 'intervention modes' to centring nature into everyday practices. These modes were distilled from 'bottom-up' cases across Europe to identify/illustrate the diverse emergent ways of going about biodiversity governance. This work is going to be derived into a policy brief (PB2). The transition pathways in the biodiversity nexus is presented in Deliverable 2.3 (changed to a scientific paper). This work will present the transition pathways that were co-created with stakeholders following the Nature Futures Framework (NFF), consequently, BIONEXT has a ‘Nature as Culture’, a ‘Nature for Nature’, and a ‘Nature for Society’ pathway. The pathways emphasise a number of key themes that they have in common (specifically societal dynamics that are not necessarily captured by the nexus) and will analyse these by emphasizing opportunities, pitfalls, theories of change, and justice implications. This paper presents the analysis of interventions, processes, and outcomes in 31 diverse biodiversity-nexus cases across Europe, applying the lens of nexus- and transformative change thinking. Subsequently, using the Formal Concept Analysis method, an archetype analysis was conducted to identify recurrent patterns of transformative mechanisms. The analysis identifies four distinct archetypes. It also clarifies which processes and interventions underlie these mechanisms. The identified archetypes can serve as guidance for policymakers designing policies to achieve transformative outcomes across multiple sectors of the biodiversity nexus, as well as for practitioners establishing new projects. In addition to the work described above, a paper on transformative governance was published (Korhonen- Kurki et al., 2025) . In this contribution, five environmental governance approaches were assessed: adaptive, earth system, evolutionary, transformative and transition governance. The elements under assessment were: characteristics of the different governance approaches, understanding of dynamics of change, and conceptualisation of the role of law. According to the literature review conducted, collaboration, leadership, learning, plurality, empowering, innovation and vision are seen as key mechanisms for change, while law is often oversimplified in these governance approaches, either as an enabler of or as a barrier to change towards sustainability. It provides a quantification of the biodiversity nexus interlinkages and supports the assessment of synergies and trade-offs between the NFF pathways. 4.4.1 Narratives and scenarios BIONEXT will produce three sets of narratives, which were co-created with stakeholders in three workshops (in Santorini, Greece; Schoorl, the Netherlands; and Teplice, Czech Republic) and a number of complementary webinars. Below, there is a synthesis of the narratives. Enriched SSP narratives . In enriched European-SSP1, the world shifts away from a market-driven economy towards moderate but steady economic growth for sustainable development. There is higher political stability and lower inequality with strongly regulated multi-level governance. Biodiversity improves due to nature restoration, mainstreaming into policy and changing human-nature relations. In enriched European-SSP3, economic woes in major economies and regional conflict fragments the EU and leads to high inequality within and between EU countries. Increasing border controls and barriers to trade result in rising energy and food prices and increasing demand for natural resources within national borders, causing severe ecosystem failures. Public spending on the military significantly increases with high carbon emissions and decreased living standards.

Biodiversity has mixed outcomes due to diverse country responses to geopolitical fragmentation and changing resource demands. In enriched European- SSP4, the world shifts strongly towards innovation leading to a high-tech green Europe with strong partnerships between business and European governments. Power is concentrated in small political and economic elites with growing inequality within and between the European countries with low quality of life. Biodiversity has mixed impacts from technology development, until inequality worsens biodiversity and counter movements return to nature. Finally, in enriched European-SSP5, the world has faith in competitive markets and innovation as a path to development. The push for economic, technological and social development is coupled with the exploitation of cheap and readily available fossil fuel resources and a lack of environmental concern. Significant investments are made in health, education, and social support with society leading high consumption lifestyles. Biodiversity declines and collapses due to uncontrolled economic development and resource extraction/use. NFF visions. In Vision 1: Dough Nadair: The way of nature (nature as culture value perspective), European society has a more pluralistic, balanced and reciprocal relationship with nature. People are guided by core principles of care and contemplation, and mainstream culture has a deeper spiritual connection with the natural world. Ecosystems are flourishing with diverse culturally embedded landscapes across Europe where human and natural processes are intertwined. In Vision 2: NaturAll (nature for nature value perspective), The importance of respecting nature for itself and giving space to natural ecological processes is highly valued among European society in 2050. Society is ecologically literate and adapts its activities to the dynamics of nature. Most people live in compact, self-sufficient cities and have lifestyles with low impact on the environment. In Vision 3: Return to nature (nature for society value perspective), European society has achieved a more balanced future for nature and people. Europe focuses on meeting the needs of nature and people with technological solutions, reduced consumption, and more highly valued biodiversity and water. NFF pathways. Under development. Scientific papers are being produced for these narratives. 4.4.2 Models The Nexus Modelling Framework is composed of three models. Europe in the models is considered as EU27 plus Norway, Switzerland and the UK. In addition to the SSP scenario and NFF pathways, models use climate scenarios (Representative Concentration Pathways, RCP). SSPs are combined with RCPs as follows: SSP1-RCP2.6, SSP3-RCP7.0 (CRAFTY-Europe) and SSP3-RCP8.5 (IAP2/JUNIPER), SSP4-RCP4.5 and SSP5-RCP8.5. All NFF pathways are combined with RCP4.5. IAP2. The IMPRESSIONS Integrated Assessment Platform (IAP2) is an extension of the CLIMSAVE Integrated Assessment Platform. They integrate a suite of ten sectoral models representing agriculture, forestry, biodiversity, water resources, fluvial and coastal flooding and urban development within a web- based platform. To facilitate the cross-sectoral model linkages and to reduce model run-time, a meta- modelling approach was used whereby computationally efficient models that emulate the performance of more complex models were developed. Two versions of IAP2 exist for Europe operating at a spatial resolution of 10 arcmin x 10 arcmin (approximately 16km x 16km) and for Scotland operating at a spatial resolution of 5km x 5km. The model produces outputs of both sector-based impact and vulnerability indicators and ecosystem services in order to link climate change impacts directly to human well-being. IAP2 outputs are European maps at 10'x10' resolution for time periods from 2010 to 2100, grouped as sectoral indicators (tourism, urban, water, floods, habitat/land cover, agriculture, forestry and biodiversity) and as ecosystem service indicators (cultural, regulating and provisioning). There are no explicit output graphs, but they can be created using the row data exported by the software. LandSyMM/CRAFTY-Europe. CRAFTY is a large-scale agent-based modelling (ABM) framework for the simulation of land use change. It is designed to allow efficient but powerful simulation of a wide range of land uses across large geographical extents, based on the decision-making of simulated land managers who generate a variety of ecosystem services. It is fully open-source and can be used without the need for any programming. CRAFTY has been applied in Europe, Sweden, Brazil, Great Britain, Scotland, and there are works in progress for its application in Germany, at global Scale, and the updated European application used in BIONEXT and other Horizon Europe projects.

CRAFTY has been applied in Europe, Sweden, Brazil, Great Britain, Scotland, and there are works in progress for its application in Germany, at global Scale, and the updated European application used in BIONEXT and other Horizon Europe projects. The model simulates the provision of a range of ecosystem services (regulating, material and non-material), and is linked to the global LandSyMM model to account for global effects including trade of food commodities. Recently, modelling extensions of CRAFTY have been developed such as LANDS-QoL to estimate quality of life (see below). In BIONEXT, the outputs of CRAFTY-Europe are analysed with emphasises on the biodiversity nexus and quality of life. CRAFTY-Europe outputs are represented as 1km grid maps showing 30 categories of land uses and 25 services (or nature’s contributions to people), for the baseline in 2020 and the target time slice 2085. Outputs also consist on large datasets of trends from 2020 to 2085 (also available up to 2100) of land uses and services, as well as Sankey diagrams of land use transitions from 2020 to 2085. LANDS-QoL is a conceptual framework and modelling approach to estimate the potential provision of human-nature quality of life (QoL) within land systems. LANDS-QoL uses nature’s contributions to people and socio-economic indicators—both linked to land use models—to spatially represent quality of life for humans and non-humans across the dimensions of material, health, social relations, security, freedom and justice & equity. The modelling approach is based on the IPBES conceptual framework, the Millennium Ecosystems Assessment and the Life Framework of Values and has been successfully applied in Great Britain, demonstrating its suitability for large spatial extents and highlighting the value of rural [Page 15] 15 areas. In BIONEXT, quality of life is modelled for Europe using CRAFTY-Europe as land use model and, therefore, the spatio-temporal simulations will be also available under the BIONEXT RCP-SSP scenarios and NFF pathways. JUNIPER is a system dynamics-based modelling framework developed to assess sustainability trade-offs across interconnected sectors such as water, energy, food, transportation, health, biodiversity, and climate. Built in STELLA Architect, it enables dynamic scenario simulations that capture environmental pressures, resource flows, and socio-economic feedbacks. The model was first developed for Greece and subsequently extended to five additional national versions—UK, Finland, Spain, Poland, and Czech Republic—reflecting diverse environmental and policy contexts. In parallel, a European-level version of JUNIPER has been developed to support integrated sustainability planning at a regional scale.

In parallel, a European-level version of JUNIPER has been developed to support integrated sustainability planning at a regional scale. By incorporating sectors like transportation and health into nexus analysis, JUNIPER provides a more comprehensive understanding of systemic interdependencies, enabling researchers and policymakers to explore synergies and manage trade-offs in complex sustainability systems. JUNIPER is being developed specifically for BIONEXT and its outputs are presented as graphs that show trends from 2000 to 2100 in water exploitation, agricultural production and emissions, energy production, GHG emissions, air pollution, Red List Index, transport activity, and life expectancy, under different scenario assumptions. It demonstrates the reasons for biodiversity loss and makes visible how biodiversity underpins every aspect of life; the water we drink, the food we eat, the health we have and much more. It focuses on the nexus meaning the connections, links and interdependences between biodiversity, water, food, energy, transport, climate and health. The project creates and offers science-based solutions and tools for halting biodiversity loss and achieving sustainable, nature-centered future and societies where biodiversity is a part of everyday choices and policymaking. The project creates new knowledge and science-based solutions on sustainable futures, for example, to the Intergovernmental Science-Policy Platform on Biodiversity and Ecosystem Services (IPBES), EU policymakers and civil society. BIONEXT brings together science and scientists from different fields and creates a network of scientists who are ambitious to create practical and effective solutions for halting biodiversity loss. The project demonstrates how biodiversity underpins every aspect of life through the nexus elements of water, food, climate, health, energy, and transport. BIONEXT’s goal is to mainstream biodiversity into policymaking and provide concrete options on how to initiate, accelerate, and upscale biodiversity-relevant transformative change in society. Task 5.2 Evaluation of Knowledge Integration Task 5.2, Evaluation of Knowledge Integration, was designed to assess and strengthen knowledge integration processes across the BIONEXT project, recognizing that transformative sustainability challenges require continuous interaction between disciplines, sectors, stakeholders and modelling approaches . Building initially on the NEOH (Network for Ecohealth and One Health) evaluation framework (EVOLvINC; Hitziger et al. 2019), the task evolved towards a more context - specific and participatory approach that better reflected the dynamic and transdisciplinary nature of BIONEXT. Rather than applying a predefined evaluation framework, the consortium chose to co- develop reflexive methods that could capture the project's emerging complexity, support learning among partners, and facilitate continuous reflection on integration processes throughout the project.

Rather than applying a predefined evaluation framework, the consortium chose to co- develop reflexive methods that could capture the project's emerging complexity, support learning among partners, and facilitate continuous reflection on integration processes throughout the project. To achieve this objective, a Reflexivity Task Force (RTF) was established in the second half of 2023, bringing together representatives from most BIONEXT partners. The RTF met regularly throughout the project and served as a collaborative platform for deve loping and implementing innovative approaches to evaluate knowledge integration. The work focused not only on understanding how knowledge integration occurred within BIONEXT, but also on generating practical tools, methods and insights that could support f uture transdisciplinary sustainability initiatives. The origination and functionality of the RTF is described in a dedicated scientific publication (Chapter 1). Description of Work The evaluation of knowledge integration was structured around three complementary strands of reflexive inquiry: researcher reflexivity, stakeholder reflexivity, and reflexive One Health Nexus modelling. Together, these activities examined knowledge generation, integration, communication and application across and beyond the BIONEXT project. Researcher reflexivity focused on understanding how BIONEXT researchers experienced collaboration and knowledge integration within a complex transdisciplinary project. A series of semi-structured interviews was developed and conducted by pairs of RTF members. Eleven interviews were completed and subsequently analysed through a systematic coding process. Preliminary findings were discussed during consortium meetings and informed the development of a draft analytical framework. Building on these insights, the team developed a Knowledge Integration Reflexivity Framework (KIRF) which was discussed with interviewees. To make these insights more practically applicable for dialogue and application, the RTF developed Knowledge Integration Reflexivity Cards (KIRC) , as a tool intended to stimulate reflection and learning in sustainability-oriented research projects and potentially other contexts. The tool was piloted within WP5, tested during the Prague consortium meeting, and further evaluated at an EU Transformative Change Cluster meeting. Lessons learned from these applications were incorporated into a refined version of the tool, alongside preparations for scientific publications and open -access [Page 5] dissemination. The development of both KIRF and KIRC are described in a dedicated scientific publication (Chapter 2). Stakeholder reflexivity explored stakeholder perspectives on knowledge integration and collaborative processes within BIONEXT.

Reflexive One Health Nexus Modelling examined how a One Health perspective could be meaningfully integrated into BIONEXT's modelling and sustainability assessments. This interest was inspired by 1) the legacy of NEOH and the experience with evaluation of knowledge integration, and 2) One Hea lth being a promising but relatively new frontier in nexus thinking, as became apparent in the course of the development of the IPBES Nexus Assessment (IPBES 2024; McFarlane et al. 2024), resulting in vast knowledge integration challenges. Initial work focused on identifying relevant One Health dimensions and indicators across human, animal, plant, ecosystem and integrated health domains. This evolved into a two -round Delphi consultation involving an international panel of One Health experts. The consultation addressed the challenge of embedding One Health considerations within nexus modelling approaches and generated extensive expert insights regarding requirements, opportunities and barriers for integrating health dimensions into sustainability transformation pathways. In addition a dedicated workshop in Athens brought together modellers and experts to assess the integration of One Health principles within the three BIONEXT models, discuss recommendations emerging from the Delphi process, and identify opportunities for strengthenin g health considerations in modelling activities. Although deeper integration of external experts into ongoing modelling work was constrained by project realities, the process generated valuable exchanges, recommendations and learning for future modelling initiatives. The collected data are currently have been synthesised for scientific publication (Chapter 3) and represent a valuable contribution to advancing One Health integration in complex systems research. Overall, Task 5.2 evolved from a framework -based evaluation exercise into a collaborative and reflexive learning process embedded within the broader BIONEXT project.

text: This Perspective draws on the experiences of the Reflexivity Task Force, a dedicated group of researchers established to embed reflexivity within the Horizon Europe BIONEXT project. We show that intentionally designed reflexive interventions can surface hidden biases, power dynamics and divergent perspectives influencing transdisciplinary research. However, barriers to engaging researchers with more conflictual or deeply entrenched dimensions of positionality and power can lead to ‘safe’ forms of reflection with limited impact on research outcomes. We argue that making reflexivity more than a mirror requires institutional transformation, moving reflexivity from an optional practice to a core scientific capacity embedded within research governance, funding and evaluation systems. Importantly, this institutionalisation of reflexivity must not come at t he cost of maintaining its provocative spirit, which requires deliberative engagement with pluralism and contestation. TOC 1. Keywords: knowledge co-production, transdisciplinary, critical, epistemology, learning [Page 10] 1. The call for reflexivity in sustainability research Transformative change is required to secure a liveable planet for people and nature (IPBES, 2024). In response, research is increasingly expected to contribute not only to understanding sustainability challenges, but to shaping solutions. Transdisciplinary research is an approach for co-producing integrative, action-oriented knowledge for sustainability by weaving together academic disciplines with the knowledge of societal actors beyond academia (Caniglia et al., 2020; Lang et al., 2012). A crucial contribution of transdisciplinary research is ensuring that solutions are actionable and grounded in dynamic complexity through a practice-based, societally embedded approach (West et al., 2019). Transdisciplinary research can be transformative by generating novel solutions that contest dominant views, structures and practices underpinning complex sustainability challenges (Augenstein et al., 2024; Fazey et al., 2020). However, this transformative potential is often impeded by unacknowledged but persistent biases and power dynamics that shape whose knowledge is recognized, how problems are framed, and which solutions are considered legitimate (Fritz et al., 2026; Lazurko et al., 2024; Wiegleb & Bruns, 2023). Misunderstanding and conflictual interpretations can emerge in collaborations across disciplines or between actors with divergent worldviews (Hertz & Schlüter, 2015; Strang, 2009; Turnhout, 2019). When the underlying power dynamics between these different perspectives are not addressed, a drive for consensus can mask divergent views (Gregory, 1996; Ulrich, 2003) or stifle transformative insights that originate from marginalised knowledge systems or are yet unknown (Bornemann & Christen, 2020; Turnhout et al., 2026). These dynamics become particularly important in science-policy settings, where research actively shapes solutions, policy options and notions of feasibility (Borie et al., 2021; Turnhout, 2024). In such contexts, unexamined power relations within transdisciplinary research risk reproducing dominant policy logics, even when participatory or integrative approaches are adopted (Turnhout et al., 2020, 2026; Wyborn et al., 2021). As researchers hold the authority to determine methodological choices and whose knowledge counts in transdisciplinary processes (Reed et al., 2023), they must also bear responsibility for the process and the outcomes of their decisions.

title: Deliverable D5.2 — section 8 of 222
text: even when participatory or integrative approaches are adopted (Turnhout et al., 2020, 2026; Wyborn et al., 2021). As researchers hold the authority to determine methodological choices and whose knowledge counts in transdisciplinary processes (Reed et al., 2023), they must also bear responsibility for the process and the outcomes of their decisions. Reflexivity has been called upon as a crucial capacity to address this responsibility (Lazurko et al., 2024; Popa et al., 2015; von Seggern et al., 2023). Reflexivity is often colloquially understood as a mirror, enabling the critical examination of one’s own biases and their influence on a situation. Positioned as a transformative capacity in sustainability research, reflexivity becomes more than a mirror: a “dynamic, embedded and collective process of self-scrutiny and mutual learning in service of transformative change” (Lazurko et al., 2025). The transformative potential of reflexivity lies in its role in surfacing and mediating the hidden biases and power dynamics that shape how diverse worldviews, disciplines and perspectives are integrated to inform solutions. Reflexivity thus enables more inclusive and adaptive research processes: for example, by creating space to elevate perspectives that appear marginalised (McIntyre et al., 2023; Staffa et al., 2022) or creating conditions that allow plurality to surface and be deliberated in ways that meaningfully influence the research outcomes (Cockburn, 2022; Turnhout, 2024). The importance of reflexivity is further acknowledged through its recognition as one of the four pillars of societal readiness, which is increasingly regarded as being as important as technological readiness in research and development projects (Francis et al., 2026). Together with inclusion, anticipation, and responsiveness, reflexivity is expected to ensure that research [Page 11] outcomes align with long-term societal values, needs, and expectations (Bernstein et al., 2022). As funding agencies increasingly require researchers to address societal readiness, there is a growing need for practical, ready-to-use tools that can be readily implemented in research projects (Braun et al., 2025). Researchers are responding to these calls for reflexivity. For example, transdisciplinary frameworks weave together multiple knowledge systems (Chilisa, 2017; Martin, 2012; Tengö et al., 2014), support iterative and collective evaluation of the research process with participants beyond academia (Hubeau et al., 2018; Mitchell et al., 2015), and help researchers reflexively choose different roles, epistemological commitments and methodological approaches (Chambers et al., 2022; Haider et al., 2018). Positionality statements are becoming more common in research outputs. Emerging critical literature highlights the limitations of the self in the mirror (Haider & Rieser, 2025) and argues that reflexivity must be provocative in order to avoid reproducing the status quo (Hakkarainen & Lazurko, 2025).

[Page 18] Fig.4: Boundary processes involved in reflexivity as a transformative capacity (Lazurko et al. 2025) The survey and resulting reflection were structured by a framework introduced in Lazurko et al. (2025), depicted in Fig. 4. This framework conceptualises reflexivity as unfolding through three interacting boundary processes: i) Boundary delineation refers to recognising and critically examining the positionality, assumptions, and power relations shaping individuals' perspectives; ii) Boundary interaction involves engaging multiple perspectives to enable inclusive and plural forms of knowledge integration, including decentring dominant boundaries and sustaining plurality and difference, which requires allowing for messy and political processes of disagreement, rather than forcing consensus; and iii) Boundary transformation describes processes of mutual learning, where individual frames transform toward a greater appreciation for difference, due to encounters with others. Together, these processes describe how individual and collective perspectives are surfaced, brought into dialogue, and potentially reshaped through engagement with others over time. This framing is particularly useful for analysing how reflexivity operates in practice, beyond individual self-reflection, by putting the relational and dynamic nature of knowledge integration at the centre. 2.4 Generating a collective reflection This paper reflects the joint perspective that emerged from the experiences and findings of the Reflexivity Task Force.

What the reflexive interventions revealed This section describes the findings of the reflexive interventions implemented by the Reflexivity Task Force in BIONEXT (Section 2.2), revealing cross-cutting insights for both researchers and participants. 3.1 Divergent perspectives exist on key aspects of transdisciplinary research Researcher insights The researcher interviews and virtual workshop together exposed multiple perspectives on key assumptions informing their approach to transdisciplinary research. These included divergent views on what transdisciplinary research is, how it should be operationalised, and whether these expectations were met in BIONEXT. The co-creation of visions and pathways toward nature- positive futures in BIONEXT was referenced as evidence of transdisciplinarity, for those who view it as a collaboration between scientists and non-academic actors to generate societally relevant knowledge. Others highlighted the nature of our research questions and methods, which required strong collaboration between disciplines. Diverse interpretations of the role of complexity in our research also emerged, with some researchers focused on complexity in the research content, such as framing sustainability challenges as interconnected systems characterised by uncertainty, emergence, and societal complexity. In contrast, others focused on the research process, including challenges of [Page 19] coordinating collaboration, integrating knowledge, and generating evidence about patterns in such complex systems. The development and testing of the reflexive tool built upon these findings to stimulate more detailed, collective discussions about divergent assumptions informing transdisciplinary research. For example, prompts from the KIRC tool stimulated critical, collective reflection on what constitutes “actionable” knowledge, how scientific robustness and rigour are understood in transformative research contexts, whether participants beyond academia are treated as equitable knowledge holders, and how researchers perceive their role in transformative change.

Researchers pointed to factors such as career stage, disciplinary background, expertise, personal motivations and values as influential in defining key research activities. The interviews also surfaced important considerations for ensuring the quality of knowledge integration in transdisciplinary research, including transparency in research design, and reflexivity and honesty in communicating the findings and limitations of the research. Researchers debated whether BIONEXT sufficiently facilitates equitable collaboration between researchers and non-academic actors, noting that researchers’ control over proposal design and methodological decisions, which is often necessary to secure funding and meet deliverables, can limit participants’ influence. This is also influenced by senior researchers who had pre-existing collaborations that influenced the proposal process. While European-level policy involvement in shaping the funding calls was seen as one way to address this lack of influence, mismatches between policy agendas and research timelines were identified as a key challenge. Participants also questioned whether the European scale hindered deeper engagement with actors embedded in specific local contexts, particularly where some ‘participants’ were themselves scientists representing policy or practice perspectives. During the workshop, process-level tensions emerged between control and flexibility in managing a highly complex research project, which may privilege certain approaches and perspectives in research. While individual researchers expressed frustration with this tension during interviews, in the workshop they discussed how this tension may be productive and inherent to transdisciplinary research: while structures such as deliverables and timelines enable coordination and progress, flexibility is essential for responding to emergent insights and enabling novel collaboration beyond ‘promised deliverables’ across a diverse project consortium. Differences in comfort with predesigned versus open-ended work highlighted a push-pull between different styles of doing science and their impacts on researchers, particularly those earlier in their careers.

Reflexive learning only became tangible when interviewees saw their perspectives synthesised with others during the virtual researcher workshop. Thus, most learning occurred within the task force, as members of the task force nuanced their own own boundary delineation through exposure to the diverse perspectives across the eleven interviewees. For participants, the reflexivity moments and interviews also clarified key factors shaping and potentially constraining personal perspectives and facilitated critical reflection on ontological and epistemological assumptions. Reflection on disciplinary hierarchies, career stage and factors related to class, age and ethnicity were mixed, indicating that, similar to the researcher-focused activities, these interventions may have failed to move beyond reflexivity as a mirror, toward more provocative, power-laden areas. Beneficial experiences for participants seemed dependent on their personalities and the dynamics of their group in workshops. For example, the involvement of two Sami individuals in one group led to important conversations about preconceived notions of their perspectives and how other participants ought to engage. This relates to a broader learning: that researchers’ frames were transformed through their interaction with workshop participants, as “participants realised several of the criteria and transmitted them to the researchers, allowing a mutual transformation.” However, despite these reflections, bigger questions about the structural power dynamics influencing how plural worldviews were discussed and incorporated, such as whether the co-creation process challenged or reinforced a European- centric framing of the biodiversity crisis, were left unaddressed. 4.2 Boundary interaction: Creating encounters across difference The reflexive interventions stewarded boundary interaction in multiple ways. For researchers, these interactions were bounded in ways that limited direct impact on research outcomes, whereas boundary interaction through co-creation with participants enabled more impactful learning. For researchers, the virtual workshop and reflexive tool partially supported boundary interaction among the research team. Discussions pushed thinking beyond disciplinary or epistemological boundaries and challenged some relatively narrow assumptions as often-unacknowledged dynamics in the group were made explicit. Anecdotally, such processes seemed to surface ‘light- bulb’ moments for certain participants and discomfort for others. However, there were also blind spots. More painful or conflictual differences in perspectives between researchers that might truly challenge academic identities and worldviews were left untouched, such as the power dynamics influencing why particular frameworks or methods are chosen or discarded. This was consequential: our approach assumed that researchers had the interest and capacity to carry these learnings with them into their work. In hindsight, we see that many researchers – including some of us in the Reflexivity Task Force – are still motivated to advocate for approaches aligned with our personal scientific agendas. Despite mixed results for researchers alone, boundary interaction when participants and researchers interacted together seems more fruitful. The co-creation workshop series enabled all of us to see how our perspectives interfaced with others in real time.

Despite mixed results for researchers alone, boundary interaction when participants and researchers interacted together seems more fruitful. The co-creation workshop series enabled all of us to see how our perspectives interfaced with others in real time. The reflexivity moments [Page 24] alongside core workshop activities were particularly effective in expanding beyond narrow boundaries and decentring dominant views, as they brought together diverse participants across sectors, geographies and organisations using creative methods and integrative approaches beyond the traditionally narrow boundaries of science. Such processes allowed novel insights to emerge and facilitated the inclusion of diverse forms of knowledge. Despite contrasting views, facilitation approaches largely managed differences productively, maintaining plurality and difference and in some cases “allowing participants to deconstruct, soften or overcome constraining positions”. The involvement of Indigenous representatives from the Sami community in the second workshop and the outdoor exercise in the third workshop (Figure 3) are noted as among the most successful in drawing out these complexities. Still, there were limitations to our approach. Highly distinct or conflictual perspectives were sometimes missing. This may be due to workshop and facilitation approaches that focused on delivering project results over participant learning. In such cases, disagreement and deliberation were allowed but not part of the workshop purpose. Participant representation also played a part, wherein participants were selected from researcher networks operating at the European scale who are already aligned to the biodiversity agenda, leading to potential biases and blind spots as more discordant viewpoints were not involved. Additionally, while workshop processes may have facilitated boundary interaction in real time, learning may be isolated to the workshop setting and does not necessarily transfer to professional lives and routines. 4.3 Boundary transformation: Learning that altered perspectives The Reflexivity Task Force appears to have facilitated boundary transformation for some researchers and participants. We were particularly effective at creating spaces to expose pluralism and difference through dialogue. As a result, both researchers and stakeholders were encouraged to consider previously unknown or unacknowledged viewpoints, which in some cases challenged, reshaped or broadened their own perspectives. While the aim was mutual learning for both researchers and participants, this learning appeared more significant for participants due to the longer-term, more relational moments in co-creation workshops that allowed participants to grow an understanding and appreciation of each other’s perspectives over time.

While the aim was mutual learning for both researchers and participants, this learning appeared more significant for participants due to the longer-term, more relational moments in co-creation workshops that allowed participants to grow an understanding and appreciation of each other’s perspectives over time. However, this success is also tied to the co-creation workshop processes beyond reflexivity moments, which aimed to stimulate learning about transformative change. Individual takeaways reveal some lasting impact of the task force. Participants beyond academia accessed new spaces to listen to and exchange with others and to reflect on their own subjective views that influence their contribution to collective research projects. Some participants and researchers intend to incorporate these insights into their future work. For example, researchers have already used individual methods such as reflexivity booklets in subsequent workshops and plan to “integrate reflexivity into the supervision of PhD students engaged in interdisciplinary research by encouraging structured reflection on assumptions, methods, and positionality.” Others have plans to “more bravely use reflexivity (moments) in my own work/research activities/meetings of the research team” and to place greater emphasis on multiple dimensions of diversity and the mechanisms underpinning transformative change. Perhaps most importantly, these impacts were limited to those who were actively engaged within the task force, which excluded researchers and stakeholders who were sceptical to begin with or more removed from the co-creation workshop series. We also received feedback that power relations between researchers were under addressed, leaving some feeling underappreciated in their role. Thus, while we have indications of boundary transformation in particular moments for [Page 25] particular people, it remains challenging to discern whether the transformative potential of reflexivity was fully realised. 5. More than a mirror: a call to action to embed reflexivity for transformative sustainability research This Perspective draws on the experiences of a transdisciplinary experiment: the Reflexivity Task Force, a specialised group of diverse researchers established to embed reflexivity within the BIONEXT project. We show that the interventions of the task force surfaced important insights, prompting important learning. However, there were numerous barriers that limited the transformative potential of our interventions, as in some cases we only partially engaged with the more provocative, power-laden undercurrents influencing transdisciplinary research. These successes and failures inform our reflections on how reflexivity can be embedded within transdisciplinary research in ways that effectively capture its transformative potential.

These successes and failures inform our reflections on how reflexivity can be embedded within transdisciplinary research in ways that effectively capture its transformative potential. 5.1 Project design should enable deeper and more widespread engagement with reflexivity Enabling more reflexive and thereby transformative transdisciplinary research requires institutional shifts that embed reflexivity into project design. Our experiences reinforce that even with the best intentions, reflexivity does not simply ‘happen’: it requires leadership, continuity, and adequate time, structure and incentives for researchers across a project consortium to engage (Lang et al., 2012). Changing research practices takes sustained effort and diverse participation with shared commitment among all (Popa et al., 2015), and cannot be achieved through singular events or initiatives involving only those researchers who are already committed to reflexive approaches (Knickel et al., 2019). In the case of BIONEXT, the Reflexivity Task Force was established as a post-proposal addition. While this allowed for experimentation, it also meant we had to advocate for our relevance within the larger project and at times had to deprioritise reflexive activities in favour of core project deliverables. This resulted in missed opportunities for impact that could be enabled if iterative self-scrutiny and mutual learning was directly tied to research outcomes across work packages and partners. Formally embedding reflexivity in the core project structure and deliverables for large consortium projects like Horizon Europe at the proposal stage would make a significant step. For example, all large transdisciplinary projects could establish a Reflexivity Task Force with specific tasks and deliverables across work packages and partners intended to mediate the biases and power dynamics influencing all processes of knowledge integration. This would help overcome the lack of resources, competition among priorities and institutional settings that limit reflexivity (Ligtermoet et al., 2025; Wyborn et al., 2019) by positioning reflexivity as not only an individual but institutional responsibility (Chakori et al., 2025). 5.2 Broader institutional shifts are required to enable reflexivity at the interface of science and society Fulfilling the transformative potential of reflexivity not only requires changes in project design: it requires a significant change in the norms and practices of scientific institutions (Loorbach & Wittmayer, 2025). Reflexivity is inherently challenging and will thus meet resistance, as researchers and participants confront the discomfort associated with recognising their own subjectivities in research processes (Hakkarainen & Lazurko, 2025).

Reflexivity is inherently challenging and will thus meet resistance, as researchers and participants confront the discomfort associated with recognising their own subjectivities in research processes (Hakkarainen & Lazurko, 2025). This points to cycles of inner and outer change that can together shift research attitudes and structures (Goldstein et al., 2025), moving reflexivity from an optional practice to an institutional capacity that supports [Page 26] societal readiness. Rather than treating reflexive activities as peripheral or supplementary, institutions can legitimise and resource them as integral to research quality, impact, and credibility – particularly in contexts where research is expected to inform policy and societal action under conditions of uncertainty, plurality and contestation (Loorbach & Wittmayer, 2025; Turnhout et al., 2020, Hebinck et al. in review). Concretely, this may involve investing in training and mentoring that support researchers in navigating positionality, power, and uncertainty; adapting incentive and evaluation systems to value learning, care-based collaboration, and reflexive practice alongside conventional outputs; and creating protected spaces and roles within projects and programmes that sustain reflexive capacity over time (Care et al., 2021). Such measures contribute to improved research practice and societal readiness, by strengthening collective capacities to engage with disagreement, ambiguity, and value-related choices as part of transformative change (Fazey et al. 2018; Horcea-Milcu et al. 2024). Without institutional support, reflexivity risks remaining dependent on motivated individuals or exceptional projects, limiting its ability to meaningfully support societal engagement with research-informed pathways. 5.3 Institutionalisation should not neutralise the provocative spirit of reflexivity Some have argued that reflexivity is only meaningful when something provocative comes of it (Hakkarainen & Lazurko, 2025; Lynch, 2000), and that transformative spaces should be “safe enough” to surface and balance tensions in a generative way (Pereira et al., 2018). We agree with these arguments in principle. However, our reflections on the transformative potential of the Reflexivity Task Force show that we encountered challenges implementing them in practice. We often felt that fully enacting them might alienate us from sceptical researchers, given our position as an optional activity outside core project deliverables. As a result, our activities in some cases failed to address the more uncomfortable but influential undercurrents influencing transdisciplinary research. We thus accompany calls for institutional shifts to enable reflexivity (Sellberg et al., 2021) with an important caveat.

As a result, our activities in some cases failed to address the more uncomfortable but influential undercurrents influencing transdisciplinary research. We thus accompany calls for institutional shifts to enable reflexivity (Sellberg et al., 2021) with an important caveat. On one hand, formalisation can be important for legitimising reflexivity in the eyes of sceptical researchers and meaningfully connect reflexive interventions to research outcomes. Yet, on the other, there is a risk that institutionalising reflexivity neutralises its provocative spirit, as it is reshaped to align within the very norms, ideologies and power structures that it is meant to challenge (Turnhout et al., 2026). In other words, reflexivity risks remaining a mirror, enabling reflection about known biases without surfacing and mediating blind spots and power dynamics in ways that meaningfully disrupt the status quo. Navigating this challenge requires taking onboard recommendations for the institutional shifts required for transformative research (Horcea-Milcu et al., 2024), while nurturing a different set of skills, competencies and priorities than those taught and incentivised in research. First, it requires creating a sense of psychological safety (Edmondson & Lei, 2014) through empathy and active listening. The Reflexivity Task Force emerged from a shared set of values, underpinned by assumptions that reflexivity is important, worthwhile and impactful. While members of the task force sometimes disagreed on particular interventions, we always came back to this shared purpose. However, engagement with the wider project consortium revealed that some researchers were unfamiliar with the concepts and language we used, feared that extensive self-scrutiny and critique might undermine scientific credibility, or were sceptical about the value of engaging with abstract or difficult-to-resolve questions. Future efforts to embed reflexivity would benefit from starting with empathetic and active listening in formal and informal [Page 27] settings to understand how researchers see themselves, how they relate to ideas of change- making, and what beliefs and values underpin their research practice. This can help build trust and a clear and inclusive purpose that recognises diverse purposes on the ‘why’ of reflexivity, moving beyond concerns that critique may undermine scientific credibility to reframe reflexive interventions as contributing to rigorous, trustworthy and impactful research. Second, it requires researchers to have the skills, bravery and institutional support required to be provocative, to push past sceptical or unsupportive responses by aligning to a higher purpose that “a better knowledge is possible” (Turnhout, 2024).

Second, it requires researchers to have the skills, bravery and institutional support required to be provocative, to push past sceptical or unsupportive responses by aligning to a higher purpose that “a better knowledge is possible” (Turnhout, 2024). The interventions of the Reflexivity Task Force emerged out of our own deliberations, in which we often discussed whether to tone down our approach to avoid language or activities that might be too confrontational for researchers and participants. In some cases, our shared values and purpose created our own blindspots, wherein we inadvertently neutralised the discussions despite our explicit desire to activate deeper learning. This speaks to the need to attend to the emotional experiences of the task force and the wider project consortium, with the help of an external facilitator or arts-based creative methods (Galafassi et al., 2018; Prall & Ounanian, 2026), to engage carefully with the fear associated with confronting more painful biases and power dynamics influencing research. It also speaks to the need to institutionalise provocation in ways that provide safety for researchers, such as mandating task forces like ours to have external chairs to ask tougher questions and legitimise the rationale and methods for reflexivity, or to provide budgets for activities of the task force that support transformative learning as a key outcome. Finally, institutionalisation of reflexivity must maintain a flexible, iterative, and emergent approach (Basta et al., 2021; Popa et al., 2015). There is no one-size-fits-all approach to embedding reflexivity, particularly given the messy nature of transdisciplinarity (Regeer et al., 2024). Our reflexive interventions in BIONEXT emerged through a combination of project opportunities, constraints, and our own learning processes. Each attempt to stimulate reflexivity prompted us to revisit our own assumptions and refine our approaches, enabling new interventions that would speak to the needs of the research project. Aligning reflexivity to project structure and deliverables must thus provide “just enough structure” (Regeer et al., 2024) to offer the motivation and context within which to steward reflexivity, without dictating exactly how and with what outcomes and while leaving room for both informal and formal modes of engagement. Importantly, to enable this kind of emergent learning, we need the transdisciplinary research community to develop repositories of reflexive interventions (e.g., as cited in (Ligtermoet et al., 2025) that could be adapted to new contexts and experiences, contributing to a shared agenda for developing context-specific and inclusive reflexive practices.

As research programmes such as Horizon Europe increasingly position projects as contributors to societal transformation, reflexivity becomes central to ensuring that interactions between science, policy, and society remain open to plurality, critical engagement, and mutual learning. In this sense, reflexivity supports not only more inclusive collaboration within projects, but also the preparedness of societal actors to engage with transformative pathways, negotiate differing values, and respond to emerging knowledge and uncertainties. Embedding reflexivity at this interface requires moving beyond assessment-oriented models of science-policy interaction toward configurations that enable experimentation, learning-by-doing, and reciprocal and provocative feedback between research, [Page 28] policy and societal practice. Reflexivity thus functions as an enabling infrastructure for societal readiness: grounding transformative ambitions in lived practice, challenging convergence around dominant framings, and strengthening legitimacy, adaptability, and responsiveness of research- informed action in complex sustainability contexts. Abstract Addressing global environmental change requires research approaches capable of engaging with complexity, uncertainty, ambiguity and diverse knowledge systems. Transdisciplinary sustainability research aims to meet this challenge through knowledge integration , which involves weaving together diverse knowledge systems to generate an enriched picture. Yet, the processes through which knowledge integration unfold remain poorly understood and are rarely made explicit in practice. In particular, limited attention has been given to how reflexivity about the research process can support the quality of knowledge integration . This study explores how the processes of knowledge integration can be conceptualized and deliberated in transdisciplinary settings. Drawing on an iterative qualitative research design within the European BIONEXT project, we conducted eleven semi-structured interviews with a heterogeneous group of researchers and practitioners, followed by thematic analys is. The analysis resulted in a Knowledge Integration Reflexivity Framework ( KIRF) capturing key research dimensions (including knowledge generation, collaboration, decision-making, adaptivity, and transparency) and recurrent challenges (including complexity, transdisciplinarity, methodological diversity, and societal relevance ).

Key words Knowledge integration, reflexivity, complexity, transdisciplinarity, dialogue support 1 Introduction As humanity continues to face complex planetary health challenges such as climate change and biodiversity loss, the limitations of traditional, discipline -bounded research approaches have become ever more apparent (1). These challenges are characterized by uncertainty, ambiguity, systemic interdependencies and feedbacks that transcend the boundaries of any individual discipline (2-5). Moreover, finding solutions for these challenges implicates diverse actors with different values and stakes in change (6, 7). As a result, scholars have argued that addressing such complexity and ambiguity requires knowledge production that is capable of transcending disciplinary silos and the boundaries of academia to engage with multiple evidence bases, including [Page 54] those held by societal actors (8-10). Over the past years, transdisciplinary sustainability research (TDS) has thus gained prominence as an approach capable of generating actionable, context - specific- insights while fostering the transformative change required to navigate planetary health crises (11, 12). TDS emphasizes collaboration among diverse scientific disciplines as well as actors beyond academia, such as government, civil society, and the private sector (13). What distinguishes it from interdisciplinary or multidisciplinary research is its explicit ambition to co -produce knowledge that is both scientifically robust and societally embedded by adopting integrative approaches that transcend the conventions of any single discipline . Central to this ambition is knowledge integration, a process through which multiple and often heterogeneous epistemologies, methods, values, and experiential insights are brought together to form new, shared understandings (14).
