text: bust and societally embedded by adopting integrative approaches that transcend the conventions of any single discipline . Central to this ambition is knowledge integration, a process through which multiple and often heterogeneous epistemologies, methods, values, and experiential insights are brought together to form new, shared understandings (14). Because natural scientists, social scientists, practitioners, and community stakeholders often operate within different knowledge systems, questions regarding what counts as evidence or valid knowledge is not merely a technical exercise but a normative and negotiated process (8) Despite its central role in transdisciplinary collaboration , knowledge integration often remains a “black box” (11). Although approaches and frameworks for connecting diverse knowledge systems exist (9), when teams work together in workshops, meetings, or field activities, the actual ways in which assumptions, conceptual frameworks, and methodological choices are bridged and influenced by various subjectivities and power dynamics tend to be implicit and rarely fully documented. As a result, the quality of knowledge integration, which may include factors such as rigor, inclusivity, societal embeddedness and transparency (15, 16), can be difficult to assess or improve. Existing frameworks frequently describe integration as a desired outcome, yet provide little guidance on how research teams can systematically reflect on, evaluate, or operationalize it during their collaboration (17-21). This gap poses a challenge for research practice, theory-building, societal impact, and the validity of the findings : without explicit attention to integration processes and the implicit factors influencing the process, it becomes difficult to understand what supports or hinders successful collaboration, and how integrative efforts influence research outcomes. In recent years, calls have intensified for more explicit reflexivity in TDS research (22-25). Reflexivity, defined as the ongoing examination of one’s assumptions, roles, positionality, and influence on the research process (26), is increasingly recognized as a critical and potentially transformative capacity for researchers and participants in transdisciplinary settings (22, 27-29). Engaging reflexively allows researchers to surface hidden tensions, power dynamics, and methodological blind spots, thereby improving the integrity and credibility of knowledge co - production (22). However, even within reflexivity scholarship, the specific question of how to reflect on the quality of knowledge integration itself remains relatively underexplored. For example, reflexivity often addresses epistemic questions, such as interrogating one’s own assumptions and the sociopolitical implications of knowledge production (30, 31).

For example, reflexivity often addresses epistemic questions, such as interrogating one’s own assumptions and the sociopolitical implications of knowledge production (30, 31). Essential to the BIONEXT project is the nexus approach that recognizes the links between biodiversity, water, food, energy, transport, climate, and health (33). The project a pproaches biodiversity loss within interconnected socio -ecological systems rather than as an isolated environmental problem. First, eleven semi -structured interviews were conducted with a purposively sampled, heterogeneous group of experts from the project to answer the first research question. Second, the interview transcripts were thematically analyzed, leading to the identification of key themes and the development of a Knowledge Integration Reflexivity Framework (KIRF) (third step). Fourth, this KIRF structured a first draft of the Knowledge Integration Reflexivity Cards (KIRC). Fifth, the draft tool was tested and discussed in an initial webinar setting as part of a member check. Sixth, insights from this feedback were used to refine the tool into a second draft. Seventh, the revised KIRC was tested in multiple TDS research settings. Finally, feedback from these applications was incorporated to produce the final version of the KIRC tool that can be taken up more widely to facil itate reflexive knowledge integration in research projects. Figure 1: outline of the multistep methodological flow. 2.1 Qualitative interview study: developing a Knowledge Integration Reflexivity Framework 2.1.1 Data collection [Page 56] The research team for this qualitative interview study consisted of an interdisciplinary group (reflexivity task force ), with experts in transdisciplinary social -ecological systems research, geography, sustainability sciences, political science, environmental health science, medical sciences and transformations research. A semi-structured interview guide was developed taking into account the existing knowledge integration challenges (appendix 1) . Overall , the interview guide focused on how individual expert characteristics shape methodological choices, perspectives on key concepts such as complexity, inter - and transdisciplinarity , and perspectives on what constitutes quality in knowledge integration. Purposive sampling took place to ensure heterogeneity (35) across the following characteristics: work packages, scientific discipline, partner institution and career stage. Eleven individual semi -structured interviews were conducted in the period March-April 2024. Each interview was conducted by two researchers from the research team (approximately 1-1,5h). Interviews were audio and video recorded after which they were transcribed verbatim. 2.1.2 Data analysis The interview transcripts were analyzed using thematic analysis (36). From this analysis, f ive overarching themes emerged: individual expert characteristics, complexity, methodological choices, knowledge positionality, quality of knowledge integration. For each theme, teams of two researchers conducted open coding, starting directly from the data in order to develop a code structure and a narrative synthesis for each overarching theme.

For each theme, teams of two researchers conducted open coding, starting directly from the data in order to develop a code structure and a narrative synthesis for each overarching theme. The analysis focused on capturing diverse perspectives rather than reaching consensus, ensuring richness in interpretation. The tool aimed to integrate key aspects derived from our thematic analysis, theoretical work and wider literature into a practical tool that could stimulate critical discussion about processes of knowledge integration, fostering individual and collective reflexivity. The tool was designed to help assess and improve knowledge integration practices. Additionally, we had to balance the inherent complexity of the key concepts with the need for clarity and ease of use, acknowledging that genuine empowerment stems from the reflexive work itself rather than from any tool alone. Questions arose about the need for accom panying facilitation or a reflexivity guide, the degree of adaptivity over time, and responsibilities for future development.

High-quality knowledge integration was seen as inseparable from rigorous attention to data quality. This is evidenced not through formal outputs, but through practice. For instance, learning occurs when researchers reach a level of mutual understanding that allows for rapid, efficient communication. However, participants noted that academic norms can unintentionally influence this by favoring "abstract conversation" over practitioner, local or experiential types of knowledge that are more grounded in practices and place. The potential of emerging tools was also noted . For example, artificial intelligence may play a role in "spotting data that’s robust" within the next few years. The KIRC approach translates the KIRF from Section 3.1 into a practical, reflexive tool for use in TDS research teams to facilitate reflection on the process of knowledge integration . The content of the tool is comprised of multiple questions that were adapted from the empirical data to enhance usability. The tool aims to s upport structured reflection on concrete transdisciplinary project activities among researchers. This can be implemented at any project stage and can be adapted to select specific aspects most relevant to their context. This modular “content menu” approach enables projects to choose either to focus broadly on at least three different aspects of their work, or to dive deeper into a single key topic deemed important through associated sub ‑questions. A facilitator with knowledge of the key tensions and needs of the research team is required to decide on and guide participants through appropriate content in the KIRC. Building on prior work demonstrating that knowledge integration processes are frequently implicit or hidden (9, 15, 16), our findings indicate that while researchers acknowledge the quality of knowledge integration as a core scientific responsibility, it remains a relatively underexamined dimension of research practice, often overshadowed by academic pressures. The KIRC approach developed in this study addresses this gap by translating abstract reflexive principles into a structured, modular dialogue tool. By doing so, it provides a practical mechanism for research teams to surface hidden assumptions and navigate the complexities inherent in co-producing knowledge for sustainability transformations.

[Page 64] A central theme emerging from our interviews is the perception of knowledge integration as an inherently "wicked" problem. Participants highlighted that as complexity increases , particularly when bridging diverse disciplinary and societal knowledge systems , the goal of "perfect" or seamless integration becomes unfeasible. This reflects a general conceptual shift: rather than viewing knowledge integration as a "technical fusion" or a deterministic mapping exercise, researchers are beginning to see it as a process defined by transparency and honesty about uncertainties (37). Our results suggest that the quality of knowledge integration is not necessarily found in the absence of tension or ambiguity, but in transparency about the research approach and limitations and the explicit documentation of the methodological choices and power dynamics that shape the integration process. By operationalizing reflexivity through the KIRC tool, this study contributes to the growing calls for more explicit reflexive practices in TDS research (22). The tool provides one option to move reflexivity from an abstract individual competency to a structured group dialogue. This transition is critical because it positions reflexivity as a relational quality assurance mechanism. Our analysis shows that researcher perceptions of knowledge integration quality encompass factors beyond traditional disciplinary rigor; such as inclusivity, societal embeddedness, and actionability. The KIRC approach helps surface the underlying differences and tensions between researchers into a dialogue, ensuring that these diverse quality aspects are explicitly considered rather than left as implicit. 4.1 Practical Utility and Challenges of the KIRC Tool The design of the KIRC tool prioritized simplicity over completeness to encourage uptake among busy researchers. Furthermore, in future research , reflexivity on knowledge integration should also be integrated in the entire research life -cycle including the conceptualization of research and outcome evaluation. 5 Conclusion Addressing interconnected planetary health issues such as biodiversity loss requires research approaches capable of engaging with complexity, uncertainty, ambiguity and diverse knowledge systems. This study shows that knowledge integration, while central to TDS research, remains insufficiently [Page 65] articulated as a reflexive and negotiated process shaped by methodological choices, epistemic differences, and power dynamics. The Knowledge Integration Reflexivity C ards approach contributes to making these dynamics explicit by operationalizing reflexivity as a structured dialogue. Rather than prescribing fixed criteria, the tool supports researchers in critically examining assumptions, improving transparency, and engaging with tensions inherent to knowledge integration. In doing so, it reframes reflexivity as a shared practice that enhances the robustness and relevance of knowledge production. Supporting such reflexive capacities is essential for producing knowledge that is both scientifically credible and socially robust. Strengthening reflexivity in knowledge integration is crucial for more effective responses to global environmental change. Advancing such models can improve sustainability governance by enabling more comprehensive and actionable insights into interconnected health challenges. Key words One Health, Nexus modelling, knowledge integration, Delphi consultation, expert workshop, interdisciplinary modellers 1 Introduction “Of course, we do One Health” Nexus modellers answer when they are asked about One Health in their models. Yet, after some deeper exploration of what they understand of and do with O ne Health, it seems that the connection with the breadth and complexity of the One Health field seems rather limited. We brought together One Health experts and interdisciplinary modellers to deepen the conversation on this topic and to exchange ideas and spark discussion. (For explanation of key terms, see the Glossary in Appendix A) Recognition of the profound interdependence between human, animal, plant and ecosystem health has elevated the One Health approach as a cornerstone of contemporary sustainability science. While we chose to work with the One Health definition ( OHHLEP et al. 2022 ), we recognize that there are closely related conceptualisations that may have evolved out of different backgrounds but are very similar to the One Health approach today. Examples are EcoHealth or Planetary Health (Penn et al. 2025 ; Savic et al. 2025 ; United Nations Environment Programme 2024; Assmuth et al. 2019 ; Mallee 2017). Yet, despite its conceptual prominence, One Health remains generally poorly understood and often misrepresented, with bias remaining to human health concerns and insufficiently embedded in the integrated systems models as well as other evidence streams that inform major policy processes (FAO et al., 2019; WHO, 2022; Yasobant et al. 2019, 2024b; United Nations Environment Programme 2019, 2025; SAPEA 2024; Milazzo et al. 2025). Nexus modelling responding to socio-economic transitions and global environmental change (Ebi et al., 2020; Su et al. 2024), linking domains such as biodiversity and ecosystems, food, water, energy, transport, and climate, has advanced rapidly in recent years (e.g., Estoque 2023; Kim et al. 2024; Harrison et al., in prep.), but its treatment of health often remains narrow, fragmented, or implicit (McFarlane et al. 2024; Harmáčková et al., 2024; Prist et al. 2024).

Most existing studies focus on bilateral interactions (e.g., agriculture–biodiversity trade‑offs or climate impacts on health) and are typically published within disciplinary silos (McFarlane et al. 2024; Prist et al. 2024) . As a result, the broader systemic drivers of health outcomes, including structural societal factors and the benefits and risks associated with nature, and especially future projections of such risks (Ebi et al., 2020; Su et al. 2024 ; Yasobant et al. 2024a ), remain underrepresented in modelling frameworks. Institutional uptake of One Health has similarly been uneven. While zoonoses, antimicrobial resistance (AMR), and food safety have received substantial attention, environmental and biodiversity dimensions of health, along with wildlife and plant health, ar e often marginalized (Caron et al. 2026; Fasina et al. 2021; Hendrickx et al. 2026; Danielsen et al. 2025; Albajes et al. 2025; Danielsen 2013). This fragmentation is also evident in coastal and marine One Health research, where integration across environmental, animal and human health dimensions remains uneven (Ioannou et al., 2025b). This imbalance limits the capaci ty of current policy support tools to address the root causes of biodiversity loss, decline in ecosystem functionality, emerging disease risks, and inequitable One Health burdens. The IPBES Nexus Assessment of thematic interlinkages between Biodiversity, W ater, Food and Health (+ Climate) (IPBES, 2024) signals growing momentum toward integrated approaches, but substantial methodological and conceptual gaps persist, as [Page 77] well as political resistance to seeing the environment as important (Pendleton et al. 2025) as well as health (Freilich & Kesselheim 2025). The BIONEXT project (www.bionext -project.eu) seeks to contribute to address these gaps by exploring the integration of One Health within leading nexus modelling frameworks. This responds to a recent inventory showing that One Health tools remain limited in supporting implementation, monitoring, prioritisation, and environmental integration (Behravesh et al., 2024). To address these gaps within a nexus-modelling context, BIONEXT expands beyond the key sectors in the IPBES Nexus Assessment, BIONEXT by also focusing on the transport and energy sectors. Building on three models and the expanding evidence based on nexus interlinkages beyond, the project intends to lay the foundations for the next generation of policy support tools capable of capturing a more comprehensive spectrum of human, animal, plant and ecosystem health dynamics and risks.

Central to this effort is an interdisciplinary process involving One Health experts from diverse disciplinary and geographical backgrounds. Through iterative consultation, BIONEXT explores how One Health sustainability principles, such as those articulated by the One Health High ‑Level Expert Panel (OHHLEP et al., 2022), can be operationalized within complex systems models (BIONEXT Consortium, 2025). To this end, the project conducted a two ‑round Delphi consultation with international One Health experts and organised a dedicated workshop together with BIONEXT modellers. These activities generated a rich body of insights regarding minimum requirements for One Health integration, relevant indicators, conceptual blind spots, and opportunities for methodological innovation. This paper synthesises the findings and examines their implications for integrated nexus modelling. Specifically, it asks: 1) how One Health experts conceptualise the interlinkages between health and nexus sectors; 2) which indicators, moderators and system features are needed to represent One Health in nexus models; and 3) how existing modelling frameworks can be adapted to support more biocentric, equitable and transformative policy -support tools. In doing so, it articulates practical pathways for strengthening One Health integration and contributes to ongoing efforts to mainstream both biodiversity and One Health considerations in sustainability governance. 2 Methods 2.1 Study Design To explore how One Health perspectives can be systematically integrated into nexus modelling within the BIONEXT project, we employed a mixed method design composed of two components: 1) a two round Delphi consultation (similar process as in Degeling et al. 2017) with international One Health experts, and 2) an One Health expert–modeller workshop dedicated to model co-development and validation. The combined approach (Figure 1) aimed to identify relevant One Health impacts and indicators, assess their compatibility with the BIONEXT nexus models, and establish priorities for future model integration. The purpose of the figure is to organize an overview of a wide diversity of elements, rather than defining a causal loop diagram. The framework has an integrative ambition and the breadth of elements it seeks to connect, recognizing that it offers a structured pathway from Nexus characteristics and activities to different forms of impact and ultimately to One Health outcomes. Nature Contributions to Nature (NCN) provide the overarching foundation, self -regulating processes of cy cling, trophic control, demographic turnover, and biodiversity maintenance that enable regeneration and constrain overabundance. Nature Contributions to Animals (here we mainly refer to wildlife in natural ecosystems) (NCA) include habitat and resource pro visioning, shelter from thermal extremes, and ecological niches that modulate exposure and immune responses; these same conditions can both dilute and amplify disease risks. Animals co -produce NCN and indirectly condition both NCA and NCP. Finally, Plant Contributions to Nature (PlCN ) include benefits in food provision and cooling, and risks in causing allergies and injuries. Together, these pathways depict a bidirectional, co-dependent system in which animals, people, plants and nature are simultaneously beneficiaries and agents. A nuance is needed here: the species they advantage may be species that would not occur naturally in the given environment in the first place, so this positive effect has also been questioned. The entanglement of energy flows with agriculture, [Page 84] transport, healthcare, and domestic life means that the One Health implications of energy systems extend across every dimension of society. They act upon the thermodynamic foundations of cohabitation and drastically change the relative leverage, i.e. through fossil fuels animal feed like soy can be transported across the globe, which would never happen if people would have to carry it by hand. This in turn facilitates high animal densities with consequences on phosphorus and nitrogen flows in soil and water. 3.1.4 Food/feed Food/feed systems operate as deeply interconnected socio -ecological networks in which decisions about how food is produced, processed, transported, and consumed shape health outcomes for humans, animals, plants and ecosystems (McMahon et al. 2025; Rushton et al. 2021). Recent scenario-based work on food and land-system transformation toward the S ustainable Development Goals further shows how food security, nutrition, greenhouse-gas emissions, biodiversity conservation, and sustainable water and nutrient use can be assessed together while making trade-offs and synergies explicit (Douzal et al., 2024). The sector extends far beyond conventional farming to include aquaculture, aquaponics, hunting, fishing, food waste management, and even pharmaceutical uses of agricultural products. Within this vast system, the pressures and dependencies that bind food, feed, and ecological processes mean that each intervention or disruption reverberates across species and environments. Overall, it is expected to generate enough food for the world's population. 3.1.5 Healthcare Healthcare, in the One Health paradigm emerges not as an isolated human service but as a coupled human– animal–plant–ecosystem system whose practices, infrastructures, and policies generate cross -species consequences. Human-, animal-, plant- and ecosystem-healthcare form interdependent domains in which clinical interventions, preventive strategies, environmental management, and human behavior shape one another. This integrated vision positions healthcare as both a beneficiary of ecological conditions and a driver of ecological change, embedding the sector firmly within the One Health and Sustainable Development Goals landscape.

Roads, railways, waterways, air routes, pedestrian networks, and emerging green corridors are not simply conduits for movement, they restructure landscapes, fragment habitats, and alter the spatial relationships among people, livestock, companion animals, wildlife, plants, and microorganisms. In this sense, mobility is both an enabler of social and economic life and a driver of ecological change, simultaneously improving access while deepening environmental pressures. 3.1.7 Water Water systems can be considered as inherently interdependent socio -ecological networks in which hydrological, ecological, and human processes continuously shape one another. Water is not simply a resource to be managed, but a multidimensional system whose availability, safety, quality, and ecological dynamics underpin the health of humans, animals, plants and ecosystems. Because water mediates contact, transmission, livelihood, and ecological functioning, any disturbance in its state reverberates across the entire One Health spectrum. Next to fresh water sources , Oceans also serve as a source of health benefits and risks: oceans play a crucial role for ecosystem and human health (Ocean and Human Health Conference Statement, 2026; Everaert et al. 2025; Laffoley et al. 2020; Sandifer and Sutton-Grier 2014). Coastal areas are particularly relevant operational settings for such integration, as they concentrate human, animal and ecosystem-health interactions within shared land–sea interfaces (Ioannou et al., 2025a). 3.1.8 Intermediary environmental impact [Page 85] The environment is a dynamic, multidimensional sphere in which ecological processes, human activities, and multispecies health are continuously intertwined. Rather than acting as a passive backdrop, environmental conditions function as active determinants of health, shaping exposure pathways, influencing ecosystem stability, and mediating interactions among humans, animals, plants, and microorganisms. Climate change, pollution, environmental degradation, biodiversity loss and novel species interactions form a constellation of pressures that collectively define the environmental determinants of One Health (IPCC 2022; United Nations Environment Programme 2019, 2025).

Rather than conceptualizing these domains as separate, biological, ecological, social, economic, and environmental processes bind them tightly together. Health outcomes flow across species; wellbeing arises from relational and multispecies interactions; and resilience is generated through adaptive capacities that link humans, animals, plants and ecological systems. Human, animal, plant and ecosystem health are separated at considerable socio -ecological risk, demonstrated by the ecological instabilities generated and expressed in terms of resource depletion, loss of biodiversity, degradation of functionality of ecosystems, disease emergence and expression and other polycrises such as climate change. Human beings have always considered technology as the solution, enabling trade -offs of human development against nature and the environment. This has proven partly true but clearly unsustainable and as society progresses there are tipping points appearing which technology will not fix. One Health is a lens to prepare for this conceptually and operationally. 3.1.10 Moderators One Health outcomes arise from human–animal–plant–ecosystem connections whose behavior is shaped by cross-cutting moderators. Environmental, socio -economic-cultural and governance context and individual characteristics modify nature –health relationships at multiple points along causal pathways. Positioning moderators as multilevel, interact ing contextual forces clarifies their role in configuring exposure, vulnerability, resilience, and the risk –benefit balance of interventions. Within this coupled system, moderators shape how sectoral activities translate into exposure, vulnerability, and u ltimately health outcomes across species. Rather than acting in isolation, moderators interact across scales to enable or constrain resilience, determining whether social –ecological change yields co -benefits or cascading risks (Marselle 2021). 3.2 Characteristics of One Health Nexus models The One Health Nexus models ideally function as comprehensive frameworks designed to capture the dense, multidirectional relationships linking human, animal, plant and ecosystem health within dynamic socio - ecological systems.

Rather than isolating health outcomes within disciplinary silos, One Health Nexus models ideally articulate how health, wellbeing and resilience emerge from interactions among biophysical processes, social structures, economic forces, governance systems, and multispecies relationships. Their overarching goal is to operationalize One Health through a structured representation of evidence, linkages, and feedback loops that reflect the real complexity of the world. At the core of these models lies a commitment to integrating diverse forms of evidence, such as epidemiological data, environmental monitoring, wildlife health metrics, socioeconomic trends, governance indicators, cultural practices, and political dynamics. This broad evidence base enables the models to explore both health and non -health outcomes, such as land -use changes, policy decisions, education systems, or resource governance, which shape the trajectories of human, animal, plant and ecosystem health i n reciprocal ways. The models are therefore not simple representations of cause and effect but relational tools that show how interventions reverberate across sectors, producing intended benefits, unintended consequences, and emergent properties. [Page 86] A defining feature of the One Health Nexus approach is that it treats all species as legitimate endpoints of health impact assessment. Systems thinking anchors the modelling philosophy: models are constructed to represent feedback loops, non-linearity, tipping points, and cross-scale interactions characteristic of complex adaptive systems. Previous W ater Energy Food (WEF) - nexus resilience modelling under climate -change scenarios provides a useful methodological foundation for representing adaptive capacity, feedbacks and system responses in integrated nexus models (Ioannou & Laspidou, 2022). Their multiscale design spans individuals, communities, landscapes, administrative regions, and global processes, with temporal dimensions that include long -term foresight. The models ideally bridge global priorities and local realities, aligning with OHHLEP principles such as equity, transdisciplinarity, and socio-ecological balance. Design and implementation principles emphasize adaptability, transparency, and co -creation. Given the uncertainty inherent in socio -ecological systems, the models explicitly embrace incomplete knowledge and encourage iterative, flexible structures that can be updated as evidence and contexts evolve.

Given the uncertainty inherent in socio -ecological systems, the models explicitly embrace incomplete knowledge and encourage iterative, flexible structures that can be updated as evidence and contexts evolve. Transparency is foundational: assumptions, functions, data gaps, uncertainties, and methodological boundaries must be documented clearly to maintain trust and ensure utility across disciplines and decision -making contexts. Codesign with stakeholders, such as policy actors, practitioners, community members, and scientists, is indispensable for ensuring that model structures reflect real needs, ethical concerns, and practical constraints. One Health nexus models sh ould not only represent system interactions but also explicitly consider how these interactions evolve over time under alternative societal pathways. To do this, scenario development cannot be reduced to varying technical parameters alone. Instead, it requ ires deliberation about the futures societies wish to pursue, recognising that alternative pathways reflect different values, priorities, political choices, perceptions of acceptable risk, and time horizons. The mapping exercise presented here provides a structured foundation for identifying relevant system components, interfaces and moderators, but it does not determine which trajectories should be explored or prioritised. That step requires iterative dialogue among all key actors to co-design plausible, desirable and equitable scenarios. In this sense, scenario development becomes a form of transdisciplinary governance, where models serve not only as analytical tools but also as boundary objects that facilitate negotiation, learning and collective decision - making under uncertainty (e.g. Yambayamba et al. 2025) . This aligns with recent work arguing that the inherent tensions of transdisciplinary research are not obstacles to be removed but productive features that should be explicitly navigated through reflexive and inclusive knowledge co -production (Harris et a l. 2024). Multicriteria analytical methods support decision -making by enabling comparison of trade -offs, synergies, and value pluralism in complex choices that rarely offer universal “win -win-win” outcomes. Similarly, WEF– SDG cross -mapping approaches can m ake nexus synergies and trade -offs more explicit for policy prioritisation (Ioannou & Laspidou, 2023). Functionally, the One Health Nexus models are positioned as decision -support tools capable of identifying trade-offs, synergies, winners and losers, and potential co -benefits across human, plant , animal, and ecosystem domains. They evaluate the consequences of policy interventions, governance reforms, and operational practices, revealing both direct and indirect impacts.

In sum, the One Health Nexus models are envisioned as adaptive, biocentric, systems -oriented tools that integrate diverse evidence and stakeholder perspectives to illuminate how health outcomes emerge from socio-ecological interactions. Their value lies no t only in computational output but in the transparent, collaborative, and interdisciplinary processes through which they are built. By representing [Page 87] interdependencies, highlighting trade-offs, and enabling informed decision-making, these models provide an essential foundation for steering societies toward ecologically grounded, equitable, and resilient futures in which human, animal, and ecosystem health can flourish together. A condensed guide to the considerations presented here is provided as a basis for future One Health model development (Appendix H). 4 Discussion This consultation set out to translate the conceptual breadth of One Health into actionable priorities for nexus modelling by combining a two -round Delphi with an expert –modeller workshop embedded in the BIONEXT project. The process yielded three overarchi ng insights. First, health is not a downstream add -on but both a driver and emergent property of coupled socio-ecological systems; as such, it must be represented across model structure and indicators, rather than appended as a single outcome variable. Second, interfaces and moderators, the places and conditions under which sectors, species and societies meet and how they change over time, are decisive in shaping risk and co-benefits, and thus need to be formalised in model design and carefully defined to embrace the complexities of anthropogenically distorted modern biomes. Third, integration requires reflexivity: iterative, codesigned processes are as important as technical choices for achieving usable, equitable models.

From sector silos to interface-centred modelling Expert feedback consistently affirmed that One Health interactions are context -dependent and often bidirectional, with benefits and risks co -existing across the major nexus domains: ecosystems and biodiversity, energy, food/feed, healthcare, transport, and water. This supports a modelling turn away from linear, sector -bounded chains toward interface -centred architectures that can represent feedbacks and trade-offs (e.g., green/blue infrastructure that improves mental health and biodiversity while, in some contexts, altering vector habitats). The proposed One Health Nexus Overview Framework (Figure 3) is useful as an organising scaffold, mapping secto ral characteristics and activities, environmental intermediaries, moderators, and One Health outcomes. Explicit representation of feedback loops, inter-domain interactions (e.g., human ↔ animal ↔ plant ↔ ecosystem), and clearer semantics around arrows and constructs such as “environmental impact” versus “ecosystem health” are recommended . Going forward, these comments point to the need for explicit systems dynamics formalisms when porting the overview into executable models. Making moderators first-class design elements Across consultation rounds, moderators emerged as the “connective tissue” of One Health. For example, governance quality, cultural values, socio -economic conditions (including equity, affordability, and access), climate change, and species/ecosystem attrib utes may alter both the direction and magnitude of potential relationships, turning potential co-benefits into harms (and vice versa) depending on who is exposed, where, and when. The implication for modelling is twofold: (i ) parameterise moderators explicitly (e.g., socio - economic indices, governance indicators, climatic envelopes, vulnerability profiles), and (ii) test cross -level interactions rather than treating moderators as background descriptors. Incorporating moderato rs directly into scenario levers (e.g., policy coherence, equity measures, or adaptive capacity) will help models explain why similar interventions succeed in one setting and fail in another, a central promise of One Health -aware decision support.

Re-centring ecosystems: seven contribution pathways The ecosystem narrative coalesced around seven complementary pathways, Nature Contributions to Nature (NCN), to Animals (NCA), to Plants (NCPl), People (NCP); People Contributions to Nature (PCN); Plant Contribution to Nature (PlCN ) and Animal Contributions to Nature (ACN), which together move beyond a human-centric framing and recognise animals, plants and ecosystems as co -producers of health. These pathways capture dualities that models should preserve: e.g., species diversity can dilute or amplify infectious disease depending on community composition and disturbance; restoration can help climate change mitigation and increase wellbeing, and while expanding some infectious disease vector niches, it may also enhance vector predators potentially neutralising negative outcomes in the long term and if well - planned; aquaculture can improve protein access while elevating antimicrobial residues in aquatic systems. [Page 88] Ecological restoration ultimately brings together positive and negative elements but overall, the balance achieved is, in a One Health context, optimal from a system-level sustainability and thus ultimately also benefits humans. Modelling these bidirectional pathways requires life cycle and landscape perspectives in which exposure pathways (contact, contamination, movement) and functional processes (nutrient cycling, trophic regulation, soil biota) are represented at appropriate spatial and temporal scales, aligning with the scale of interventions and human ecosystem modification. A further refinement may be to combine PCN, ACN and PlCN as Domestic Animal, Plant and People Contribution to Nature (DCN) to simplify framing. Removal of all animals from industrial systems will enhance wellbeing/welfare of remaining domestic animals kept for food or draught, but may increase cost of protein for people. Responsible pet ownership has significant benefits for human wellbeing but not at the cost of the environment or wildlife, where nature -health benefits are of a much greater impact. Contribution of this study The study contributes a shared, expert-informed agenda for operationalising One Health in nexus models: (i) treat interfaces and moderators as first -class elements; (ii) elevate ecosystem processes and non -human endpoints; (iii) represent feedbacks , trade-offs, and equity explicitly; and (iv) embed reflexive codesign and transparent uncertainty throughout. Moderator: environmental, socio -economic-cultural and governance context and individual characteristics modify nature –health relationships at multiple points along causal pathways. Moderators are multilevel, interacting contextual forces configuring exposure, vulne rability, resilience, and the risk –benefit balance of interventions. Moderators shape how sectoral activities translate into exposure, vulnerability, and ultimately health outcomes across species. Rather than acting in isolation, moderators interact across scales to enable or constrain resilience, determining whether social –ecological change yields co -benefits or cascading risks (Marselle 2021). Multispecies health : concepts and practices of health that are equitable across human and nonhuman lifeforms (Rubio-Ramon and Srinivasan, 2026) Nature Contributions to Animals (NCA): ( here we mainly refer to wildlife in natural ecosystems ) include habitat and resource provisioning, shelter from thermal extremes, and ecological niches that modulate exposure and immune responses; these same conditions can both dilute and amplify disease risks. Nature Contributions to Nature (NCN): provide the overarching foundation, self -regulating processes of cycling, trophic control, demographic turnover, and biodiversity maintenance that enable regeneration and constrain overabundance. Nature Contributions to People (NCP): encompass climate regulation, pollination, storm buffering, food and biofuel production, medicinal resources, clean air and water, and support to the human microbiome, benefits that coexist with hazards linked to contact, vectors, and extreme events. Originally coined within IPBES (Diaz et al. 2018): it builds on the ecosystem service concept popularized by the Millennium Ecosystem Assessment. But as we detail below, NCP as defined and put into practice in IPBES differs from earlier work in several important ways. First, the NCP approach recognizes the ce ntral and pervasive role that culture plays in defining all links between people and nature. Second, use of NCP elevates, emphasizes, and operationalizes the role of indigenous and local knowledge in understanding nature's contribution to people. Nature contributions to Plants (NCPl): (here we mainly refer to wild plants) include benefits in habitat provision and pollination, and risks such as natural hazards and invasive alien species. Their overarching goal is to operation alize One Health through a structured representation of evidence, linkages, and feedback loops that reflect the real complexity of the world One Health: the health of humans, animals, plants and the environment is closely linked and interdependent within the environments they share and shape across time and space . SESs are composed of multiple subsystems and internal variables within these subsystems at multiple levels analogous to organisms composed of organs, organs of tissues, tissues of cells, cells of proteins, etc. (1). In a complex SES, subsystems such as a resource system (e.g., a coastal fishery), resource units (lobsters), users (fishers), and governance systems (organizations and rules that govern fishing on that coast) are relatively separable but interact to produce outcomes at the SES level, which in turn feed back to affect these subsystems and their components, as well other larger or smaller SESs (Ostrom 2009; de Garine- Wichatitsky 2021).

Regional Office for Eu rope 2021; IPBES 2020; Assmuth et al. 2020; Lauwers et al. 2020; Marselle et al. 2019; Rüegg et al. 2018; Romanelli et al. 2015; Whitmee et al. 2015). The draft set was shared with participants in an online survey. Experts were asked to 1) Evaluate propose d human health impacts (HHI), animal health impacts (AHI), and ecosystem health impacts (EHI), 2) Propose additional integrated One Health impacts (OHI); 3) Provide comments and sector specific recommendations; 4) Suggest key literature and relevant datasets. Incorporating One Health in a truly integrated manner in leading policy support models, is still in its infancy, when considering the rich potential and importance of the One Health perspective. A significant body of literature exists describing different nexus interlinkages between biodiversity, food, water, health, transport and energy in the context of climate change. However, much of this literature focuses on 2 -way interactions, e.g. between agriculture and biodiversity, or single drivers of change, e.g. climate change impacts on biodiversity. In addition, the literature is highly fragmented, often being reported in single discipline journals. Furthermore, even though the One Health approach offers a holistic view of nature-related health risks and benefits, it remains poorly integrated with the wider nexus interlinkages affecting biodiversity loss. Institutional adoption of One Health has also been mostly narrowly focused on zoonosis, anti-microbial resistance (AMR) and food safety and from a domestic animal and human perspective, with under -representation of institutions with a mandate in environment, biodiversity and wildlife health. The BIONEXT project In the BIONEXT project we aim to contribute to the design of the next generation policy support models incorporating all elements, including One Health. We aim to build on existing leading nexus models and key scientific evidence on the nexus. As One Health is a main missing perspective, the interdisciplinary involvement of One Health experts is of vital importance, covering human health, animal health, ecosystem health. Ideally, we can involve a relevant mix of different forms of One Health expertise and geographical spread within Europe. BIONEXT will address these shortcomings by advancing conceptual and practical integration of nexus interlinkages with the One Health approach, overcoming differences in framing and implementation challenges across disciplines and sectors to promote a balanced and systemic approach ( One Health High -Level Expert Panel 2022). This will include a focus on the health benefits from nature as well as risks ( WHO-CBD 2015 ) and better integration of structural societal One Health drivers, which are critical for advancing transformative and preventative actions within the One Health approach, taking it beyond development of vaccines and culling of ‘dangerous’ animals (Wallace et al. 2015). This will underscore the urgency of tackling the root causes of biodiversity loss with fair and equitable policies and promote the mainstreaming of both biodiversity and the One Health approach in policy making.

BIONEXT models IAP The Integrated Assessment Platform (IAP) is a user-friendly, interactive web-based tool that allows stakeholders to assess climate change impacts and vulnerabilities for a range of sectors, including agriculture, forests, biodiversity, coasts, water resour ces and urban development. The linking of models for the different sectors enables stakeholders to see how their interactions could affect European landscape change. The relationship between choice, uncertainty and constraints is a key cross -cutting theme in the conduct of past participatory IA. Integrating scenario development processes with an interactive modelling platform is shown to allow the exploration of future uncertainty as a structural feature of such complex problems, encouraging stakeholders to explore adaptation choices within real-world constraints of future resource availability and environmental and institutional capacities. CRAFTY + LANDS-QoL LANDS-QoL is a holistic and inclusive land system-based conceptual framework to estimate the potential provision of Quality of Life (QoL) for people and nature at high resolution for large scales. QoL is operationalised through six elements: basic material for a good life, one health, social relations, security, freedom of choice and action, and socio-ecological justice and equity. The framework is composed of a modelling approach that contains a five-steps method with a cell-based spatially explicit index. This means that the outputs reflect the level of QoL that could be provided in a specific location given the characteristics of the land system but not the actual QoL perceived there. These characteristics can be explored under different scenarios and con sist of non -nature’s and nature’s contributions to people, as well as of socio -economic indicators associated to a land use model like CRAFTY. All together, these characteristics form a list of variables that is flexible and can influence QoL in multiple ways.

JUNIPER JUNIPER relies upon a detailed framework concerning the mapping and quantification of the interrelations of the seven nexus elements — water, energy, food, transport, health, biodiversity and climate (emissions) — along with the detailed analysis behind each component. JUNIPER model is based on the structure of a System Dynamic Model (SDM) developed in Stella Architect (isee) environment. JUNIPER maps data by country and by sector from large databases for the pilot national case study of Greece and the European Union (EU) level. The model uses as input data annual time series for years 2000 to 2019 to simulate the 7 Nexus inte rlinkages. JUNIPER is a dynamic tool running different scenarios-policies to help policymakers and stakeholders to unveil a package of policy initiatives with the aim to set the EU on the path to a green transition and reach climate neutrality. After developing the baseline scenario models, JUNIPER runs SSPs and RCPs scenarios until 2100. (more on decision support below) [Page 127] One Health experts’ reflections on the usefulness of the One Health nexus models Recurring model design questions posed by One Health experts were ”who is your audience?” and related, ”what is the pupose of your model?”. Below some inspiration for the models. Models as decision & policy & practice & research support tool Models can provide valuable decision support towards a sustainable balance between people and nature. One of the key targets of models can be capacity building for children. In addition, models are considered key decision suport tools for policy makers, researchers and practitioners. In order to do so, models should clarify data linkages and translate their outcomes in a One Health relevant cheklist, which can be adapted to the needs of different sectors and end-users. On a critical note, the usefulness of models should not be overestimated: “Models are not the priority. It is all about the interaction between all systems in a semi -quantitative way”. ”Models provide insight into unintended or unexpected consequences of a policy or an action”. Model (co-)design principles Ideally, models are co -designed, co -created with end -users, stakeholder communities, policymakers. This engagement is useful to identify their information needs from the models, and for deciding the importance/weights of model linkages. It would be interesting to have an approach on how to include knowledge of local people in a One Health model. It is important that models are open access: no restrictions in order to avoid that only one specific group of people will understand/use the model. In addition, having clear outputs is key: “Connections should: be visible, convincing, long-term impact, applicable in policy-making” and “Model to be clear/practical/useful to the new generation and inspire OH practitioners/researchers/trainers for transformative change”. Potentially linking to best practices (role model) by demonstrating concrete measures that have already been applied. In addition, we should be aware of a human bias: “Need neutral ecological hierarchies in the design - natural order rather than human dominated order, in models to understand optimal ecosystems outcomes. In reality trade -offs are made but rarely do models take into account the biasing input variables and outputs favouring of one or few species”. One Health relevant key foci for the models Several key foci are proposed by the One Health experts, as models can lead to change. The food system is critical for One Health and biodiversity loss.

One Health relevant key foci for the models Several key foci are proposed by the One Health experts, as models can lead to change. The food system is critical for One Health and biodiversity loss. A critical reflection is that one of the leading One Health narratives is animal health for consumption, so perhaps not all One Health narratives are compatible with transformation of the food system. The food system perspective moreover is also relevant for mental health, not only for physical health, as diets have a significant impact on mental health, e.g. in connection with differences in the microbiome. Biodiversity is considered another key focus as biodiversity underpins health for all, including future generations , and ecosystems functionality. Models can consider restoration and effects on the food system. At the global UN level, the Global Biodiversity Framework underlines that it should be applied in line with the One Health approach. In addition, at the request of UN member states a biodiversity and human health plan of action is drafted and under discussion. It would be good to explore with the models how One Health interventions affect biodiversity and vice - versa. Currently, there is lack of articulation of One Health interventions, One Health is mainly articulated in terms of objectives. Another key focus relevant to explore with models is prevention. The health systems are mainly focussed on pathogenic and curative interventions. Prevention or a salutogenis approach is considered very important for One Health challenges, including transformation of the food system. Models as intervention explorer Models can be useful in exploring feasible connections which may inspire interventions. The modellers ask for concrete One Health examples of interventions to focus on. One concrete example could be ”What will happen if we don’t have mosquitos anymore?”. Another good example is “What if we lose natural animal microbiomes which are much more diverse and complex than domestic (species) microbiomes?”. Similar consequences of soil microbiome and water microbiome losses are unquantified. More concrete example actions can be found in the OHHLEP Plan of action and in this OHHLEP document One Health Theory of Change. I use it when I teach ecological fallacy/bias to epidemiology students, because it is a short read, and it is in a respectable journal. Here is a short definition of ecological fallacy/bias from Wikipedia: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ecological_fallacy An ecological fallacy (also ecological inference fallacy [1] or population fallacy) is a formal fallacy in the interpretation of statistical data that occurs when inferences about the nature of individuals are deduced from inferences about the group to which those individuals belong. Studies are ecologically biased when data are collected at one level/scale (i.e., the group, or population) and inferences are made at a different level/scale (i.e., the individual). For example; there are many studies that use country level data about an exposure such as the amount of fish consumed on average per person in a year (total Kgs of fish sold in markets in the country in a year divided by the population), to make inferences about the cause of specific cancers also using country level data, for example the risk of developing leukaemia (total number of cases of Leukaemia reported for the country in one year divided by the country population). However, cancer occurs at the ind ividual level, not at the country level. From the data (country level fish consumption and country level cancer incidence) it is not possible to determine how much fish was eaten by individuals who developed Leukaemia. text: d - Introduction The second Delphi round was conducted between late 2024 and early 2025, building directly on the findings of the first round and the feedback generated during the Athens workshop. This round consolidated and extended the insights gained from earlier stages of the research. Specifically, the second round had four primary objectives. First, it sought to synthesise and validate the interlinkages between One Health principles and the nexus sectors (i.e., biodiversity, climate, food, water, energy, transport, an d health). Second, the round aimed to refine the list of suggested data sources that could support integrated nexus modelling. Third, it attempted to prioritise a set of design principles for developing One Health –informed nexus models. Finally, the round assessed experts’ willingness to engage in future collaborative research activities beyond the Delphi process itself. Before administering the second -round questionnaire, participants were provided with a set of background documents to ensure a common level of knowledge across the panel. These documents included a synthesis of One Health –nexus interlinkages derived from t he first round, an overview of related trade -offs and win -wins (Appendix D), a summary of modelling considerations for incorporating One Health perspectives, a curated list of key data sources, and the full report from the Athens workshop (Appendix B). Participants were then invited to complete the second-round questionnaire (Appendix C). They were encouraged to comment selectively based on their area(s) of expertise, recognising the broad disciplinary scope of One Health. The questionnaire was designed to validate the interlinkages, rate the usefulness of proposed data sources, and rank the importance of various modelling design principles. [Page 154] Appendix F Participant Reflections and Limitations Appreciation and willingness to engage The general feedback to the consultations reveals a mixture of appreciation, difficulty, and concern, reflecting the complexity of the task and the diversity of participant backgrounds. Many respondents expressed gratitude for being invited to contribute a nd acknowledged the ambitious nature of the work. They recognized the consultation’s breadth, noting that it encouraged reflection and critical thinking rather than simple completion. Several participants described a willingness to remain engaged in subseq uent phases, including analysis and policy development, and expressed admiration for the materials and framing the One Health challenges addressed by the survey. Difficulty and need for orientation Despite this appreciation, respondents consistently reported significant challenges in completing the surveys. Due to the multi-and-transdisciplinary nature of the study, many found sections difficult to understand, often citing a lack of expertise in specialized domains. The absence of a preparatory webinar or orientation session was mentioned repeatedly as a barrier, with participants noting that more contextual explanation would have helped them grasp the process, objectives, and expectations.

Experts also suggested scientific literature for specific topics, often though more generally for whol e sections, like a nexus sector. We combine the specific references in the te xt with suggestions for further reading for each of the below presented specific sections. Ecosystem Ecosystems and biodiversity form a dynamic, interdependent web in which the social -ecological system, including animals, humans, plants, and other organisms (such as fungi, bacteria), and their physical environments continually co -produce and are impacted by One Health outcomes (de Garine -Wichatitsky 2021). From a One Health perspective, these interactions are inseparable: ecological structure and function determine exposure pathways, resilience, and the distribution of risks and benefits across species and societies. Importantly, to emphasise the high leverage of human activities on other forms of life and represent the central role of humans in decision -making, humans can be considered human animals, and other animals as non-human animals despite the lack of biological justification. Healthy ecosystems perform core functions, habitat provision, nutrient and carbon cycling, trophic regulation, and microclimate buffering, that sustain life and shape health trajectories. Ecosystem contributions are not intrins ically beneficial or harmful but context dependent, varying with landscape structure, biotic assemblages, and anthropogenic pressures. For example, species diversity can moderate infectious disease through dilution or amplification effects (Johnson et al., 2015; Kilpatrick et al., 2017; Morand, 2018; Civitello et al. 2015; Randolph 2012), distributing pathogens across hosts with heterogeneous competence; yet under disturbance, altered host communities and vector dynamics can trigger amplification effects th at raise transmission among wildlife and livestock.

text: or amplification effects (Johnson et al., 2015; Kilpatrick et al., 2017; Morand, 2018; Civitello et al. 2015; Randolph 2012), distributing pathogens across hosts with heterogeneous competence; yet under disturbance, altered host communities and vector dynamics can trigger amplification effects th at raise transmission among wildlife and livestock. As human activities draw wildlife, livestock, and people into human domains, at shared water resources, in agricultural mosaics, and along restoration corridors, opportunities for spillover (bidirectional humans – animals (wildlife and domesticated) increase and antimicrobial resistance concerns intensify (Vanhove et al. 2021). Renaturing, e.g. in urban environments like cities, or ecosystem restoration, can expand vector habitats or interface areas between humans and wild and domestic animals, demonstratin g that well - intentioned restoration may carry unintended consequences for human and animal health if not well planned. Natural hazards remain inherent components of ecosystems but species in nature are adaptive to floods, storms, droughts, harmful algal bl ooms, toxic plants, and envenomation events. Green/blue spaces illustrate a similar duality: early -life exposure can protect against allergies, whereas sensitized individuals may experience exacerbation of symptoms. Ecosystem quality and biodiversity underpin all other elements, with restoration emerging as a high-leverage response option capable of improving multiple nexus outcomes at once. For example, soil biodiversity plays a crucial role in food production, nutrient cycling, and resistance to antimicrobial pressures. It is important to note that One Health is characterized by interdependence and feedbacks: changes in one component propagate across the system and co-evolve. Environ Int. 2024;187:108662. doi:10.1016/j.envint.2024.108662 [Page 163] Energy Renewable, fossil and nuclear energy sources each generate complex, context-dependent effects. Renewable technologies provide clear climate and pollution benefits by reducing greenhouse gas emissions and airborne contaminants. Yet these systems also produce ecological pressures: solar and wind installations require land conversion, potentially disrupt wildlife migration and behaviour, and can cause injuries to birds and bats (Katovich, 2024; Lin 2017; Marques et al., 2020; Rydell et al., 2010 ) and disruption to marine life (Koschinski et al., 2003 ).Hydropower dams dramatically alter riverine systems, influencing biodiversity and sediment dynamics. Bioenergy illustrates an especially multilayered case: although regarded as a renewable source capable of supporting decarbonization, bioenergy crop expansion competes with food production, fragments habitats, and can modify vector ecology ( Živković et al., 2018). Furthermore, both photovoltaic and battery technologies introduce end -of-life waste challenges, while the mining of rare earth elements, often externalized to regions outside Europe, imposes significant health and ecological burdens on workers, communities, and biodiversity. Renewable systems inter act with healthcare as well, since energy efficiency and clean power availability affect medical service quality, reducing environmental footprints and improving health outcomes. Fossil fuels, though currently offering affordability and short-term accessibility to lower-income populations, generate predominantly harmful environmental outcomes. Their production and use contribute heavily to pollution, climate change, and long -term ecological degradation. Even in cases where fossil infrastructures inadvertently create ecological stepping stones, these effects coexist with substantial damage to marine ecosystems (Galaiduk et al. 2024; Coolen et al. 2020; Adams et al. 2014). Finally, nu clear energy presents low-emissions benefits but poses risk of catastrophic accidents and nuclear waste challenges.

title: Deliverable D5.2 — section 173 of 222
text: Even in cases where fossil infrastructures inadvertently create ecological stepping stones, these effects coexist with substantial damage to marine ecosystems (Galaiduk et al. 2024; Coolen et al. 2020; Adams et al. 2014). Finally, nu clear energy presents low-emissions benefits but poses risk of catastrophic accidents and nuclear waste challenges. The overall One Health picture presented is one in which renewables are essential for long -term planetary health but cannot be considered impact-free, while fossil fuels and nuclear power remain deeply harmful across human, animal, and environmental domains. Adopting a life-cycle perspective on energy systems is key, as is energy use that should not exceed the energy available through sustainable harvesting. This includes tracing health and ecological consequences from extraction, where mining can disrupt habitats, contaminate soil and water, and expose humans and animals to toxic substances, to infrastructure deployment, operational emissions, and end -of-life material flows. Indicators for material recovery, recycling processes, and waste management need to be considered. Co- benefits need to be presented honestly while avoiding greenwashing, acknowledging that even well - intended transitions toward sustainable energy may introduce new pressures, inequities, and vulnerabilities. Energy infrastructure emerges as an important determinant of multispecies health (Rubio -Ramon and Srinivasan, 2026). Infrastructure shapes land-use patterns, accessibility, and exposure to secondary systems such as transport corridors and fuel stations. Re source extraction is similarly central, with mining, both terrestrial and underwater, affecting entire ecosystems, from microorganisms and soils to plants, animals, and human communities. Extraction sites generate lasting losses, damages, and risks that extend far beyond the point of excavation. Energy types and usage practices are equally important: health impacts arise when mismatches occur between energy type and context, such as the reliance on polluting fuels for indoor cooking, which has particularly harmful effects on women and children. Climate change is deeply intertwined with energy systems and human, animal, plant and ecosystem health, because changes in temperature, precipitation, and weather extremes impose simultaneous stresses across species. Pollution, though expressed differently across technologies, remains a pervasive concern, spanning air, soil, and water contamination. A sustainable energy transition must integrate climate mitigation, pollution reduction, biodiversity protection, land-use planning, social equity, and the differentiated vulnerabilities of human and nonhuman communities. Deeper consideration of land systems, soil biodiversity, and ecosystem functioning is essential, as these ecological foundations underpin every feasible pathway toward a just and health-promoting energy future.

They range from intensive monocultures to sustainability-oriented approaches such as agroforestry, agroecology, conservation agriculture, and local agropastoral practices. These models coexis t with small -scale forms of food provision, including home gardening and urban indoor cultivation. All depend on foundational inputs, land and soils, energy, water, and pollinators, while potentially drawing on chemical inputs such as fertilizers, pesticid es, and herbicides. Decisions about crop genetic resources, including the use of wild relatives, resistant cultivars, and high-yield varieties, directly influence agrodiversity, resilience, and the long -term ecological footprint of farming landscapes. Animal agriculture is equally diverse, spanning intensive industrial systems and more traditional or local agropastoral approaches.

Animal agriculture is equally diverse, spanning intensive industrial systems and more traditional or local agropastoral approaches. These systems are tightly interlinked with feed crop production and rely heavily on land, water, energy, and antimicrobial i nputs. Their waste streams including; pathogens and resistomes, methane emissions, and pollutant outputs shape environmental quality, climate dynamics, human, animal and ecosystem health. Across the entire (domestic) animal sector, resource use sits on a continuum between renewable and recyclable inputs on one end and fossil -fuel dependency on the other. The patterns of accessibility, affordability, and technological development within this resource base play central roles in shaping equity and the environm ental and health impact of food systems. The health impact of intensive livestock systems at present are confined largely to the absence of disease for animals that live drastically truncated lives (Pohl & Lee 2024; Schmidt 2023). Health outcomes emerging from food/feed systems are inherently mixed. Intensive crop and livestock systems improve food availability and can lower costs for consumers, contributing to nutrition and reducing inequities for low-income populations. The exposure to pathogens from domesticated animals, over the last 8000 years, has accounted for over 60% of known human pathogens, and many wildlife diseases, causing considerable impacts over the millennia (Sikora et al 2025; Morand et al. 2014). New candidate "domestic" animal species have increased dramatically in modern times and as biodiversity declines, a few species adapt to human domains (most pertinent examples, where disease transfer has b een a major issue for human epidemics are rodents (e.g. brown and black rat, house mice), bats (e.g. fruit bats with Nipah and Hendra virus); Lord et al., 2025), overall increasing pathogen pollution once again. Zoonoses continue to be acquired from these same systems which enable pathogens and zoonotic and vector-borne disease opportunities. This is mediated through land use change, biodiversity loss and loss of ecological resilien ce and the creation of a peridomestic interface and artificial water sources, which leads to changes in community ecology, in relative host abundance. Amplified environmental pressures, pollution, soil structural degradation and loss of fertility, and gree nhouse gas emissions, further degrade ecosystem functions essential for long -term food security, especially for humans. In contrast, small-scale self-provisioning and gardening reconnect people to local foodscapes, strengthen social cohesion, and support m ental well-being as well as provide fresh food with supply chain issues limited to inputs.

Simultaneously we have to recognize that while more than 50% of the world population lives in urban settings, self -provisioning in urban contexts is only to a very l imited extend feasible. Extensive pastoral and nomadic livestock systems retain a degree of ecological resilience, whilst it may reduce herbivore diversity and altering host -pathogen and parasite dynamics. Sustainable dietary choices, particularly those th at reduce reliance on animal -sourced foods and ultra -processed products, tend to lower environmental impacts while aligning with improved human and wildlife health outcomes. In addition, value -chain actors between production and retail need to be considere d, as food processing industries and other intermediaries strongly influence production practices, food quality, and health outcomes. Significant reduction in animal -based food systems would release large areas of land for biodiversity and ecosystem’s reco very, reduce greenhouse gases (GHGs) and disease transmission and emergence risks, at little cost to the global economy and human nutrition. Remaining focus on pastoral and agroecological livestock systems would provide a local optimal protein source in regions where crop agriculture is untenable Willett et al. (2019). Men are often more involved in agricultural and extractive activities with high environmental impact, whereas women are more frequently responsible for subsistence farming and daily resource management, [Page 168] generally relying on more diversified practices and lower use of chemical inputs. Women are also often more vulnerable to the effects of climate and food crises due to more limited access to land, resources, and economic protection, while simultaneously carrying a disproportionate burden of caregiving and household food provision (Boriani et al. 2025). Throughout the consultation, antimicrobial resistance (AMR) and zoonotic diseases emerge as repeatedly emphasized threats. AMR relates to the use and abuse of pharmaceuticals in both humans, non -human animals and agriculture. Creating resistant organisms i n the microbial communities increasingly prevents treatment, management and resolution of infections. Endemic zoonoses are a relatively minor cause of human morbidity, when compared to anthroponoses, non -communicable disease and trauma but in some regions can be numerically significant due to particular cultural practices e.g. food borne trematodiasis , and where treatment is not available (Di Bari et al. 2023). Zoonotic origin human pathogens are a quite different category and should be considered independently of zoonosis.

Zoonotic origin human pathogens are a quite different category and should be considered independently of zoonosis. These are acquired over time primarily from close associations between humans, domesticated and peridomestic animals, and spillover, with the force of infection paralleling the rapid growth in their populations. In modern times, novel emergence has been observed from disrupted ecologies involving several species, especially from the rodent and chiroptera taxa and from effectively, of vectors that become anthropophilic, especially mosquitos such as those belonging to Aedes. Nutrition and feed provision appear as foundational drivers of the system, shaping land use, resource flows, biodiversity pressures, and health risks. Food - and land-system transformation scenarios can support this framing by linking food security and nutrition with greenhouse-gas reduction, biodiversity conservation, and sustainable water and nutrient use, while explicitly considering SDG trade -offs and synergies (Douzal et al., 2024). Sustainable agriculture, soil and water quality, where feasible, biodiversity integration into farming systems, reduction in animal -based food and reduction of food loss and waste all emerge as central pillars for transforming food –feed systems toward resilience and e cological regeneration. Consequently, urban planning must include food-systems, to address the needs of most of humanity. Dietary patterns, particularly high-meat and highly processed food consumption, are major levers influencing agricultural demand, environmental degradation, and human health. Behavioral change and education, especially among younger generations, are described as critical for shifting societal norms toward sustainability, biodiversity conservation, and reduced food waste. Human behavior is the most significant determinant of both beneficial and harmful outcomes within the food–feed nexus (Rockström et al. 2025). Energy -intensive technologies, sterilization processes, pharmaceutical production, transport dependence, and medical waste generat ion introduce air, soil, and water pollutants and greenhouse gas emissions that circulate back through ecosystems, ultimately affecting human and animal health (Andrieu et al, 2022 ; Hu et al., 2022 ; Tennison et al. , 2021)) . Animal use in research is another example: scientific advances to some extend still depend on laboratory species, but these practices entail ethical and welfare tradeoffs that must be carefully managed (Kiani, et al ., 2022 ). Salutogenic and preventive approaches, including healthy lifestyle promotion with nature contact (Maller et al., 2006), highlight the system’s dual nature. Such measures reduce disease burdens and resource consumption, but increased human –nature contact may for example disturb ecosystems or lead to higher rates of exposure if not designed with ecological sensitivity and clear risk communication (Stanley and Galbraith, 2024). Healthcare infrastructures influence ecological and social outcomes. Human over -population beyond ecological capacities (requiring multiple planetary systems to sustain a European lifestyle) has been aided by medical advances and healthcare. Biodiversity l oss, climate change and pollution have been a trade -off for human population growth (Cafaro et al. , 2022)Whilst essentially damaging, dependency on nature on a micro-scale goes further into the very essence of “Greened” healthcare facilities, featuring nature -based design, improved thermal resilience, and integrated green spaces, can simultaneously support patient recovery (Park and Mattson, 2009 ), reduce environmental burdens, and increase biodiversity in urban landscapes (Robinson and Breed, 2019). However, the sector also relies on extensive transportation networks that increase emissions, and its pharmaceuticals contribute to antimicrobial resistance and chemical pollution. These patterns demonstrate how healthcare can generate both co -benefits a nd risks across species. Animal healthcare follows similar patterns. Veterinary services support animal welfare through vaccination, antimicrobial use, disease management, and emergency care, yet these same actions contribute to domestic animal over -population (>90% of global mamm al and bird biomass is now domestic), energy use, waste production, and antimicrobial resistance (AMR) dynamics. Interventions such as translocation for conservation may connect veterinary medicine to ecosystem stewardship, while companion animal care generates psychological benefits for humans but also adds to environmental pressures through biodiversity loss (Gómez-Serrano 2025; Schaffner 2023; Crowley et al 2020), natural resource consumption and waste. Intensive livestock systems amplify these interdepe ndencies: they ensure food security but heighten vulnerability to epidemics, accelerate AMR dissemination, and impose huge environmental burdens that compromise long -term human and ecosystem health. Along with humans, a large portion of domestic animals ar e now largely isolated from their environments, unable to develop adaptive physiologies or resilience to disease through natural evolutionary processes, creating endless dependencies on medical technologies and expenditure (Gobbin 2025). Whilst welfare is a priority or duty of care with human and non- human (domestic) animals, the overarching consequences are unconsidered in human development and future risk framing. The cycle is never broken as owner and farmer wellbeing emerges as a key determinant linking animal healthcare with social systems, as poor mental or physical health among owners/farmers undermines animal care quality and increases system-level risks (Bourque 2017). Rising costs to animal care, a consequence of corporatization of veterinary medicine, cause more animals being untreated which raises real welfare/wellbeing concerns among the animals and their caregivers.
